name: Cercospora leaf spot
summary: A Cannabis leaf-spot disease that often begins on older lower leaves as yellow flecks and develops into round lesions with pale centers, dark borders, and yellow halos. Conidiophore and laboratory evidence are needed because several pathogens make similar spots.
indicators: Small yellow flecks appear first on older lower foliage
Lesions become round, approximately 2 to 6 mm, with tan-to-white centers
Dark brown to purplish raised borders and yellow halos may develop
Melanized conidiophores can become visible in lesion centers
exclusions: Dark pycnidia support Septoria
Sooty underside masses support Pseudocercospora
Shot-hole lesions with Colletotrichum evidence support anthracnose
Laboratory testing identifies another pathogen

progression.description: Small yellow flecks appear on older lower leaves.
Round lesions enlarge and centers pale while dark borders and halos become clearer.
Spots can coalesce and lesion centers may break down.

confirmation: Inspect lesion centers with magnification and submit tissue for fungal identification.
Use morphology and/or molecular testing before assigning Cercospora cf. flagellaris at species level.
immediateActions: Document early lower-canopy distribution and preserve representative lesions.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed leaf-spot disease management and sanitation appropriate to the setting.
prevention: Scout older foliage and reduce avoidable leaf wetness.
Avoid moving symptomatic material into clean areas.
warnings: Round pale-centered lesions are not unique to Cercospora.
Cercospora often appears as part of a multi-pathogen field leaf-spot complex.

sources.title: First Report of Cercospora cf. flagellaris on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Cercospora leaf spot began on older lower-canopy hemp leaves as small yellow flecks and progressed to round 2 to 6 mm lesions with tan-to-white centers, dark brown-to-purplish borders, and yellow halos.
Melanized conidiophores could become visible in lesion centers before centers disintegrated.
Whole-plant inoculation reproduced similar symptoms and the fungus was recovered again, supporting pathogenicity rather than visual association alone.

sources.title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria were the prevalent hemp leaf-spot diseases evaluated in Kentucky field trials.
Septoria generally appeared first, followed by Bipolaris, while Cercospora developed later in reproductive stages; cultivar susceptibility varied.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean distribution, timing, microscopy, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.

name: Exserohilum / Helminthosporium leaf blight
summary: A confirmed outdoor hemp leaf and stem spot disease. Round brown-to-black lesions with dark margins are compatible, but abundant conidia and laboratory identification are needed because the lesion appearance overlaps other leaf spots.
indicators: Round brown-to-black lesions develop on leaves or stems
Lesions have distinctly darkened margins
Abundant large conidia can be observed within compatible lesions
ITS/RPB2 or equivalent fungal identification supports Exserohilum/Setosphaeria
exclusions: Pycnidia strongly support Septoria
Pale-centered lesions with Cercospora structures support Cercospora
Sooty underside masses support Pseudocercospora
No fungal evidence exists and chemical or mechanical injury follows an exposure pattern

progression.description: Round dark lesions appear on foliage or stems.
Lesion burden and necrotic tissue increase and can contribute to leaf distortion or blight.

confirmation: Examine lesion structures microscopically and use culture plus molecular identification for organism-level confirmation.
Photograph both surfaces and stem lesions before sampling.
immediateActions: Preserve representative lesions and reduce transfer of symptomatic debris into clean areas.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed leaf-blight management and sanitation appropriate to the production system.
prevention: Scout field foliage and stems and reduce prolonged leaf wetness where practical.
warnings: “Helminthosporium” is a historical/common disease name and does not by itself identify the modern fungal taxon.
Dark round spots are not Exserohilum-specific.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

name: Fusarium foliar, flower and head blight complex
summary: A Cannabis Fusarium disease complex affecting leaves, flowers, drying floral material, stems and grain heads. It must be separated from Fusarium root/crown rot because infection site, symptom pattern and confirmation evidence differ.
indicators: Floral surfaces develop abundant hyphae with light-brown necrotic tips
Leaves develop roughly circular light-brown lesions with darker brown margins and gray-brown aging centers
Blight is centered on floral/head tissue rather than beginning as root decay
Fusarium macroconidia, culture, sequence or species-specific molecular evidence accompanies compatible tissue
exclusions: Root/crown rot and vascular wilt dominate without foliar or floral lesions
Gray fuzzy sporulation and diagnostic evidence identify Botrytis
White mold and sclerotia identify a Sclerotinia or southern-blight differential
No Fusarium evidence is present and drying/heat/mechanical injury explains floral browning

progression.description: Localized leaf lesions or necrotic flower tips develop and surface hyphae may become visible.
Necrosis expands through affected foliar or floral tissue.
F. graminearum may be detectable before obvious blight, especially around flowering, so visual absence is not proof of absence.

confirmation: Submit representative fresh lesion/flower tissue for culture and molecular identification when Fusarium species matters.
For suspected F. graminearum, species-specific molecular assays can detect infection that is not yet visually obvious.
immediateActions: Separate suspect floral material from clean material and preserve diagnostic samples before treatment or disposal.
Inspect roots/crowns separately so root Fusarium is not conflated with foliar/flower blight.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-supported disease management and sanitation appropriate to the production stage and local crop rules.
prevention: Use clean propagation/seed sources where applicable and reduce movement of symptomatic plant debris.
Track humidity, rainfall/leaf wetness, and flower-stage disease development without treating environment as proof of pathogen identity.
warnings: Fusarium flower browning is not visually species-specific.
The 2020 survey identified both F. equiseti and F. graminearum in the foliar/flower blight complex; do not collapse every lesion into F. graminearum.
Image-only absence cannot exclude latent F. graminearum infection.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

sources.title: First Report of Fusarium graminearum Causing Head Blight on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Wisconsin
supportedClaims: Fusarium graminearum was reported causing blight of hemp grain heads, strengthening evidence that Fusarium flower/head disease is a distinct Cannabis diagnostic target from Fusarium root/crown rot.
The disease note used isolation and pathogen identification from symptomatic grain heads rather than relying on flower appearance alone.

sources.title: Detection and Quantification of Latent Infection by Fusarium graminearum, Causal Agent of Fusarium Head Blight on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Fields in Kentucky
supportedClaims: A multi-site hemp field study used species-specific qPCR to detect and quantify F. graminearum in asymptomatic and symptomatic tissues.
Latent infection occurred before visible disease and infection was more prominent during flowering, so absence of visible blight cannot exclude infection and image-only confirmation is unsafe.

name: Powdery mildew
scientificName: Golovinomyces ambrosiae / Podosphaera macularis complex on Cannabis sativa
summary: Cannabis powdery mildew is a disease class marked by superficial whitish mycelium and conidia that expand across living foliage and sometimes stems or flowers. The phenotype can strongly support powdery mildew, but images cannot distinguish the documented Cannabis pathogens Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis.
indicators: Small whitish, powdery, superficial colonies occur on either leaf surface; colony texture sits on the tissue rather than appearing only as internal chlorosis.
Colonies enlarge and coalesce, producing irregular white coverage that may spread among leaves, petioles, and stems; susceptible plants can show extensive surface mycelium and conidia.
Under severe adult-plant pressure, white colonies can extend onto sugar leaves, petioles, stem tissue, flower bracts, or buds.
Affected leaves can lose vigor, yellow, become necrotic, or defoliate as disease severity increases, but these secondary changes are nonspecific.
No universal leaf-age onset is established: capture the oldest, newest, upper, lower, interior, and exterior symptomatic and apparently clean foliage rather than assuming a nutrient-mobility pattern.

Powdery-mildew colonies may become visible within roughly one week under favorable conditions, while one controlled Cannabis experiment reported susceptible leaf and stem colonies within 45 days of germination under continuous inoculum pressure.
exclusions: Foliar spray or mineral residue often follows droplet edges or application patterns, may occur on nonliving surfaces, and lacks hyphae, conidiophores, and an advancing colony margin.
Normal glandular trichomes are regularly distributed structures anchored to floral tissue rather than irregular spreading white mycelial patches.
Spider-mite silk forms threads or sheets associated with mites, eggs, cast skins, and feeding stippling rather than a powdery fungal colony.
Botrytis produces advancing brown or water-soaked flower decay and gray-brown sporulation, often including internal tissue breakdown, rather than only superficial white colonies.
Downy mildew is associated with angular chlorotic-to-necrotic lesions and corresponding gray-to-purplish underside sporulation under wet or humid conditions.
Leaf bleaching, variegation, nutrient chlorosis, and camera overexposure remain within tissue and do not resolve into fungal hyphae and conidia under magnification.

progression.description: A clean image is symptom-negative only; resistant genotypes can suppress visible colonization, and visually clean tissue is not a universal pathogen-negative control.
Few small superficial white colonies appear. In the PM2 study scale, grade 1 represented restricted, nonspreading colonies covering less than 25% of the leaf.
Colonies enlarge and merge. Study grades 2 and 3 represented 25–50% and 50–75% leaf-area coverage.
Study grade 4 represented 75–100% leaf coverage; petioles, stems, sugar leaves, bracts, or buds may also be colonized under severe adult-plant pressure.
Leaves may yellow, become necrotic, or defoliate, and flower quality can decline; these effects require the active colony to preserve the powdery-mildew label.

lookAlikes: Botrytis gray mold or bud rot
confirmation: Do not assign a powdery-mildew species from a photograph or video. Capture whole-canopy distribution plus sharp upper- and lower-surface macros from several symptomatic and adjacent apparently clean leaves.

At the active colony edge, use magnification to document superficial hyphae and chains of conidia; include a scale and a gentle side-lit video or focus stack that separates fungal growth from residue and trichomes.
Record whether material transfers when touched, but do not use wipe behavior alone as confirmation because residue and fungal spores can both move.

For organism-level ground truth, submit fresh tissue to a qualified plant diagnostic laboratory for microscopy and molecular testing; both Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis are documented on hemp.

Record cultivar or genotype, plant age, growth stage, organ, canopy position, production setting, first-observed date, repeated fixed-area coverage, temperature, humidity, and recent foliar applications.
Treat absent colonies as a symptom-negative observation, not proof of resistance or pathogen absence; controlled resistance claims require replicated inoculation and appropriate susceptible controls.
immediateActions: Separate or flag affected plants, minimize handling and airflow disturbances that can disperse conidia, and preserve a fresh diagnostic sample before removal.
Map affected plants and organs, capture pre-intervention colony coverage, and inspect nearby plants on both leaf surfaces and flower-adjacent tissue.
correctivePlan: Use only legal, crop-, site-, and growth-stage-appropriate disease management selected for the production system; follow the product label and local testing requirements.
Remove heavily affected material without dispersing spores where permitted, clean tools and contact surfaces, and track new colony development rather than persistent old discoloration.
Review humidity, air movement, canopy density, intake material, and cross-room movement as epidemiological context without treating any single environmental reading as diagnostic proof.
prevention: Inspect incoming plants and clones under magnification and maintain cultivar/source identity so repeated susceptibility can be recognized.
Scout fixed leaves and flower-adjacent tissues across canopy zones, recording new colony area over time and retaining source-group identity for image sequences.
warnings: The 2019 Kentucky DOI originally identified Golovinomyces spadiceus; later taxonomy generally includes that name within G. ambrosiae. Preserve the original title and do not silently rewrite historical species labels.
At least two powdery-mildew fungi, Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis, have been PCR-confirmed on hemp, so disease-class imagery is not species-level ground truth.
The PM2 0-to-4 leaf-coverage scale is a controlled resistance-study scale, not a universal field severity, yield-loss, or intervention threshold.

Cultivar, genotype, pathogen isolate, organ, plant stage, and inoculum pressure can change visible severity; adult plants in one study sometimes appeared more susceptible than their earlier clone assay.
The linked CC BY 4.0 susceptible-versus-resistant Figure 2 is a shared-experiment composite. It remains training-ineligible, and the resistant panel is not an independent universal negative sample.
Do not consume visibly mold-contaminated material, and do not apply unapproved products to Cannabis or flowering tissue.

sources.title: First Report of Powdery Mildew Caused by Golovinomyces spadiceus on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: The Kentucky report identified a powdery mildew on industrial hemp as Golovinomyces spadiceus using fungal morphology and ITS plus 28S sequence evidence.
The historical G. spadiceus name in this report is now generally treated within the amended G. ambrosiae concept; the DOI must not be cited as though its original title named G. ambrosiae.

sources.title: Characterization of Powdery Mildew Fungi Affecting Hemp in the Pacific Northwest
supportedClaims: Surveys of 74 hemp fields in Oregon and Washington across three time points in 2021 and 2022 found powdery mildew later in the season in Oregon but not at the early survey point.
Diagnostic PCR detected both Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis on hemp, so a white powdery-mildew phenotype does not resolve the causal species.
Among assayed survey samples, G. ambrosiae was much more frequent than P. macularis, but the regional and seasonal sample does not establish a universal species prior for other production systems.

sources.title: Discovery and Genetic Mapping of PM1, a Powdery Mildew Resistance Gene in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Patchy white mycelial colonies developed on Cannabis foliage and flowers and were associated with reduced vigor, but colony presence did not by itself identify every possible powdery-mildew species.

In two segregating Cannabis populations, susceptible plants developed white colonies on leaves and stems within 45 days of germination under continuous inoculum pressure, while PM1-bearing plants showed complete resistance to the tested Pacific Northwest G. ambrosiae isolate.

Plants were followed through flowering, and 55 clonal replicates were reinfected to validate scores; resistance or absence of visible colonies in this experiment is genotype- and isolate-specific rather than a universal negative control.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 susceptible-versus-resistant Cannabis comparison; its panels share experimental source context and must not be treated as independent training samples without source grouping and review.

sources.title: Mapping and Characterization of a Novel Powdery Mildew Resistance Locus (PM2) in Cannabis sativa L.
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Seifi et al.)
supportedClaims: The study used a leaf-area severity scale of 0 for no symptoms, 1 for less than 25% coverage with few restricted nonspreading colonies, 2 for 25–50%, 3 for 50–75%, and 4 for 75–100% powdery-mildew coverage.

Under severe adult-plant disease pressure, susceptible genotypes could show colonization of flower sugar leaves, petioles, and stem tissue; adult susceptibility sometimes exceeded the earlier clone-assay result.

PM2 resistance strongly suppressed conidia generation and involved a localized microscopic hypersensitive response without macroscopic chlorotic spots, so symptom-negative or visually clean tissue is not proof that all pathogen interaction is absent.
The scale and response were generated in controlled inoculation and resistance-mapping experiments and are not universal field severity, yield-loss, or intervention thresholds.

sources.title: Field Guide to Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Diseases
sources.publisher: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension
supportedClaims: On hemp, powdery fungal mycelium and spores can appear as whitish spots or patches on both leaf surfaces and can spread across leaves, petioles, stems, flower bracts, and buds within about a week under favorable conditions.
Increasing severity can lead to leaf necrosis and defoliation, while high humidity favors infection even though free leaf wetness is not required.

The guide recommends diagnostic-center confirmation for hemp diseases; its powdery-mildew image is credited to Nicole Gauthier and does not carry an explicit reusable-media license on the page, so it is not copied or indexed as training media here.

media.alt: Cannabis powdery mildew experiment comparing a susceptible plant with dense powdery mycelial growth and a resistant phenotype without visible colonies.
media.caption: Cannabis powdery mildew resistance experiment showing a susceptible phenotype with dense mycelial growth beside a resistant phenotype without visible powdery mildew colonies (Mihalyov and Garfinkel 2021, Figure 2).
media.creator: Paul D. Mihalyov and Andrea R. Garfinkel
media.requiredAttribution: Mihalyov PD, Garfinkel AR. 2021. Discovery and Genetic Mapping of PM1, a Powdery Mildew Resistance Gene in Cannabis sativa L. Frontiers in Agronomy 3:720215. CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: powdery-mildew — Cannabis powdery mildew susceptible/resistant phenotype comparison
useLimitations: Reference-only phenotype comparison from a controlled disease-resistance experiment.
Dense white mycelial growth can strongly support powdery mildew, but organism identification remains separate when the causal species matters.
Do not use the resistant panel as a negative training control without source-group and experimental-context review.

name: Pseudocercospora olive / sooty leaf spot
summary: A molecularly documented Cannabis leaf-spot disease characterized in one report by olive-to-pale lesions and sooty sporulation on the lower leaf surface. The underside view is important because upper-surface spots alone overlap many pathogens.
indicators: Olive or pale yellowish leaf spots are present
Lesions can be vein-limited, irregular to subcircular, and several millimeters across
Lower leaf surfaces develop grey-brown to sooty conidial masses associated with lesions
exclusions: No underside sporulation is present and a different leaf-spot pathogen is confirmed
Pycnidia support Septoria
White-centered round lesions with Cercospora structures support Cercospora

progression.description: Olive or pale discoloration develops in leaf tissue.
Irregular or subcircular lesions expand along vein-limited areas.
Sooty conidial masses become visible on the lower leaf surface.

confirmation: Photograph both leaf surfaces and inspect underside growth with magnification.
Use fungal morphology plus multilocus molecular identification for species-level confirmation.
immediateActions: Preserve sporulating tissue for diagnosis and reduce movement of symptomatic leaves.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed fungal leaf-spot management appropriate to the production system.
prevention: Scout both leaf surfaces and reduce prolonged foliage wetness.
warnings: Olive spots alone are not diagnostic.
The strongest modern Cannabis evidence is regional and species identification depends on morpho-molecular methods.

sources.title: First Molecular Phylogenetic Identification and Report of Pseudocercospora cannabina Causing Leaf Spot Disease on Cannabis sativa in Thailand
supportedClaims: Cannabis in Thailand developed olive leaf spot associated with Pseudocercospora cannabina.
Lesions were vein-limited to irregular or subcircular, pale yellowish, approximately 2 to 6 mm, with sooty conidial masses especially on the lower surface.
Morphology, multilocus phylogeny, pathogenicity testing, re-isolation, and identification fulfilled a molecularly supported disease report.

name: Sclerotinia white mold / crown rot complex
summary: A confirmed Cannabis Sclerotinia disease complex that can involve white-mold, crown-rot, wilt, and yellowing syndromes. S. sclerotiorum and S. minor are both documented on Cannabis/hemp; organism-level evidence is required because Botrytis, Fusarium, southern blight, and other molds overlap visually.
affectedParts: flowering tissue depending on infection site
indicators: White fungal growth occurs on symptomatic Cannabis tissue with associated wilt or yellowing
Affected tissue declines in a pattern consistent with an active stem/crown or aerial infection
Laboratory isolation or DNA evidence identifies Sclerotinia sclerotiorum
exclusions: Gray mold and laboratory evidence identify Botrytis
Root/crown testing identifies Fusarium or Pythium instead
White residue is nonliving spray/mineral material
No organism evidence accompanies nonspecific wilt

progression.description: Affected tissue develops mold and localized decline.
Stem or crown involvement can contribute to yellowing and wilt.
Tissue collapse can become extensive; appearance overlaps other mold diseases.

confirmation: Use culture and molecular identification for Sclerotinia confirmation.
Photograph infection site, internal stem/crown condition when available, and whole-plant distribution.
immediateActions: Isolate strongly affected plants and preserve diagnostic tissue before disposal.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-confirmed disease management and sanitation appropriate to the setting.
prevention: Limit carryover of infected plant debris and conditions that keep susceptible tissue wet for extended periods.
warnings: White mold appearance is not specific to Sclerotinia.
The 2025 Cannabis pathogenicity report supports the organism as a real disease cause but not image-only species identification.
Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and S. minor should not be separated by canopy appearance alone; crown signs, sclerotia, culture, and molecular evidence carry more weight.

sources.title: Emerging Fungal and Oomycete Diseases of Cannabis in South Africa: First Reports and Pathogenicity Confirmation
supportedClaims: Cannabis samples from an aeroponic facility with wilting, yellowing, white mold, and gray mold were investigated with DNA sequence data and pathogenicity testing.

Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, Botrytis cinerea, Fusarium oxysporum, and Pythium myriotylum were all confirmed capable of causing disease, demonstrating strong visual overlap among mold and wilt syndromes.
Sclerotinia diagnosis therefore requires organism-level evidence rather than white mold appearance alone.

sources.title: First Report of Sclerotinia Crown Rot Caused by Sclerotinia minor on Hemp
supportedClaims: Sclerotinia minor caused crown rot on field-grown hemp; foliage wilted and dried while the soil-contact crown developed white-to-gray mycelium and small irregular black sclerotia.
The crown-centered S. minor disease overlaps white-mold syndromes but requires organism-level confirmation rather than a canopy-only label.

name: Septoria leaf spot complex
summary: A lower- and inner-canopy hemp leaf-spot syndrome caused by Septoria species. Dark pycnidia within expanding brown-gray lesions are useful evidence, but modern work shows more than one Septoria species can infect Cannabis.
indicators: Disease often begins on lower or inner-canopy leaves
Small irregular brown-to-gray spots expand to several millimeters
Dark round pycnidia can be visible within lesions
Older leaves may defoliate as disease advances
exclusions: Sooty conidial masses on the underside support Pseudocercospora
White-centered round lesions with a pronounced dark border support Cercospora as a differential
Shot-hole lesions and Colletotrichum evidence support anthracnose
No fungal structures or lab evidence are present and an abiotic exposure fits the distribution better

progression.description: Small discolored spots appear on older or inner leaves.
Brown-to-gray lesions enlarge and reproductive structures may become visible.
Lesions multiply and older foliage can yellow and drop.

confirmation: Examine lesions for pycnidia and submit representative tissue for fungal identification when species matters.
Use morphology and molecular sequence data for species-level Septoria classification because S. cannabis and S. cannabicola cannot be separated by a generic spot photo.
immediateActions: Document lower-versus-upper canopy distribution and both leaf surfaces.
Limit movement of symptomatic foliage into clean production areas.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed-disease sanitation and environmental management appropriate to the system.
Track new lesion development after intervention.
prevention: Scout lower and inner canopy foliage early.
Reduce prolonged leaf wetness and carryover of infected debris where practical.
warnings: Septoria species taxonomy on Cannabis is not reducible to visual symptoms.
Do not train a species classifier from mixed Septoria figures without organism-confirmed labels.

sources.title: Reemergence of Septoria Leaf Spot Caused by Septoria cannabis on Hemp in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Septoria leaf spot was documented on hemp primarily on lower leaves and inner canopy, with small irregular brown-to-gray lesions expanding to roughly 5 to 7.5 mm and dark pycnidia in lesions.
Eight isolates were tested for pathogenicity on greenhouse-grown hemp and diagnostic loci were sequenced; morphology and sequence evidence supported Septoria cannabis in the Kentucky material.
Visual lesion appearance alone cannot separate Septoria from other hemp leaf-spot pathogens.

sources.title: Septoria cannabicola, a new species on Cannabis sativa from Japan
supportedClaims: Molecular phylogeny and morphology demonstrated that Cannabis leaf spot historically attributed to Septoria cannabis can involve a distinct species, Septoria cannabicola.
Natural symptoms began as indistinct yellow spots on lower leaves and progressed to brown irregular lesions and premature defoliation of older leaves.
Species-level Septoria naming therefore requires laboratory evidence rather than lesion appearance alone.

sources.title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria were the prevalent hemp leaf-spot diseases evaluated in Kentucky field trials.
Septoria generally appeared first, followed by Bipolaris, while Cercospora developed later in reproductive stages; cultivar susceptibility varied.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean distribution, timing, microscopy, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.

name: Southern blight
summary: A warm-condition soilborne Cannabis disease centered at the soil line, crown and taproot. White cottony mycelium plus tan-to-brown spherical sclerotia at the plant base are strong signs, but wilt alone is nonspecific.
indicators: Dark brown-to-tan discoloration develops near the soil line
Rot extends into crown or taproot while foliage yellows and the plant wilts/collapses
White cottony mycelium develops on basal tissue or adjacent soil
Numerous spherical tan-to-dark-brown sclerotia occur with compatible basal rot
exclusions: No basal rot, mycelium or sclerotia are present and measured drought explains wilt
Laboratory evidence identifies Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, Pythium or another root/crown pathogen
White growth is confined to leaves/flowers without basal disease

progression.description: Dark tan-brown discoloration appears at the soil line.
Rot moves into crown and taproot as foliage yellows.
Whole plants can wilt and collapse while white mycelium and brown sclerotia accumulate at the base.

confirmation: Inspect the soil line/crown/root surface for characteristic mycelium and sclerotia and submit tissue/culture for organism confirmation.
Record temperature/moisture context, but do not use hot wet conditions as diagnostic proof.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone material and prevent movement of contaminated soil or debris to clean areas.
Preserve basal tissue and sclerotia for diagnostic testing.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed soilborne-disease sanitation and crop-legal management appropriate to the setting.
Address excess moisture where measured without assuming moisture correction eliminates established pathogen inoculum.
prevention: Avoid moving contaminated soil or plant debris between production areas.
Monitor crown/root health during warm wet periods.
warnings: Whole-plant wilt alone cannot identify southern blight.
Sclerotia and laboratory evidence are substantially stronger than canopy appearance.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

sources.title: First Report of Southern Blight Caused by Sclerotium rolfsii on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Sicily and Southern Italy
supportedClaims: Infected hemp developed dark brown-to-tan discoloration at the soil line, crown and taproot rot, foliar yellowing, whole-plant collapse, white cottony mycelium, and tan-to-dark-brown spherical sclerotia.
Pathogenicity was reproduced on hemp and Sclerotium rolfsii was reisolated while noninoculated controls remained symptomless.
High summer temperatures and high soil moisture were associated with the reported outbreak but are risk context, not diagnostic proof.

name: Stable chlorotic sectoring / suspected genetic variegation
summary: Sharply bounded chlorotic or chlorophyll-deficient sectors can be consistent with somatic mutation or mosaicism in Cannabis, but no published Cannabis image morphology proves genetic cause; treat this as an exclusion-based phenotype until serial lineage evidence and appropriate laboratory work support the attribution.
affectedParts: successive leaves from one shoot or meristem
whole plant only when a documented cultivar trait is established
stages: flowering; stage specificity is not established
indicators: Abrupt yellow, cream, pale-green, or near-white tissue adjoining normally green tissue within the same leaf
Sector-shaped or longitudinal pigment loss rather than uniform whole-leaf yellowing
The same shoot position or clonal lineage is mapped across successive leaves and time rather than inferred from one detached leaf
Affected tissue retains its boundary while new observations document whether the pattern remains localized, expands, disappears, or is joined by distortion and stunting
Matched images preserve upper and lower leaf surfaces, whole-plant distribution, branch identity, scale, cultivar, developmental stage, and camera-lighting conditions
exclusions: Validated testing detects a virus or viroid consistent with the sampled tissue and syndrome
Mosaic, mottling, line patterns, curling, brittle growth, shortened internodes, stunting, or reduced inflorescence performance progress beyond the original sector
Chlorosis follows leaf age, interveinal or marginal patterns, or a measured tissue-nutrient, substrate-pH, or root-zone-EC abnormality better than a branch lineage
Microscopy or organism sampling confirms thrips, mites, leafminers, or another pest associated with the marks
The distribution maps to a lamp, spray, pesticide, plant-growth regulator, abrasion, heat event, or other documented exposure
Camera white balance, glare, shadow, senescence, or cultivar pigmentation explains the apparent color boundary

progression.description: Capture calibrated whole-plant, branch, upper-surface, and lower-surface views; assign a symptom-only chlorotic-sector label, not a genetic ground-truth label.

Mark the shoot and record successive leaves and any cuttings over time. A stable lineage association increases suspicion of a developmental or genetic origin but does not exclude latent or localized infection.
Compare matched healthy tissue and evaluate pests, root-zone pH and EC, nutrient status, exposure history, and a region- and facility-appropriate virus/viroid panel before narrowing the cause.

Use genetic or meristem-lineage analysis when a genetic claim matters. Cannabis somatic mosaicism has been sequenced within one mother plant, but published evidence does not establish a universal visible phenotype or inheritance rule.

lookAlikes: Mosaic, mottling, or line-pattern syndrome of unresolved cause
Lettuce chlorosis virus or other regional virus
Iron, manganese, magnesium, or nitrogen disorder
Camera color, glare, or shadow artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm genetic variegation, chimerism, mutation, virus freedom, or training ground truth from a photograph or video.
Record the exact leaf, node, branch, plant, cultivar, propagation source, date, stage, lighting, and serial change; include healthy plants of the same cultivar and environment.
Inspect both leaf surfaces and protected growth with magnification, and document pest organisms or their absence separately from the color phenotype.

Measure root-zone pH and EC and review irrigation, tissue or solution analysis, nutrient history, spray records, lamp position, temperature, and mechanical injury before assigning a developmental explanation.

Submit symptomatic and matched asymptomatic tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory for a locally appropriate validated virus/viroid differential; a negative targeted assay excludes only the agents and sample covered by that assay.
When a genetic attribution is operationally important, compare mapped sectors and clones and use qualified genetic or meristem-lineage analysis; persistence alone is supportive context, not proof.
immediateActions: Keep the visual label at “chlorotic sectoring—cause unresolved” and flag it for human review.
Pause distribution of suspect cuttings and separate them from verified genetic-trait references until infectious causes are reasonably excluded.
Preserve serial imagery and matched tissue before pruning or discarding the affected shoot.
correctivePlan: Correct only measured root-zone, nutrient, pest, or exposure problems and document whether new growth changes.
If validated pathogen testing is positive, move the sample to the confirmed pathogen class and follow the facility’s sanitation and plant-health protocol.
If differential testing is negative and the pattern tracks a shoot or clone, retain a “suspected genetic/developmental” label unless genetic evidence supports a stronger claim.
prevention: Maintain cultivar, mother-plant, cutting-position, and clone-lineage records.
Use tested propagation stock and tool-sanitation practices so a stable-looking pattern is not assumed noninfectious.
Capture healthy reference plants under repeatable lighting and camera settings for color comparison.
warnings: “Genetic mosaicism” describes within-organism genetic variation; a visible “mosaic symptom” is not evidence of that mechanism.
The Cannabis mosaicism sequencing study sampled one mother plant and did not link its variants to visible leaf sectors.
The VIGS bleaching experiment was an intentionally virus-vector-induced gene-silencing phenotype and must not be treated as proof that natural bleaching is inherited or noninfectious.

The composite reference image mixes four unresolved mosaic-like presentations with panel e, which the authors characterize as somatic-mutation-associated chlorotic sectors; preserve panel labels and never train the entire composite as one genetic class.
Negative molecular, microscopy, or indicator-host findings are bounded by sample quality, agent coverage, assay performance, and observation time.
This reviewed record validates an uncertainty-bounded workflow, not image-only genetic ground truth; all symptom-only samples remain human-review items.

sources.title: Accumulation of somatic mutations leads to genetic mosaicism in cannabis
sources.publisher: Wiley on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America
supportedClaims: Deep whole-genome sequencing of top, middle, and bottom samples from one 1.5-year-old Cannabis mother plant detected many variants unique to individual canopy samples, demonstrating within-plant genetic mosaicism in that plant.
The study examined a single mother plant and did not validate a visible leaf-sector pattern as a diagnostic marker of somatic mutation, heritability, or clonal stability.

sources.title: Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Experimental silencing of Cannabis phytoene desaturase and magnesium-chelatase-subunit-I genes produced spotted leaf bleaching, 70–73% lower target-transcript expression, and corresponding carotenoid or chlorophyll-a reductions.

This deliberately induced, virus-vector phenotype shows that perturbing pigment-related gene expression can create visible bleaching; it does not establish that naturally occurring sectors are genetic or safe from infectious differentials.

sources.title: Challenges to Cannabis sativa Production from Pathogens and Microbes—The Role of Molecular Diagnostics and Bioinformatics
sources.organization: International Journal of Molecular Sciences (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: The authors documented Cannabis leaves with mosaic, mottling, and line patterns that superficially resembled viral symptoms, and separately illustrated sharply chlorotic, chlorophyll-deficient sectors attributed to somatic mutation in Figure 4e.

Defined broad-spectrum and specific RT-PCR assays did not detect the targeted viruses in tested OG Kush and Headband tissues; positive controls worked, no virus-like particles were seen in the examined Cannabis samples by transmission electron microscopy, and inoculated indicator hosts remained symptomless for three weeks.

Those negative results apply only to the sampled tissues, agents, assays, and observation period and therefore do not establish genetic causality or exclude every virus, viroid, pest, nutrient, root-zone, or chemical cause.

media.caption: Rights-cleared reference composite from the author preprint corresponding to the peer-reviewed Punja et al. paper. Only panel e is presented by the authors as somatic-mutation-associated chlorotic sectoring; panels a–d are visually overlapping, unresolved mosaic-like differentials. It is not genetic ground truth.

useLimitations: Reference URL only; the asset is not copied into the repository.
Panel e is the suspected somatic-mutation comparison; panels a–d are unresolved mosaic-like differentials and must not inherit the genetic label.
No panel is sequence-confirmed as the cause shown; retain panel labels, caption context, and human review.
CC BY permits automated use with attribution, but this composite is excluded from training eligibility because its panels contain different and incompletely resolved labels.
media.severity: mixed chlorotic and mosaic-like foliar patterns

name: Armyworm caterpillar feeding complex
summary: A late-season caterpillar feeding differential for hemp. Armyworm larvae can defoliate foliage and enter buds or flowers, but species-level identification requires larval morphology rather than damage pattern alone.
indicators: Caterpillar larvae are present with fresh irregular chewing injury
Severe feeding skeletonizes or strips leaves toward the midribs
Larvae entering buds or flowers leave feeding injury together with silk and frass
Larval head/body markings support fall armyworm, true armyworm, or another armyworm identification
exclusions: No larvae or fresh frass are found and damage is old
Characteristic looping larvae support cabbage looper
Adult Japanese beetles are actively skeletonizing tissue

progression.description: Larvae chew irregular holes and remove expanding leaf area.
High feeding pressure can skeletonize leaves or strip tissue to major veins.
Later larvae can enter reproductive tissue, leaving silk, frass, and damaged floral material.

confirmation: Collect or clearly photograph representative larvae and use morphology for species-level assignment.
Treat frass plus an active larva as stronger evidence than holes alone.
immediateActions: Inspect fresh feeding fronts, buds, and flowers for larvae and frass.
Record larval size and density because damage potential changes with instar and population.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM response based on confirmed caterpillar identity, population, crop stage, and locally legal hemp options.
prevention: Scout late-season foliage and reproductive tissue for egg masses and young larvae.
Use monitoring and beneficial-conservation practices where appropriate.
warnings: Armyworm damage overlaps other caterpillar feeding.
Do not identify species from leaf holes or frass alone.

sources.title: Insect Pests of Industrial Hemp in Missouri
supportedClaims: Spotted cucumber beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and floral tissue, producing holes and ragged edges, while larvae can feed on root hairs and root tips.
Tarnished plant bug feeding on young hemp leaves, stems, buds, and flowers can produce chlorotic spots, leaf curling, terminal stunting, distorted buds, and bud abortion.
Dectes texanus larvae can bore inside hemp stems and pith, producing internal galleries, wilting, dieback, swollen or split stems, and increased breakage risk.
Cabbage looper larvae feed on hemp leaves, often from lower-leaf undersides upward, producing large irregular holes and potentially damaging floral buds.
Japanese beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and can skeletonize leaves between veins; adults are metallic green with bronze wing covers and often aggregate.
Armyworm larvae can create irregular holes and skeletonization and may enter hemp buds or flowers, where silk and frass can accompany feeding injury.
Hemp insect pressure varies by region, growth stage, and variety, so damage morphology without organism evidence should not be treated as species confirmation.

name: Cabbage looper feeding injury
summary: A caterpillar chewing pest documented on hemp foliage and floral buds. Irregular holes are low-specificity; the looping green larva and fresh feeding site make the diagnosis substantially stronger.
indicators: Green caterpillars with pale side striping move in a characteristic looping gait on hemp
Large irregular chewing holes begin on leaf tissue, often from lower-leaf undersides
Severe feeding strips foliage or damages/deforms floral buds
exclusions: No larvae, frass, or active chewing are found
Larval morphology supports armyworm or another caterpillar
Skeletonization occurs with aggregating adult Japanese beetles

progression.description: Larvae chew localized holes, often from leaf undersides.
Irregular holes enlarge and feeding moves upward.
Late feeding can deform or destroy portions of marketable flower heads.

confirmation: Find and document the larva on or near fresh damage and use morphology/behavior for identification.
Use chewing pattern only as supporting evidence.
immediateActions: Inspect undersides and flowers for larvae, eggs, frass, and fresh chewing.
Record larval density rather than treating one old hole as an active infestation.
correctivePlan: Use threshold-aware IPM and locally legal hemp controls for confirmed active feeding.
prevention: Scout lower foliage and reproductive tissue during late-season moth activity.
Conserve beneficial predators and parasitoids where compatible with the IPM program.
warnings: Irregular holes are shared by many chewing insects.
Old feeding damage can remain after the pest is gone.

name: Dectes stem-borer injury
summary: A stem-boring beetle differential for hemp. Internal pith galleries plus a compatible larva or adult are much stronger evidence than wilting or stem breakage alone.
indicators: Internal stem or pith galleries are present
Cream-colored longhorn-beetle larvae occur inside affected stems or compatible gray long-antenna adults are found nearby
Infested stems may swell, split, wilt, die back, or break where internal tunneling weakens them
exclusions: Stem interior lacks galleries and a vascular/root pathogen explains wilt
Boring is produced by another identified stem-boring insect
Breakage is purely mechanical with healthy intact pith

progression.description: Larvae enter stems and tunnel through internal pith.
Transport and structural integrity decline as galleries expand.
Affected stems can wilt, die back, split, or break under stress.

confirmation: Split a representative symptomatic stem lengthwise and document galleries and larvae.
Identify the insect when species-level attribution matters.
immediateActions: Flag and inspect affected stems before disposal so internal evidence is preserved.
Scout adjacent plants for adults, entry sites, or galleries.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM plan appropriate to confirmed stem-borer pressure and locally legal hemp practices.
prevention: Scout stems for swelling, entry injury, and adults during the relevant field season.
Remove or manage infested residues when locally appropriate.
warnings: Wilt and stem breakage are nonspecific.
A gallery without an identified insect should remain a generic stem-borer diagnosis.

name: Japanese beetle feeding injury
summary: A documented outdoor-hemp defoliator and flower feeder. Fresh skeletonization plus an adult with metallic-green head/thorax, copper-bronze wing covers, and twelve white abdominal hair patches is strong field evidence; feeding damage without the adult is only a low-specificity chewing-injury label.
affectedParts: major and minor veins left after feeding
indicators: Adults on hemp have a metallic-green head and thorax with copper-bronze wing covers
Five white hair patches along each abdominal side plus two posterior patches form twelve visible tufts when the adult is photographed from above and slightly behind
Fresh chewing removes interveinal leaf tissue while leaving a lace-like network of veins
Adults are present on the same leaf, shoot, or developing flower as fresh feeding injury
Multiple adults and newly expanding damage occur in a localized plant or field cluster
Flower feeding is directly observed rather than inferred from missing or browned floral tissue
exclusions: No adult or specimen is recovered after repeat scouting and another defoliator is found at the fresh feeding front
The beetle lacks the twelve discrete white abdominal hair patches or morphology supports green June beetle, another scarab, or a metallic beetle
Holes contain caterpillars, silk, or frass and do not preserve the characteristic interveinal lace pattern
Small round shot holes with flea beetles support flea-beetle injury
Irregular holes or ragged margins occur with spotted cucumber beetles rather than Japanese beetles
Damage is mined within intact epidermis rather than removed from the leaf surface
Skeletonization is old, dry, and unchanged across serial observations, with no active organism established
Root decline is attributed to Japanese beetle solely because adults occur above ground; hemp-root grub feeding has not been confirmed

progression.description: One or more adults occupy exposed foliage or developing flowers; small fresh interveinal feeding windows begin near the occupied tissue.
Interveinal tissue is progressively removed and intact veins create a lace-like pattern; neighboring leaves or flowers should be checked to map whether injury is clustered.
More adults and fresh injury may accumulate on a subset of plants or canopy positions. Record actual adult counts and new injury because a single frame cannot establish temporal growth.

Large populations can remove substantial leaf area or completely defoliate plants, but serious hemp defoliation was rare in the early multi-state literature and no universal loss threshold was established.
Skeletonized tissue persists after adults leave. Old lace-like leaves without adults or newly expanding injury must not be labeled as a current Japanese beetle infestation.

lookAlikes: Green June beetle or another scarab beetle
confirmation: Capture a whole-plant or row view to show the distribution of affected and unaffected plants, then record upper, middle, and lower canopy zones separately; published hemp sources do not establish a preferred leaf age or canopy position.
Photograph fresh injury and the adult together before disturbance, then obtain dorsal, lateral, and posterior macro views with a scale reference.
Verify the metallic-green head/thorax, copper-bronze wing covers, and twelve discrete white abdominal hair patches; preserve a representative adult when morphology is unclear.
Revisit marked leaves or plants and record new feeding and adult counts so old residual skeletonization is separated from an active infestation.
For image/video datasets, require an organism-level frame linked to the damage sequence; do not use skeletonization-only frames as species-level ground truth.
Submit an intact adult to an Extension entomologist or diagnostic laboratory when a similar scarab, green June beetle, or incomplete view prevents confident identification.
Do not infer larval root injury from adult canopy presence; confirm grubs in the root zone and identify them separately if root damage is suspected.
immediateActions: Mark sampled plants, count adults, estimate current defoliation, and record whether flowers are being fed on before choosing an intervention.
Scout several plants across several locations so one conspicuous aggregation is not treated as a field-wide population estimate.
Preserve pre-intervention photographs and a representative specimen when the diagnosis or future label review depends on species identity.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM response based on confirmed adults, fresh injury, crop stage, local pressure, and products currently legal for hemp in the jurisdiction.
Track new injury and adult counts at fixed plants; old skeletonized tissue will not recover and should not be used alone to judge control.
Protect pollinators and flowering-crop quality when evaluating any response on developing flowers.
prevention: Include adult-morphology and fresh-damage views in routine outdoor scouting records.
Map clusters and repeat counts through the adult activity period instead of relying on cumulative season-long damage.
Treat pheromone traps as monitoring tools only after evaluating placement; attraction near the crop can confound local abundance and damage.
warnings: Skeletonization, irregular holes, or flower injury alone are not Japanese beetle ground truth; species-level image labels require the adult and diagnostic morphology.
A close-up adult specimen image can teach organism morphology but cannot establish Cannabis host association, active feeding, severity, canopy distribution, or yield impact.
Published hemp observations do not establish a preferred leaf age or canopy position, so those fields must be recorded from the sampled plant rather than imputed.

The 2019 multi-state synthesis called Japanese beetle potentially significant but also reported serious defoliation as rare across the broader defoliator complex; apparent severity must remain case-specific.
No universal hemp economic threshold, symptom-to-yield conversion, or cultivar response is established by these sources.
The UNH hemp photograph is institutional and creator-credited but has no explicit reuse license on its landing page; store only its reference metadata unless permission is obtained.
All damage-only, incomplete-morphology, unlinked specimen/damage, and root-injury samples require human review.

sources.title: Developing Insect Pest Management Systems for Hemp in the United States: A Work in Progress
sources.organization: Journal of Integrated Pest Management (Cranshaw et al.)
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Japanese beetle was observed on hemp east of the Mississippi as a highly visible, potentially significant defoliator that also feeds readily on hemp flowers; Figure 4 documents an adult on hemp.

Across the broader hemp defoliator complex, serious defoliation had only rarely been observed and experiments were still needed to connect defoliation with seed, fiber, cannabinoid, and biomass outcomes.

sources.title: Hemp Pests in New Hampshire
sources.organization: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
sources.publisher: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
supportedClaims: Adult Japanese beetles feed on hemp leaves and developing flowers; leaf feeding produces skeletonization, and large populations may completely defoliate plants.
Japanese beetle grubs may damage roots, but turfgrass is their preferred larval habitat; an adult observed on hemp should not be used to infer that hemp roots contain grubs.
Representative field scouting should cover multiple plants and locations and record the pest, plant injury, crop context, and collected specimens rather than relying on one image.

sources.organization: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program
sources.publisher: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

The institutional specimen image is credited to Clemson University–USDA Cooperative Extension Slide Series, Bugwood.org, and is licensed CC BY 3.0 US.

sources.title: Japanese beetles in yards and gardens
supportedClaims: Adult Japanese beetles are approximately one-third to one-half inch long, with a metallic-green head and thorax, copper-brown wing covers, five white hair patches along each abdominal side, and two patches at the abdominal tip.

In Minnesota, adults primarily feed during July and August and can persist into September; damaged leaves emit odors that attract other beetles, producing concentrated clusters while neighboring suitable plants may remain lightly infested.
The seasonal timing is regional context rather than a universal Cannabis calendar, and the larval white-grub stage requires separate ventral-spine examination for positive identification.

name: Spotted cucumber beetle feeding injury
summary: A documented industrial-hemp chewing pest. Adult beetles can damage foliage and floral tissue while larvae can injure root hairs and root tips; organism evidence is needed because ragged holes and weak roots are not species-specific.
indicators: Yellow-green adult beetles with twelve dark spots are present on hemp
Leaves or floral tissue show fresh holes and ragged chewing edges while adults are feeding
Root injury or weak anchorage occurs together with compatible rootworm larvae in the root zone
exclusions: No compatible beetles or larvae are found and another chewing pest is present
Damage consists mainly of stippling, silvering, mining, or sap-feeding distortion rather than chewing
Root decline occurs without root-feeding larvae and a pathogen or irrigation disorder is better supported

progression.description: Adults chew foliage and reproductive tissue, leaving holes and ragged margins.
Where larvae are present, root-hair and root-tip feeding can reduce anchorage and contribute to stunting.

confirmation: Photograph or collect the beetle/larva with the damaged tissue; identify the organism rather than assigning species from holes alone.
Inspect roots only when root symptoms or lodging are present.
immediateActions: Scout nearby plants for adults and fresh feeding damage.
Document root-zone larvae separately from above-ground beetles.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM response appropriate to confirmed pest pressure, crop stage, and locally legal hemp options.
prevention: Scout field margins and foliage during vegetative to early flowering growth.
Reduce weed or alternate-host reservoirs where agronomically appropriate.
warnings: Chewing holes are not diagnostic of spotted cucumber beetle.
Root damage can coexist with root pathogens; finding beetle larvae does not exclude disease.

name: Tarnished plant bug feeding injury
summary: A piercing-sucking hemp pest that can injure expanding leaves, shoots, buds, and flowers. Terminal distortion and chlorotic spotting overlap mites and abiotic injury, so a compatible Lygus insect should be observed before assigning this diagnosis.
indicators: Fast-moving mottled brown bugs with a pale or yellow triangular marking are present on symptomatic hemp
Young tissue develops chlorotic feeding spots, curling, or distorted terminal growth
Developing buds are malformed or abort while compatible plant bugs are feeding
exclusions: No compatible insects are found after repeated scouting
Microscopy confirms broad or russet mites
Distortion follows a chemical, heat, or mechanical exposure pattern
Chewing holes dominate rather than piercing-sucking injury

progression.description: Adults or nymphs feed on young vegetative or reproductive tissues.
Expanding leaves or terminals can curl or stunt and buds may become misshapen.

confirmation: Capture or clearly photograph the insect on symptomatic tissue and use morphology for species-level identification.
Treat terminal distortion alone as low-specificity evidence.
immediateActions: Scout young leaves, terminals, and buds for nymphs/adults.
Record whether injury is clustered along field edges or alternate-host vegetation.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed-pest IPM and locally legal hemp controls only when population and injury justify intervention.
prevention: Monitor weeds and field margins that can harbor plant bugs.
Scout during rapid terminal and bud development.
warnings: Curling and distorted buds are not Lygus-specific.
Do not infer this pest from one deformed leaf without organism evidence.

sources.title: Insect Pests of Industrial Hemp in Missouri
supportedClaims: Spotted cucumber beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and floral tissue, producing holes and ragged edges, while larvae can feed on root hairs and root tips.
Tarnished plant bug feeding on young hemp leaves, stems, buds, and flowers can produce chlorotic spots, leaf curling, terminal stunting, distorted buds, and bud abortion.
Dectes texanus larvae can bore inside hemp stems and pith, producing internal galleries, wilting, dieback, swollen or split stems, and increased breakage risk.
Cabbage looper larvae feed on hemp leaves, often from lower-leaf undersides upward, producing large irregular holes and potentially damaging floral buds.
Japanese beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and can skeletonize leaves between veins; adults are metallic green with bronze wing covers and often aggregate.
Armyworm larvae can create irregular holes and skeletonization and may enter hemp buds or flowers, where silk and frass can accompany feeding injury.
Hemp insect pressure varies by region, growth stage, and variety, so damage morphology without organism evidence should not be treated as species confirmation.

name: Thrips feeding injury
summary: Onion thrips and western flower thrips are documented on hemp; feeding can produce vein-associated white flecks or irregular silvery scars, dark fecal spots, and distortion of leaves damaged while expanding, but symptoms alone cannot identify the insect or its species.
indicators: Irregular white flecks or silvery scarred patches, often following or crossing veins
Small dark fecal spots occur within or beside fresh feeding scars
Minute elongated yellow, tan, or yellow-brown insects are recovered from symptomatic tissue
Wingless creamy-yellow larvae or slender adults with narrow fringed wings are visible under magnification
Leaves fed on while developing later expand with localized distortion or uneven scarred areas
Indoor or protected-crop injury increases over serial observations while matched uninfested plants remain unchanged
exclusions: No thrips, larvae, shed skins, or dark fecal spots are found after repeat inspection, foliage tapping, and sticky-card monitoring
Fine webbing, round eggs, and two-spotted mites are present
Microscopic cigar-shaped mites with two pairs of legs are present
Only residue is visible and it wipes or dissolves without damaged epidermal tissue beneath it
The pattern follows a nutrient-mobility gradient by leaf age rather than localized feeding scars
Circular or angular lesions enlarge independently and have halos, fungal growth, bacterial streaming, or pathogen-positive laboratory results
Distortion is restricted to the newest protected tissue and broad mites or dotted broad-mite eggs are confirmed
Abrasion aligns uniformly with a fan, rubbing surface, spray event, or physical contact and no organisms are recovered

progression.description: Small white flecks or short irregular silver scars appear, commonly along veins; a single image may omit the tiny insect and remains low confidence.
Fresh scars accumulate on multiple leaves with dark fecal spots, and larvae or adults can be recovered by direct inspection or tapping.
Tissue fed on while young expands unevenly, leaving localized distortion and larger scarred areas even if insect abundance later changes.

In one preliminary indoor Cannabis experiment, plants begun with five onion thrips produced less fresh yield than uninfested plants; this does not define a universal visual severity scale or action threshold.

confirmation: Inspect both leaf surfaces, veins, folds, growing tips, and flowers with at least a 10× hand lens; record whether scars, dark fecal spots, larvae, adults, and shed skins occur together.
Tap symptomatic foliage and flowers over white paper or a collection tray, then preserve representative insects for magnified examination.
Use blue or yellow sticky cards as population and movement monitors, not as proof that a particular damaged leaf was caused by thrips.

For species-level labels, submit intact adults to an entomology or plant diagnostic laboratory for morphological or validated molecular identification; color and a routine phone photograph are insufficient.
Capture serial whole-plant, leaf-surface macro, opposite-surface, vein-level, and organism-magnification views with scale and production context; compare with a matched healthy plant.
immediateActions: Separate or clearly mark suspect plants and inspect neighboring propagation material, young growth, flowers, weeds, and sticky cards before moving plants.
Preserve representative insects and pre-treatment images before intervention when species or causal confirmation is needed.
Avoid applying an unverified pesticide or coating simply because silver injury is present.
correctivePlan: Use only a control program legal for Cannabis or hemp, the jurisdiction, production system, and growth stage, following the current product label and worker-safety requirements.
Track fresh scars and organism counts at fixed sampling sites; old silver scars and distorted leaves will not heal and should not be used alone to judge control.
Address confirmed entry or reservoir points such as infested transplants, weeds, crop debris, flowers, or unscreened openings while conserving identified beneficial thrips and other natural enemies.
prevention: Quarantine and hand-lens inspect incoming clones and transplants.
Scout representative plants and canopy zones on a fixed schedule, including young leaves and flowers rather than relying only on sticky cards.
Maintain clean plant and weed-free buffer practices appropriate to the production system and record thrips detections by stage and location.
warnings: Silver flecks, black specks, or distorted leaves alone are not thrips ground truth; confirm the organism and feeding context.

A group-level thrips label does not establish onion thrips, western flower thrips, tobacco thrips, or another species; species identification requires suitable adult specimens and specialist examination.
The controlled yield study was preliminary and used defined indoor infestation treatments; it does not establish a universal economic threshold or symptom-to-yield conversion.
Predatory thrips can be beneficial, so the presence of a thrips-shaped insect is not sufficient to assign a damaging-pest label.
The two institutional Cannabis images below have no explicit reuse license; they are hidden metadata references, not copied assets or training samples.

sources.title: Onion thrips, Thrips tabaci (Thysanoptera: Thripidae), reduces yields in indoor-grown cannabis
supportedClaims: A controlled preliminary study identified onion thrips, Thrips tabaci, proliferating on indoor-grown Cannabis and compared plants initially receiving zero, one, or five thrips.

Plants initially receiving five thrips had lower fresh yield than plants receiving zero thrips; the result supports monitoring but does not establish an image-only diagnosis or a general action threshold.
The experiment was limited to defined indoor conditions and infestation treatments, so yield effects and severity must not be generalized across cultivars, production systems, or thrips species.

sources.title: Thrips
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Onion thrips and western flower thrips occur on field- and greenhouse-grown hemp; adults are minute, elongated, yellow to yellow-brown insects with fringed wings and larvae are creamy yellow and wingless.
Feeding on hemp produces white flecks or silvery scars with dark fecal spots, often along veins, and feeding on developing leaves can distort them.
Field injury is usually minor in Utah, economic damage is more likely indoors, and no industrial-hemp treatment threshold is established.
The two hemp symptom photographs on the page are credited collectively to the USU Extension IPM Program, while the page provides no explicit reuse license.

sources.title: Developing Insect Pest Management Systems for Hemp in the United States: A Work in Progress
sources.organization: Journal of Integrated Pest Management (Cranshaw et al.)
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Onion thrips was the species commonly found on hemp foliage in eastern Colorado and could cause serious foliage damage during indoor production, while outdoor populations generally failed to reach damaging levels.
Western flower thrips was also identified on Colorado hemp but was associated mainly with flowers and pollen; tobacco thrips was reported on young plants in an earlier Mississippi survey.
Thrips on hemp remained incompletely characterized, so visual injury cannot safely assign species or predict economic impact without organism sampling and production context.

name: Broad mite
summary: A microscopic tarsonemid mite that hides in protected young tissue; feeding injury appears later as hardened, puckered, cupped, or strap-like new leaves, bronzing, short internodes, and deformed buds.
indicators: Warped, puckered, or hardened newest leaves
Cupped or strap-like new growth
Bronze, copper, or dark discoloration on young tissue
Short internodes and stunted growing tips
Deformed or aborted flower buds
Oval mites or dotted translucent eggs under magnification
exclusions: Cigar-shaped mites with only two pairs of legs are present instead
Fine webbing and round spider-mite eggs are present
Only older leaves follow a mobile-nutrient symptom pattern
Injury is uniform on the brightest upper canopy and measured leaf temperature or light is excessive
No mites or dotted eggs are found after repeat sampling of adjacent fresh growth and protected sites

progression.description: Tiny mites and eggs occupy leaf undersides, axils, buds, and other protected young tissue; visible injury may be absent or lag behind feeding.
Expanding leaves become puckered, cupped, hardened, strap-like, or bronze while internodes shorten and growing tips slow.
New growth is markedly stunted, buds deform or abort, and damaged tissue can remain symptomatic after mites move to fresher growth.

confirmation: Inspect fresh expanding tissue adjacent to the worst damage, including undersides, axils, growing tips, and buds, at about 20× or with a dissecting microscope.
Confirm translucent oval adults and clear oval eggs bearing raised pale dots; adult females may show a pale dorsal stripe.
Separate broad mite from cigar-shaped, two-pair-legged russet mites and from cyclamen mites, whose eggs lack the characteristic dotted surface.
Treat a negative sample cautiously because injury can persist after mites leave badly damaged tissue; repeat sampling across plants and time when suspicion remains.
immediateActions: Quarantine suspect plants and stop moving cuttings or shared tools into clean areas.
Microscope-screen neighboring plants before choosing any control.
correctivePlan: Use only controls legal for the crop, jurisdiction, and growth stage, following the current label.
Track mites or eggs on fixed fresh-growth sampling sites; do not judge response from old distorted leaves.
Remove severely infested material without spreading mites and sanitize shared tools between plants.
prevention: Start with inspected propagation material.
Quarantine and magnification-screen incoming clones.
Include protected new-growth sites in routine scouting rather than inspecting only mature fan leaves.
warnings: Leaf distortion, bronzing, or short internodes alone are not diagnostic.
The two media assets below show the organism without a host and are morphology references, not cannabis symptom ground truth.
Although their licenses permit reuse, both remain reference-only and excluded from automated training pending a separate training and dataset-split review.

sources.title: Broad Mite
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Broad mite (Polyphagotarsonemus latus) is documented on hemp and occupies shaded, protected leaf surfaces and crevices.
Adults are extremely small, oval to round, and light yellow to green; eggs are laid on leaf undersides.
Feeding can produce malformed, warped, or hardened young leaves and flower buds, bronzing, stunting, and aborted growth.

sources.title: Assessing the impact of piercing-sucking pests on greenhouse-grown industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Broad mites are recognized among the most significant piercing-sucking pests of greenhouse-grown hemp.

Piercing-sucking pest injury in hemp can overlap visually with cupping, yellowing, leaf loss, and reduced reproductive performance, so pest presence must be confirmed rather than inferred from canopy symptoms.

sources.title: Broad Mite
supportedClaims: Broad mites prefer young, protected tissue and may no longer be present on the most damaged tissue because visible injury can persist after feeding.
Clear oval broad-mite eggs have raised pale dots, while cyclamen-mite eggs are smooth and russet mites have a narrow, conical body form.
Broad-mite injury can resemble plant-growth-regulator herbicide injury, nutrient problems, and other abiotic disorders; inspection at about 20× or by microscope is recommended.
