The composite contains three diagnosis classes: only the left column is manganese deficiency; the middle is boron deficiency and the right is copper deficiency, so a whole-image single-class label is invalid.
The rows are a severity sequence from one experiment; preserve source grouping and do not split related panels across training and evaluation.
Reference display only until every panel is bounded, class- and stage-annotated, independently reviewed, and assigned a leakage-safe dataset split.
media.stage: initial, intermediate, and advanced vegetative deficiency

name: Low molybdenum analytical state — no validated visual phenotype
summary: A deliberate abstention class: Cannabis grown without molybdenum for nine weeks had a 96% lower foliar Mo concentration but no visual symptoms and no significant dry-weight reduction. Image-only “molybdenum deficiency” should therefore be rejected by the diagnostic engine.
affectedParts: most-recent mature leaf for tissue testing
indicators: Laboratory tissue analysis documents very low molybdenum relative to an appropriate healthy comparison
No stable Cannabis-specific visual symptom pattern is required or validated
exclusions: A diagnosis is based only on yellow, orange, pink, curled, or narrow leaves from a generic internet chart
Another measured nutrient, pH, EC, root, pest, or pathogen condition explains visible symptoms

progression.description: No visible symptom progression developed during nine weeks of complete Mo withholding in Cannabis sativa T1 despite strongly reduced tissue Mo.

confirmation: Use calibrated tissue analysis and nutrition history; a photograph cannot confirm low molybdenum in Cannabis.
Keep photo-only confidence near zero unless future Cannabis-specific controlled evidence establishes a reproducible phenotype.
immediateActions: Do not apply molybdenum based on image color alone.
Review complete fertilizer composition and laboratory results.
correctivePlan: Correct only a laboratory-supported under-supply using a measured nutrition plan.
prevention: Use complete micronutrient formulations and periodic analytical monitoring when warranted.
warnings: The best controlled Cannabis evidence currently contradicts popular image charts that assign a distinctive Mo-deficiency leaf appearance.
This record exists partly to prevent false-positive model predictions.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Single-element withholding in Cannabis sativa T1 documented boron deficiency, manganese toxicity, and the absence of a visible molybdenum-deficiency phenotype during the nine-week experiment.
Boron-deficient plants developed growing-tip stunting, distorted new leaves, marginal necrosis, death of growing tips, root-tip loss, and severe wilting in advanced stages.

In Cannabis sativa T1, manganese-toxicity symptoms appeared seven weeks after treatment: marginal yellowing began on lower leaves, intensified inward toward the midrib, and advanced to marginal necrosis, severe chlorosis, and occasional leaf abscission.

The manganese-toxicity treatment used a tenfold increase over the complete formula (180 micromolar Mn versus 18 micromolar), but treated foliar Mn was 47.88 mg/kg, within the cited 41–93 mg/kg survey range; dry weight did not differ significantly from controls and the authors called for higher-concentration work to refine the threshold.
Figure 5 is a six-panel composite: manganese toxicity occupies the left column and boron toxicity the right, with initial, intermediate, and advanced symptom rows.

Molybdenum-withheld plants had foliar Mo 96% lower than controls yet developed no visual symptoms and no significant dry-weight difference by nine weeks, so a camera-visible Mo-deficiency phenotype was not established.
The experiment used one cultivar and complete withholding or tenfold treatments; tissue values and timing are experimental observations rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

name: Nitrogen deficiency
summary: A nitrogen-status disorder with controlled Cannabis evidence for stunting and chlorosis that begins on older or lower fan leaves and progresses upward. Flowering-stage evidence adds leaflet-tip and interveinal onset, red-brown petioles, stem yellowing or browning, fan-leaf senescence, and later sugar-leaf involvement, but none of these visual features is nitrogen-specific.
affectedParts: fan leaves across the lower two-thirds as injury progresses
petioles of severely affected fan leaves
main stem and lower-order branch stems in prolonged flowering deficiency
older and larger sugar leaves near inflorescence bases in advanced flowering deficiency
whole plant for height, width, canopy gradient, and vigor comparison
roots and root zone for availability checks
stages: vegetative evidence from transplant-onward complete withholding in T1
flowering weeks three onward after withholding began at photoperiod change in Gelato 29
late flowering where normal senescence is a major confounder
indicators: Slight stunting precedes or accompanies visible chlorosis relative to a healthy same-cultivar control
Vegetative T1 first develops slight general paling or yellowing of lower foliage
Flowering Gelato 29 first develops very slight yellowing at leaflet tips on lower-canopy fan leaves
Chlorosis expands through older fan leaves and upward through the canopy rather than beginning in recently expanded top growth
Flowering fan-leaf chlorosis may be initially strongest between veins before broad whole-leaf yellowing
Within affected flowering leaflets, severity can increase from base toward tip even though the first visible cue was tip yellowing
Severely affected fan leaves become fully yellow, then brown or necrotic and senesce or abscise
Petioles may shift from dull green to red-brown and prolonged deficiency may yellow then brown stems
Sugar-leaf chlorosis begins later than fan-leaf injury and is strongest first on older, larger, lower-position sugar leaves
Serial neutral-light images show a lower-to-upper and older-to-younger gradient instead of isolated color change
exclusions: Recently expanded upper foliage is affected first while older lower foliage remains healthy, favoring an immobile-micronutrient, sulfur, exposure, or growing-point disorder
Older leaves have sharply interveinal chlorosis with persistent green veins and tissue evidence supports magnesium rather than nitrogen status
Chlorosis is marginal, lesion-based, mosaic, sectoral, stippled, silvered, or associated with distortion rather than a mapped age-position gradient
The pattern appears only in late flowering and matches healthy same-cultivar controls with adequate solution and tissue nitrogen
Root-zone EC is high, fertilizer salts are concentrated, or solution nitrogen is adequate, making indiscriminate nitrogen addition unsafe
Root-zone pH, saturation, hypoxia, temperature, root binding, root loss, or vascular/root disease better explains impaired uptake
Mites, thrips, aphids, eggs, webbing, cast skins, frass, or feeding scars are found on magnified inspection
Discrete lesions, surface growth, vascular discoloration, soft rot, odor, or laboratory evidence supports a pathogen
A lamp, heat, drought, spray, herbicide, salt, or other exposure gradient fits the distribution and timing
Color change disappears under neutral calibrated lighting or follows camera exposure, white balance, cultivar pigmentation, or genetic variegation
Molecular testing and systemic signs support virus, viroid, phytoplasma, or another infectious syndrome
Only one detached yellow leaf is available without node, canopy, root-zone, nutrition, stage, and serial context

progression.description: After six weeks of complete nitrogen withholding from transplant, plants were slightly stunted and lower foliage developed slight overall paling or yellowing.
Yellowing intensified and advanced from the bottom-most leaves into middle foliage; advanced leaves became completely yellow, then necrotic and abscised.
During flowering week three, very slight yellowing appeared at leaflet tips of lower-canopy fan leaves, together with visibly reduced vegetative expansion relative to other treatments.
Most fan leaves in the lower two-thirds showed yellowing. Detached-leaf views showed mild-to-severe progression; chlorosis was initially strongest between veins before broad whole-leaf yellowing.
Nearly all fan leaves were yellow with a bottom-to-top severity gradient; the worst fan leaves browned and senesced, petioles became red-brown, stems began yellowing, and sugar-leaf chlorosis began.

By weeks six and seven, most fan leaves had senesced, yellowing advanced through older basal and lower-position sugar leaves, and stems became brown. This severe endpoint is a loss state, not a treatment target or routine training reference.
Track expansion, color, and injury in subsequent leaves plus root-zone and analytical measurements; old yellow, necrotic, or abscised foliage will not become a clean visual reference.

lookAlikes: Normal late-flower leaf aging or senescence
Iron, manganese, zinc, or other micronutrient availability disorder
Overwatering, root hypoxia, root binding, drought, or root loss
Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, root aphid, fungus gnat, or root-knot injury
Light, heat, cold, or excessive vapor-demand stress
Herbicide, foliar spray, fertilizer contact, or salt injury
Spider mite, broad mite, hemp russet mite, thrips, or aphid injury
Virus, viroid, phytoplasma, or unresolved systemic decline
Leaf-spot, vascular, crown, or root pathogen
Camera white-balance, exposure, or grow-light color shift
confirmation: Do not confirm nitrogen deficiency from yellow color, lower-leaf loss, red petioles, stem color, stunting, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected label until the photographed plant is linked to nutrition, root-zone, and analytical context.

Capture serial whole-plant views and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy fan leaves of known node and physiological age, both leaf surfaces, petioles, stems, roots, and inflorescence sugar leaves under neutral repeatable lighting with a color reference, scale, and healthy same-cultivar control.

Record cultivar, propagation cohort, vegetative or flowering day, nitrogen concentration and form, complete fertilizer recipe, source water, irrigation history, substrate or solution type, recent feed changes, and whether nutrients were intentionally withheld.
Measure input and root-zone pH and EC, water content or container mass, temperature, drainage, and oxygenation as appropriate; inspect washed roots before adding nitrogen.

Submit correctly positioned upper- and lower-canopy leaf tissue plus appropriate fertilizer solution, leachate, substrate, soil, and source-water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret nitrogen with other nutrients using crop-, cultivar-, organ-, stage-, and method-appropriate references.

Do not use one tissue number as a universal threshold: in the flowering study, visible nitrogen symptoms occurred even though upper- and lower-canopy foliar nitrogen values overlapped controls and other treatments at symptom onset.

Inspect both leaf surfaces, growing points, stems, and roots with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when arthropods, root disease, vascular disease, viruses, viroids, or other pathogens remain plausible.

Compare the rate and age-position pattern with untreated healthy same-cultivar plants; response of subsequent growth after correcting a documented cause is supporting evidence, not retrospective ground truth for the original image.
immediateActions: Mark the plant and preserve pre-treatment serial images, fertilizer and irrigation records, root-zone measurements, and representative upper- and lower-canopy tissue before changing nutrition.
Correct documented pH, salinity, saturation, temperature, oxygenation, irrigation, or root-health problems before assuming nitrogen concentration is inadequate.
Avoid adding nitrogen from color alone, especially when EC is elevated, roots are impaired, or plants are in late flowering.
correctivePlan: When analytical and production records support inadequate nitrogen supply or availability and roots are functional, restore a balanced crop- and system-appropriate nitrogen program gradually under current local agronomic guidance.
Track subsequent foliage, internode and leaf expansion, new injury, root growth, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue or solution results rather than recovery of old yellow leaves.
If nitrogen status is adequate or the pattern continues, reopen senescence, magnesium, sulfur, micronutrient, root disease, arthropod, pathogen, environmental, exposure, and genetic differentials.
prevention: Record total nitrogen and nitrogen form, complete fertilizer composition, source-water chemistry, pH, EC, irrigation, and crop stage against plant and media identifiers.
Use routine same-position upper- and lower-canopy tissue sampling and production-system-appropriate root-zone or soil testing before visible injury.
Maintain healthy same-cultivar references and neutral-light serial imaging across fan-leaf ages, canopy thirds, stems, sugar leaves, and flowering weeks.
Do not intentionally force severe deficiency or visible fade as a proxy for maturity, quality, or harvest readiness.
warnings: The vegetative T1 six-week onset, 1.62% most-recent-mature-leaf nitrogen value, 50% biomass difference, and sequence came from one cultivar in silica sand with complete withholding and are not universal thresholds.

The flowering Gelato 29 week-three onset and progression came from three deep-water-culture plants per treatment with withholding initiated at photoperiod change; weeks, colors, tissue distribution, and loss estimates must not be generalized.

Flowering-study tissue nitrogen at visible symptom onset overlapped controls and other treatments, demonstrating that sample position, timing, stage, cultivar, and analytical context can outweigh a single number.

Healthy control plants in the flowering study developed lower-fan-leaf chlorosis during weeks six through eight despite adequate nutrient solution and measured foliage, so late-cycle yellowing is not nitrogen-deficiency ground truth.
Red or brown petioles, interveinal yellowing, stem color, and lower-leaf loss are not nitrogen-specific and require explicit confounder checks.

The licensed flowering figure combines four panels, organs, views, weeks, and severity states; the separate vegetative Figure 2 combines nitrogen, phosphorus, and calcium classes. Both remain excluded from automated training until panels are bounded, individually annotated, scientifically reviewed, source-grouped, and assigned leakage-safe splits.
All symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, late-flower, unmeasured-root-zone, and unlinked-tissue samples require human review.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Cannabis sativa T1 plants were grown in silica sand with a complete modified Hoagland solution or a solution withholding one nutrient, observed daily, photographed through initial, intermediate, and advanced symptoms, and sampled at first symptom expression for most-recent-mature-leaf tissue analysis.

Nitrogen-withheld plants developed symptoms after six weeks: slight stunting and lower-foliage paling progressed upward into middle foliage, then affected leaves became fully yellow, necrotic, and abscised.

At first symptom expression, nitrogen-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.62% nitrogen dry weight compared with 4.28% in controls, and treated plants produced 50% less dry biomass under the experiment conditions.
Only the left column of Figure 2 represents nitrogen deficiency; the center and right columns are phosphorus and calcium deficiency and must retain separate labels.
The one-cultivar, silica-sand, complete-withholding experiment does not establish universal onset timing, tissue thresholds, production symptoms, or response to partial nitrogen limitation.

Phosphorus-withheld plants first showed slight stunting and irregular olive-green spots on lower and older leaflets after seven weeks; spots enlarged, appeared sunken and almost wet, developed some marginal necrosis, and advanced to extensive olive spotting and large necrotic portions.

At first phosphorus-deficiency symptom expression, phosphorus-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.09% phosphorus dry weight compared with 0.43% in controls, a 79% difference under the experiment conditions.

The study used one cultivar, began nutrient withholding at transplant, and reported no statistically significant biomass difference for phosphorus-withheld plants at the symptom-onset harvest, so its timing, tissue value, and appearance are not universal diagnostic thresholds.
Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced nitrogen-, phosphorus-, and calcium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1.

In calcium-withheld T1 plants, symptoms appeared after five weeks as slight stunting and irregular growing tips and newly expanding leaves; leaflet bases stayed narrow and paler than tips, then basal and interveinal chlorosis, marginal necrosis, distorted geometry, growing-tip death, and axillary branching developed.

At first calcium-deficiency symptom expression, most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.39% calcium dry weight compared with 3.73% in controls, but the one-cultivar silica-sand withholding experiment does not establish a universal tissue threshold or field sequence.

Iron-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks: slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases, progressed to interveinal chlorosis on growing-tip and newly expanding leaves and spread through the upper half while middle and lower foliage remained healthy dark green.

At first iron-deficiency symptom expression, iron-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 60.08 mg/kg iron compared with 111.75 mg/kg in controls, 46% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.
Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 composite with initial, intermediate, and advanced iron-deficiency images in its left column and zinc-deficiency images in its right column.

Manganese-withheld T1 plants developed bright-yellow netted interveinal chlorosis on upper and central foliage after six weeks; the netting began near leaflet midribs, spread toward margins, retained green veins, and later developed small tan necrotic regions.

At first manganese-deficiency symptom expression, manganese-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 7.56 mg/kg manganese compared with 29.40 mg/kg in controls, 74% lower under the experiment conditions; dry biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

The control manganese concentration was itself below the cited general crop survey range, and the study used one cultivar in silica sand with complete withholding, so neither treatment value is a universal Cannabis diagnostic threshold.

Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced manganese-, boron-, and copper-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its left column represents manganese deficiency.

Copper-withheld T1 plants first developed visible symptoms after nine weeks, beginning with slight whole-plant stunting and mild distortion of newer and expanding leaves, especially narrowed and slightly yellow leaflet bases.

As copper-withholding symptoms advanced, basal narrowing and distortion intensified, marginal interveinal chlorosis developed, and the whole leaf progressed to fine interveinal chlorosis with slightly inward- and downward-curled margins and reduced turgidity.

At first copper-deficiency symptom expression, copper-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.41 mg/kg copper compared with 4.65 mg/kg in controls, 70% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 45% less biomass.

The control copper concentration of 4.65 mg/kg was itself slightly below the general crop survey range cited by the authors, and the one-cultivar complete-withholding result does not establish a universal Cannabis threshold.

The published Figure 4 caption and column labels identify initial, intermediate, and advanced copper-deficiency panels in the right column, although the copper subsection text cites Figure 5; Figure 5 is captioned as manganese- and boron-toxicity progression, so this source-level numbering inconsistency must remain attached to copper panel review.

Magnesium-withheld T1 plants first developed slight interveinal yellowing on lower and older foliage after seven weeks; the contrast between green veins and yellow interveinal tissue intensified and some regions became necrotic.

At first magnesium-deficiency symptom expression, magnesium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.12% magnesium compared with 0.61% in controls, 80% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced sulfur-, magnesium-, and potassium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its center column represents magnesium deficiency.

Potassium-withheld T1 plants first developed yellowing at leaflet margins and saw-tooth serrations on lower and older foliage after nine weeks; yellowing intensified and moved inward toward the midrib, followed by tan necrosis concentrated along serrated margins.

At first potassium-deficiency symptom expression, potassium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.41% potassium compared with 2.85% in controls, 86% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 27% less biomass.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite whose right column shows initial, intermediate, and advanced potassium-deficiency phenotypes; the sulfur and magnesium columns are separate diagnoses and the asset is indexed once under the magnesium record to avoid duplicate media hashes.

Zinc-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks as marginal yellowing on newer and expanding leaves, concentrated along leaflet margins and toothed portions; tan, irregularly shaped marginal necrosis developed as the disorder progressed.

At first zinc-deficiency symptom expression, zinc-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 10.70 mg/kg zinc compared with 25.33 mg/kg in controls, 58% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

Sulfur-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after seven weeks as slight overall yellowing, especially in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases; yellowing intensified at leaflet bases and on newly expanding leaves, then advanced to very pale yellow tissue around the midrib and leaflet bases.

At first sulfur-deficiency symptom expression, sulfur-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.11% sulfur compared with 0.41% in controls, 73% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

sources.title: Foliar Symptomology, Nutrient Content, Yield, and Secondary Metabolite Variability of Cannabis Grown Hydroponically with Different Single-Element Nutrient Deficiencies
supportedClaims: Three Gelato 29 plants per treatment were grown in aerated deep-water culture; single-element withholding began with the switch to a 12-hour flowering photoperiod, plants were examined daily and photographed weekly, and upper- and lower-canopy foliage was laboratory analyzed at symptom onset.
Nitrogen-withheld plants showed reduced vegetative expansion before foliar symptoms; during week three, very slight yellowing began at leaflet tips of lower-canopy fan leaves.

By week four, most fan leaves in the lower two-thirds were yellowing; chlorosis was initially strongest between veins before broad whole-leaf yellowing, and severity within leaflets progressed from base toward tip.

By week five, nearly all fan leaves were yellow with severity increasing from bottom to top; petioles became red-brown, some fan leaves browned and senesced, stems began yellowing, and sugar-leaf chlorosis began.

By weeks six and seven, most fan leaves had senesced, older and lower-position sugar leaves progressively yellowed or browned, and stems became brown; the authors considered this prolonged severe endpoint commercially damaging.

At symptom onset, upper- and lower-canopy foliar nitrogen concentrations did not differ and overlapped the control and other treatments, illustrating limitations of a single tissue analysis later in production.

Healthy control plants developed lower-fan-leaf chlorosis in weeks six through eight despite adequate nutrient solution and foliar concentrations, demonstrating that natural late-flower senescence can visually confound nitrogen deficiency.

Nitrogen-withheld plants had 73% less aboveground vegetative fresh mass and approximately 72% less fresh inflorescence mass than controls under this three-plant treatment; these are experiment-specific loss estimates, not universal predictions.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage nitrogen-deficiency progression spanning lower-canopy onset, detached fan-leaf severity, canopy distribution, fan-leaf senescence, stem color, and beginning sugar-leaf chlorosis.

In the calcium-withheld treatment, lower fan leaves developed interveinal spots with yellow rings and necrotic brown centers in week three; by week four symptoms occupied mostly the lower two-thirds and were concentrated near leaflet margins and tips.

By week five, spots coalesced into irregular marginal necrosis, serration points browned, injury moved upward into younger fan and sugar leaves, and upper fan-leaf tips curled upward; by week six most fan and sugar leaves were affected.

The flowering-stage lower-leaf onset differed markedly from the vegetative-stage T1 study and from the usual expectation for an immobile nutrient; lower-canopy foliage also contained almost three times the calcium of upper-canopy foliage at symptom onset.

Calcium-withheld plants averaged 621 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls under this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; those values do not establish a universal yield-loss estimate.
Figure 5 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel Cannabis calcium-deficiency progression from week-three spotting through widespread marginal necrosis and upward curling in week six.

Despite foliar iron concentrations less than half those of controls, iron-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants showed no visible deficiency symptoms and no significant aboveground biomass reduction by the end of the 7.5-week treatment.

The symptom-negative flowering result came from three plants in one cultivar and one deep-water-culture experiment; it demonstrates that absence of a visible syndrome cannot exclude inadequate iron status, not that flowering Cannabis never shows iron-deficiency symptoms.

In sulfur-withheld flowering Gelato 29, recently developed upper sugar leaves yellowed in week four; by week five upper fan leaves angled upward and lower fan leaves developed interveinal chlorosis from midrib to margins, later progressing through fan leaves to total yellowing and senescence while early sugar-leaf chlorosis changed little except for browned tips and marginal teeth.

Sulfur-withheld foliage had substantially lower sulfur than all other treatments, with no significant upper-versus-lower canopy concentration difference; inflorescence yield was 34% lower than control while vegetative biomass, root biomass, and cannabinoid concentrations showed no major effect in the three-plant treatment.

Figure 7 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel sulfur-deficiency progression showing younger sugar-leaf yellowing, upward-angled upper fan leaves, a fan-leaf chlorosis sequence, and the later whole-plant distribution.

The flowering study contrasted with the vegetative T1 study in first described canopy location and progression direction, and cautioned that late-flower nutrient symptomology can be confounded with natural foliar senescence.

No visually obvious manganese-deficiency signs developed in the manganese-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants; at week seven their apical inflorescences were similar to controls in size, shape, and color, and the treatment did not reduce biomass or cannabinoid concentrations.

At harvest, manganese-withheld upper-canopy foliage was extremely low in manganese relative to lower-canopy foliage and other treatments, yet the plants remained visually similar to controls, so a symptom-negative image cannot exclude low manganese status.

The authors state that nutrient diagnosis should integrate fertilizer and leachate composition, symptomology, and strategically timed and positioned foliar analysis because cultivar, environment, maturity, and sample location affect tissue concentrations.

Figure 9 is a CC BY 4.0 side-by-side comparison of manganese-withheld and control apical inflorescences during week seven; it is a controlled symptom-negative reference rather than a visible-deficiency example.

Magnesium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for three weeks; mild interveinal chlorosis began on lower fan leaves in week four between the midrib and margins, then rapidly predominated on smaller, younger fan leaves while older fan leaves and inflorescence sugar leaves were less affected.

Severely affected flowering leaves developed interveinal necrosis that increased from leaflet bases toward tips; by week five symptoms were widespread except at apical inflorescences, and by week six most smaller fan leaves and sugar leaves were yellow except at the midrib and extreme margins while some older fan leaves remained largely unaffected.

At symptom onset, lower-canopy foliage in the magnesium-withheld treatment contained about one-third the magnesium of upper-canopy foliage; the treatment averaged 748 g fresh inflorescence mass versus 1110 g in controls, approximately 30% lower in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment, while cannabinoid concentrations were not significantly affected.

Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel flowering-stage magnesium-deficiency progression spanning the first mild lower-fan-leaf chlorosis, whole-plant distribution, detached-leaf severity, inflorescence context, and advanced whole-plant symptoms.

Potassium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for two weeks; in week three, larger sugar leaves developed dark-brown lesions around secondary branch veins, while lower fan leaves developed lighter browning at leaflet tips and marginal teeth one week later.

By week five both potassium-deficiency pathways appeared on the same plant: sugar-leaf lesions predominated near the top and fan-leaf injury was strongest in the middle third, with light-brown fan-leaf injury moving inward especially through interveinal tissue.

By week six, green tissue was largely limited to inflorescences, sugar-leaf midribs, and some lower fan leaves; by week seven most non-inflorescence leaves were brown, curled, and dry, and some inflorescence leaves developed tip browning.

Potassium-withheld plants averaged 535 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls and had the second-lowest root dry mass in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; higher THCA concentration did not offset the lower plant-level yield.
Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage potassium-deficiency progression showing distinct sugar-leaf and fan-leaf symptoms at week four and their middle-canopy distribution by week five.

media.alt: Four-panel flowering Cannabis nitrogen-deficiency progression showing lower-canopy fan-leaf onset, detached-leaf severity, lower-two-thirds canopy chlorosis, fan-leaf senescence, stem color change, and initial sugar-leaf chlorosis
media.caption: Controlled flowering Gelato 29 nitrogen-withholding composite. Panels document week-three lower fan-leaf onset, week-four leaf and canopy progression, and week-five fan-leaf senescence with stem and early sugar-leaf involvement.
media.creator: David Llewellyn, Scott Golem, A. Maxwell P. Jones, and Youbin Zheng
media.requiredAttribution: Llewellyn D, Golem S, Jones AMP, Zheng Y (2023), Plants 12(3):422, Figure 2, CC BY 4.0; link the source and license and indicate modifications.
useLimitations: One cultivar, three plants per treatment, flowering-stage deep-water culture, and complete nitrogen withholding do not establish universal production symptoms, timing, yield effects, or tissue thresholds.

The four panels combine close-up, detached-leaf, canopy, stem, and inflorescence-context views from weeks three through five; every panel requires separate view, tissue, stage, and severity annotation.
Late-flower senescence, magnesium or sulfur status, root-zone dysfunction, and lighting must remain active confounders for yellow foliage.
Preserve source grouping across all panels and derivatives and do not split related observations across training and evaluation.
Reference display only until panels are bounded, individually annotated, scientifically reviewed, and assigned a leakage-safe dataset split.

name: Phosphorus deficiency
summary: A Cannabis nutrient disorder that, in one controlled T1-cultivar withholding study, began on lower and older leaves as irregular olive-green spotting with slight stunting and progressed to sunken wet-looking olive areas, marginal necrosis, yellowing, and large necrotic portions. The appearance is contextual and requires root-zone and tissue evidence.
affectedParts: petioles as an institutional context feature
roots and root zone for exclusion checks
stages: vegetative evidence from a transplant-onward withholding experiment
flowering as institutional field context; no universal timing established
indicators: Slight whole-plant stunting relative to matched healthy plants
Irregular olive-green spots begin along leaflets on lower and older leaves
Olive spots enlarge and appear sunken or almost wet
Some marginal necrosis develops as the olive spotting expands
Advanced older leaves show extensive olive spotting, yellowing, and large necrotic portions
Bluish-green foliage, purple petioles, or copper to purplish-brown lower-leaf blotches may occur in institutional hemp guidance but were not the defining sequence in the controlled T1 study
Serial images show an older-leaf-first distribution rather than isolated contact injury
exclusions: Uniform older-leaf yellowing without olive or sunken spotting and tissue analysis supports nitrogen deficiency
Older leaves show sharply interveinal chlorosis with green veins and measured context supports magnesium deficiency
Necrosis begins primarily at saw-tooth margins and progresses inward in the potassium-deficiency pattern
Discrete water-soaked lesions, halos, fungal structures, or a plant-diagnostic result supports a pathogen
Fine stippling, silver scars, webbing, fecal spots, mites, or thrips are found on magnified inspection
Damage maps to spray droplets, rubbing points, a lamp-facing surface, or another documented exposure and stops after the exposure ends
Roots are decayed or oxygen-stressed, or pH, EC, temperature, or water content is abnormal enough to explain impaired uptake
Tissue phosphorus is adequate for the cultivar, sampled organ, stage, and laboratory method, or another nutrient result explains the symptoms better

progression.description: Growth or yield can be affected before a reliable image label is available; establish a same-cultivar baseline and measure root-zone conditions rather than waiting for color alone.
After seven weeks of phosphorus withholding from transplant in Cannabis sativa T1, plants were slightly stunted and lower, older leaflets developed irregular olive-green spots.
Olive-green spots enlarged, became sunken and almost wet in appearance, and developed some marginal necrosis.
Yellowing older leaves became extensively olive-spotted, with large symptomatic areas and, in severe cases, large necrotic portions.
New growth and new-lesion rate are the useful response measures; established necrotic tissue will not return to a clean visual reference state.

lookAlikes: Cultivar anthocyanin or camera color shift
confirmation: Do not confirm phosphorus deficiency from purple color, olive spotting, one photograph, or one video; preserve the label as suspected until nutritional and root-zone evidence is linked to the photographed plant.

Capture serial whole-plant, lower-canopy, upper-canopy, symptomatic upper-surface, opposite-surface, lesion-margin, root, and root-zone views under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched healthy same-cultivar plant.

Record leaf node and physiological age, growth stage, cultivar, fertilizer phosphorus input, irrigation history, substrate or soil type, root-zone pH, EC, water content, temperature, drainage, and recent environmental or product changes.

Submit representative leaf tissue from the correct plant part to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory and interpret phosphorus concentration using a crop-, organ-, stage-, and method-appropriate reference; the controlled-study 0.09% value is not a universal cutoff.

Use substrate, solution, water, or soil testing appropriate to the production system to separate low phosphorus supply from high pH, salinity, cold, saturation, poor drainage, root injury, or nutrient antagonism.

Inspect both leaf surfaces and roots, and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when pathogens or arthropods remain plausible; a nutritional response after correction supports the differential but does not retroactively make the original image ground truth.
immediateActions: Mark the plant and preserve pre-treatment images, root-zone measurements, feed records, and representative tissue before changing nutrition.
Correct documented drainage, temperature, pH, EC, or root-health problems before assuming more phosphorus is required.
Avoid stacking phosphorus-rich products while the root-zone and tissue result are unknown.
correctivePlan: When testing supports inadequate phosphorus supply and roots are functional, restore balanced crop- and stage-appropriate nutrition gradually and follow current local agronomic guidance.
Track new leaf appearance, new-lesion rate, growth, root-zone measurements, and tissue results; do not judge correction by recovery of old necrotic leaves.
If phosphorus is adequate or symptoms continue, reopen nitrogen, magnesium, potassium, root disease, waterlogging, pest, pathogen, exposure, and normal-senescence differentials.
prevention: Use routine same-position tissue sampling and production-system-appropriate root-zone or soil testing before visible injury.
Keep input and drainage pH, EC, phosphorus concentration, temperature, water-content, and irrigation records linked to plant and image identifiers.
Avoid universal bloom-booster schedules: controlled Cannabis studies show phosphorus responses depend on cultivar, stage, system, and tested concentration range.
warnings: The primary visual sequence used one Cannabis sativa T1 cultivar in silica sand with phosphorus withheld from transplant; seven weeks, 0.09% tissue phosphorus, and the pictured colors are experiment-specific, not universal thresholds.
Purple petioles or leaves are not phosphorus-deficiency ground truth because genetics, temperature, maturation, lighting, and camera rendering can produce similar color.
Adding phosphorus cannot correct root hypoxia, root disease, unsuitable pH, cold roots, or high salinity and may worsen nutrient imbalance or environmental losses.
A high-THC flowering study found a cultivar- and system-specific quadratic phosphorus response; its solution concentrations must not be converted into a universal feed recipe.
The CC BY figure is a mixed nitrogen/phosphorus/calcium composite and remains excluded from automated training until panel-level crops, labels, and dataset splits are reviewed.
All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

sources.title: Nutrient Deficiencies
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: USU describes hemp phosphorus-deficiency context as slowed growth with bluish-green foliage, purple petioles, copper to purplish-brown lower-leaf blotches, contortion or downward curl, and bronze or purple necrosis in heavily affected leaves.

USU states that high-pH soil above 7, cold soil, and clayey, poorly drained, soggy conditions can limit phosphorus uptake, so tissue appearance cannot distinguish inadequate supply from impaired root-zone availability.
The page recommends soil and nutrient analysis to guide amendments and states that excess phosphorus can resemble iron or zinc deficiency, supporting measurement before corrective fertilization.
The phosphorus photographs on the page have mixed USU and commercial-vendor credits and no explicit reuse license, so they are not admitted as verified media or ground truth.

USU describes hemp calcium-deficiency context as contorted or curled leaves, irregular yellow-brown spotting while intervening tissue remains green, slowed flower-bud development, and root-tip dieback, and states that excess water, salinity, or root damage can impair calcium transport.

The USU calcium page localizes pictured spotting to lower leaves, which is compatible with a flowering-stage hydroponic study but differs from the newly expanding growth sequence in the vegetative T1 study; canopy location alone is therefore not diagnostic.

sources.title: Optimisation of Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium for Soilless Production of Cannabis sativa in the Flowering Stage Using Response Surface Analysis
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Bevan et al.)
supportedClaims: A high-THC Cannabis cultivar grown in deep-water culture during flowering showed quadratic inflorescence-yield responses to nitrogen and phosphorus, with predicted optima near 194 mg per litre nitrogen and 59 mg per litre phosphorus under the tested conditions.

Inflorescence yield decreased markedly outside approximately 160–230 mg per litre nitrogen and 40–80 mg per litre phosphorus, demonstrating that flowering plants still respond materially to nutrient supply.
Those solution concentrations are experiment- and cultivar-specific and must not be converted into universal feed targets, tissue sufficiency ranges, or visual thresholds.

media.alt: Nine-panel Cannabis nutrient-deficiency figure with nitrogen, phosphorus, and calcium columns and initial, intermediate, and advanced rows
media.caption: Controlled-study composite. The center column shows phosphorus-withheld Cannabis sativa T1 progressing from lower-leaf olive spotting to enlarged sunken-looking spots with marginal necrosis and then extensive olive and necrotic areas. Nitrogen and calcium columns are separate classes.
media.creator: Paul Cockson, Hunter Landis, Turner Smith, Kristin Hicks, and Brian E. Whipker
media.requiredAttribution: Cockson P, Landis H, Smith T, Hicks K, Whipker BE (2019), Applied Sciences 9(20):4432, CC BY 4.0; link the source and license and indicate modifications.
useLimitations: Scientific reference only until the center phosphorus panels are separately cropped, bounded, and assigned a dataset split.
The composite contains three diagnosis classes: nitrogen in the left column, phosphorus in the center, and calcium in the right; do not train or infer one label from the full image.
One cultivar and withholding protocol do not establish universal symptom timing, colors, tissue thresholds, or production-system response.

name: Sulfur deficiency
summary: A sulfur-status disorder with controlled Cannabis evidence for pale new or growing-point tissue followed by broader chlorosis. Vegetative T1 first showed middle-canopy and leaflet-base yellowing, while flowering Gelato 29 began on upper sugar leaves before later interveinal chlorosis became most severe on lower fan leaves.
affectedParts: newly expanding leaves and localized growing points
middle-canopy foliage in the vegetative T1 sequence
upper fan leaves and leaf angle
lower fan leaves during later flowering progression
leaflet bases, midribs, margins, tips, and marginal teeth
roots and root zone for availability checks
whole plant for distribution and senescence comparison
stages: vegetative evidence from a transplant-onward withholding experiment
flowering weeks four onward in a deep-water-culture withholding experiment
late flowering where natural senescence is a major confounder
indicators: Slight general yellowing first emphasized in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases in vegetative T1
Yellowing intensifies at leaflet bases and on newly expanding leaves, with advanced tissue very pale around the midrib and base
Recently developed upper sugar leaves yellowed first during flowering week four in Gelato 29
Upper fan leaves developed a pronounced upward angle by flowering week five
Lower fan leaves then developed interveinal chlorosis extending from the midrib to the margins
Later fan-leaf chlorosis progressed toward total yellowing and senescence while the initial sugar-leaf chlorosis changed little except for browned tips and marginal teeth
Serial canopy mapping distinguishes movement through leaf classes from a single yellow leaf or static exposure artifact
exclusions: Uniform yellowing begins on the oldest lower fan leaves and progresses upward in a pattern better supported by nitrogen deficiency or late-cycle senescence
Older leaves show sharply interveinal chlorosis with green veins and tissue analysis supports magnesium deficiency
Young-leaf interveinal chlorosis and analytical evidence support iron, manganese, or zinc status more strongly
The upward leaf angle follows high light, heat, vapor-demand, irrigation, or root-zone changes and maps to exposure rather than nutrient treatment
Brown tips or marginal teeth follow high EC, fertilizer application, spray contact, or another documented exposure
Fine stippling, silver scars, webbing, mites, thrips, eggs, or fecal spots are present on magnified inspection
Discrete lesions, surface growth, vascular discoloration, root decay, or laboratory evidence supports a pathogen
Mosaic, vein clearing, distortion, brittle growth, or a molecular result supports a virus or viroid
Chlorosis follows a stable cultivar sector or camera, white-balance, grow-light, or exposure artifact
Root-zone pH, EC, temperature, oxygenation, saturation, or damaged roots explain impaired uptake better than inadequate sulfur supply

progression.description: After seven weeks of sulfur withholding from transplant, foliage became slightly yellow overall, especially in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases.
Basal yellowing intensified and became stronger on newly expanding leaves; advanced leaves became very pale, especially around midribs and leaflet bases.
In week four, recently developed upper sugar leaves showed general yellowing.
Upper fan leaves angled upward, while lower fan leaves developed interveinal chlorosis extending from midribs to margins.

Fan-leaf chlorosis spread and became most severe low in the canopy, progressing toward total yellowing and senescence; early sugar-leaf chlorosis remained comparatively stable except at tips and teeth.
Track subsequent leaves, growing points, leaf angle, new injury, and analytical values; old chlorotic or senescent leaves will not return to a clean visual reference.

lookAlikes: Waterlogging, root-zone hypoxia, or root disease
Light, heat, or high vapor-demand stress
Broad mite, spider mite, or thrips injury
Camera white-balance, exposure, or grow-light color shift
confirmation: Do not confirm sulfur deficiency from yellowing, interveinal chlorosis, upward leaf angle, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected label until root-zone and analytical evidence are linked to the photographed plant.

Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, growing points, sugar leaves, fan leaves of known node and physiological age, both leaf surfaces, roots, and inflorescences under neutral repeatable lighting with a healthy same-cultivar reference.

Record cultivar, stage and flowering week, sulfur concentration and sulfate-containing inputs, complete fertilizer recipe, source-water sulfur and alkalinity, irrigation history, substrate or solution type, and recent environmental or product changes.
Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content, temperature, drainage, and oxygenation as appropriate to the production system, and inspect washed roots before changing sulfur supply.

Submit correctly positioned upper- and lower-canopy leaf tissue plus appropriate solution, substrate, soil, or water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret sulfur with nitrogen, magnesium, iron, manganese, zinc, and competing nutrients using crop-, organ-, stage-, and method-appropriate references.
Inspect both leaf surfaces, growing points, and roots with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when arthropods, root disease, viruses, viroids, or other pathogens remain plausible.
Treat response of subsequent growth as supporting evidence only; improvement after correcting a documented cause does not retroactively make the original image ground-truth sulfur deficiency.
immediateActions: Mark the plant and preserve pre-treatment serial images, fertilizer and irrigation records, root-zone measurements, and representative upper- and lower-canopy tissue before changing nutrition.
Correct documented pH, salinity, saturation, temperature, oxygenation, or root-health problems before assuming sulfur concentration is inadequate.
Avoid adding sulfate or complete fertilizer from leaf color alone, particularly during late flowering when normal senescence and nitrogen status can closely overlap.
correctivePlan: When analytical and production records support inadequate sulfur supply or availability and roots are functional, restore a balanced crop- and system-appropriate sulfur program gradually under current local agronomic guidance.
Track subsequent foliage, growing points, leaf angle, new-lesion rate, root growth, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue results rather than recovery of old yellow leaves.
If sulfur status is adequate or the pattern continues, reopen nitrogen, senescence, magnesium, micronutrient, root disease, arthropod, pathogen, environmental, exposure, and genetic differentials.
prevention: Record sulfur and nitrogen concentrations, sulfate-bearing inputs, complete fertilizer composition, source-water chemistry, pH, EC, and irrigation conditions against plant and media identifiers.
Use routine same-position upper- and lower-canopy tissue sampling and production-system-appropriate root-zone or soil testing before visible injury.
Maintain healthy same-cultivar references and neutral-light serial imaging across growing points, sugar leaves, fan-leaf ages, canopy thirds, and flowering weeks.
warnings: The vegetative T1 seven-week onset, 0.11% most-recent-mature-leaf sulfur value, middle-canopy description, and base-to-tip sequence came from one cultivar in silica sand and are not universal thresholds.

The flowering Gelato 29 week-four onset, upper-sugar-leaf presentation, later lower-fan-leaf severity, and 34% inflorescence-yield difference came from three deep-water-culture plants per treatment and must not be generalized.
Controlled studies differed in first described canopy location and progression direction; canopy position alone is not sulfur-deficiency ground truth.
Nitrogen deficiency and natural late-flower senescence can closely overlap the yellowing sequence, while upward leaf angle can reflect environmental or water-status responses.

The CC BY figure contains four panels spanning different organs, views, and severity states; it remains excluded from automated training until panels are bounded, individually annotated, source-grouped, scientifically reviewed, and assigned a leakage-safe split.
All symptom-only and late-flower samples require human review and linked analytical evidence before ground-truth use.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Cannabis sativa T1 plants were grown in silica sand with a complete modified Hoagland solution or a solution withholding one nutrient, observed daily, photographed through initial, intermediate, and advanced symptoms, and sampled at first symptom expression for most-recent-mature-leaf tissue analysis.

Nitrogen-withheld plants developed symptoms after six weeks: slight stunting and lower-foliage paling progressed upward into middle foliage, then affected leaves became fully yellow, necrotic, and abscised.

At first symptom expression, nitrogen-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.62% nitrogen dry weight compared with 4.28% in controls, and treated plants produced 50% less dry biomass under the experiment conditions.
Only the left column of Figure 2 represents nitrogen deficiency; the center and right columns are phosphorus and calcium deficiency and must retain separate labels.
The one-cultivar, silica-sand, complete-withholding experiment does not establish universal onset timing, tissue thresholds, production symptoms, or response to partial nitrogen limitation.

Phosphorus-withheld plants first showed slight stunting and irregular olive-green spots on lower and older leaflets after seven weeks; spots enlarged, appeared sunken and almost wet, developed some marginal necrosis, and advanced to extensive olive spotting and large necrotic portions.

At first phosphorus-deficiency symptom expression, phosphorus-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.09% phosphorus dry weight compared with 0.43% in controls, a 79% difference under the experiment conditions.

The study used one cultivar, began nutrient withholding at transplant, and reported no statistically significant biomass difference for phosphorus-withheld plants at the symptom-onset harvest, so its timing, tissue value, and appearance are not universal diagnostic thresholds.
Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced nitrogen-, phosphorus-, and calcium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1.

In calcium-withheld T1 plants, symptoms appeared after five weeks as slight stunting and irregular growing tips and newly expanding leaves; leaflet bases stayed narrow and paler than tips, then basal and interveinal chlorosis, marginal necrosis, distorted geometry, growing-tip death, and axillary branching developed.

At first calcium-deficiency symptom expression, most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.39% calcium dry weight compared with 3.73% in controls, but the one-cultivar silica-sand withholding experiment does not establish a universal tissue threshold or field sequence.

Iron-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks: slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases, progressed to interveinal chlorosis on growing-tip and newly expanding leaves and spread through the upper half while middle and lower foliage remained healthy dark green.

At first iron-deficiency symptom expression, iron-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 60.08 mg/kg iron compared with 111.75 mg/kg in controls, 46% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.
Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 composite with initial, intermediate, and advanced iron-deficiency images in its left column and zinc-deficiency images in its right column.

Manganese-withheld T1 plants developed bright-yellow netted interveinal chlorosis on upper and central foliage after six weeks; the netting began near leaflet midribs, spread toward margins, retained green veins, and later developed small tan necrotic regions.

At first manganese-deficiency symptom expression, manganese-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 7.56 mg/kg manganese compared with 29.40 mg/kg in controls, 74% lower under the experiment conditions; dry biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

The control manganese concentration was itself below the cited general crop survey range, and the study used one cultivar in silica sand with complete withholding, so neither treatment value is a universal Cannabis diagnostic threshold.

Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced manganese-, boron-, and copper-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its left column represents manganese deficiency.

Copper-withheld T1 plants first developed visible symptoms after nine weeks, beginning with slight whole-plant stunting and mild distortion of newer and expanding leaves, especially narrowed and slightly yellow leaflet bases.

As copper-withholding symptoms advanced, basal narrowing and distortion intensified, marginal interveinal chlorosis developed, and the whole leaf progressed to fine interveinal chlorosis with slightly inward- and downward-curled margins and reduced turgidity.

At first copper-deficiency symptom expression, copper-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.41 mg/kg copper compared with 4.65 mg/kg in controls, 70% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 45% less biomass.

The control copper concentration of 4.65 mg/kg was itself slightly below the general crop survey range cited by the authors, and the one-cultivar complete-withholding result does not establish a universal Cannabis threshold.

The published Figure 4 caption and column labels identify initial, intermediate, and advanced copper-deficiency panels in the right column, although the copper subsection text cites Figure 5; Figure 5 is captioned as manganese- and boron-toxicity progression, so this source-level numbering inconsistency must remain attached to copper panel review.

Magnesium-withheld T1 plants first developed slight interveinal yellowing on lower and older foliage after seven weeks; the contrast between green veins and yellow interveinal tissue intensified and some regions became necrotic.

At first magnesium-deficiency symptom expression, magnesium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.12% magnesium compared with 0.61% in controls, 80% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced sulfur-, magnesium-, and potassium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its center column represents magnesium deficiency.

Potassium-withheld T1 plants first developed yellowing at leaflet margins and saw-tooth serrations on lower and older foliage after nine weeks; yellowing intensified and moved inward toward the midrib, followed by tan necrosis concentrated along serrated margins.

At first potassium-deficiency symptom expression, potassium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.41% potassium compared with 2.85% in controls, 86% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 27% less biomass.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite whose right column shows initial, intermediate, and advanced potassium-deficiency phenotypes; the sulfur and magnesium columns are separate diagnoses and the asset is indexed once under the magnesium record to avoid duplicate media hashes.

Zinc-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks as marginal yellowing on newer and expanding leaves, concentrated along leaflet margins and toothed portions; tan, irregularly shaped marginal necrosis developed as the disorder progressed.

At first zinc-deficiency symptom expression, zinc-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 10.70 mg/kg zinc compared with 25.33 mg/kg in controls, 58% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

Sulfur-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after seven weeks as slight overall yellowing, especially in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases; yellowing intensified at leaflet bases and on newly expanding leaves, then advanced to very pale yellow tissue around the midrib and leaflet bases.

At first sulfur-deficiency symptom expression, sulfur-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.11% sulfur compared with 0.41% in controls, 73% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

sources.title: Foliar Symptomology, Nutrient Content, Yield, and Secondary Metabolite Variability of Cannabis Grown Hydroponically with Different Single-Element Nutrient Deficiencies
supportedClaims: Three Gelato 29 plants per treatment were grown in aerated deep-water culture; single-element withholding began with the switch to a 12-hour flowering photoperiod, plants were examined daily and photographed weekly, and upper- and lower-canopy foliage was laboratory analyzed at symptom onset.
Nitrogen-withheld plants showed reduced vegetative expansion before foliar symptoms; during week three, very slight yellowing began at leaflet tips of lower-canopy fan leaves.

By week four, most fan leaves in the lower two-thirds were yellowing; chlorosis was initially strongest between veins before broad whole-leaf yellowing, and severity within leaflets progressed from base toward tip.

By week five, nearly all fan leaves were yellow with severity increasing from bottom to top; petioles became red-brown, some fan leaves browned and senesced, stems began yellowing, and sugar-leaf chlorosis began.

By weeks six and seven, most fan leaves had senesced, older and lower-position sugar leaves progressively yellowed or browned, and stems became brown; the authors considered this prolonged severe endpoint commercially damaging.

At symptom onset, upper- and lower-canopy foliar nitrogen concentrations did not differ and overlapped the control and other treatments, illustrating limitations of a single tissue analysis later in production.

Healthy control plants developed lower-fan-leaf chlorosis in weeks six through eight despite adequate nutrient solution and foliar concentrations, demonstrating that natural late-flower senescence can visually confound nitrogen deficiency.

Nitrogen-withheld plants had 73% less aboveground vegetative fresh mass and approximately 72% less fresh inflorescence mass than controls under this three-plant treatment; these are experiment-specific loss estimates, not universal predictions.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage nitrogen-deficiency progression spanning lower-canopy onset, detached fan-leaf severity, canopy distribution, fan-leaf senescence, stem color, and beginning sugar-leaf chlorosis.

In the calcium-withheld treatment, lower fan leaves developed interveinal spots with yellow rings and necrotic brown centers in week three; by week four symptoms occupied mostly the lower two-thirds and were concentrated near leaflet margins and tips.

By week five, spots coalesced into irregular marginal necrosis, serration points browned, injury moved upward into younger fan and sugar leaves, and upper fan-leaf tips curled upward; by week six most fan and sugar leaves were affected.

The flowering-stage lower-leaf onset differed markedly from the vegetative-stage T1 study and from the usual expectation for an immobile nutrient; lower-canopy foliage also contained almost three times the calcium of upper-canopy foliage at symptom onset.

Calcium-withheld plants averaged 621 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls under this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; those values do not establish a universal yield-loss estimate.
Figure 5 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel Cannabis calcium-deficiency progression from week-three spotting through widespread marginal necrosis and upward curling in week six.

Despite foliar iron concentrations less than half those of controls, iron-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants showed no visible deficiency symptoms and no significant aboveground biomass reduction by the end of the 7.5-week treatment.

The symptom-negative flowering result came from three plants in one cultivar and one deep-water-culture experiment; it demonstrates that absence of a visible syndrome cannot exclude inadequate iron status, not that flowering Cannabis never shows iron-deficiency symptoms.

In sulfur-withheld flowering Gelato 29, recently developed upper sugar leaves yellowed in week four; by week five upper fan leaves angled upward and lower fan leaves developed interveinal chlorosis from midrib to margins, later progressing through fan leaves to total yellowing and senescence while early sugar-leaf chlorosis changed little except for browned tips and marginal teeth.

Sulfur-withheld foliage had substantially lower sulfur than all other treatments, with no significant upper-versus-lower canopy concentration difference; inflorescence yield was 34% lower than control while vegetative biomass, root biomass, and cannabinoid concentrations showed no major effect in the three-plant treatment.

Figure 7 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel sulfur-deficiency progression showing younger sugar-leaf yellowing, upward-angled upper fan leaves, a fan-leaf chlorosis sequence, and the later whole-plant distribution.

The flowering study contrasted with the vegetative T1 study in first described canopy location and progression direction, and cautioned that late-flower nutrient symptomology can be confounded with natural foliar senescence.

No visually obvious manganese-deficiency signs developed in the manganese-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants; at week seven their apical inflorescences were similar to controls in size, shape, and color, and the treatment did not reduce biomass or cannabinoid concentrations.

At harvest, manganese-withheld upper-canopy foliage was extremely low in manganese relative to lower-canopy foliage and other treatments, yet the plants remained visually similar to controls, so a symptom-negative image cannot exclude low manganese status.

The authors state that nutrient diagnosis should integrate fertilizer and leachate composition, symptomology, and strategically timed and positioned foliar analysis because cultivar, environment, maturity, and sample location affect tissue concentrations.

Figure 9 is a CC BY 4.0 side-by-side comparison of manganese-withheld and control apical inflorescences during week seven; it is a controlled symptom-negative reference rather than a visible-deficiency example.

Magnesium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for three weeks; mild interveinal chlorosis began on lower fan leaves in week four between the midrib and margins, then rapidly predominated on smaller, younger fan leaves while older fan leaves and inflorescence sugar leaves were less affected.

Severely affected flowering leaves developed interveinal necrosis that increased from leaflet bases toward tips; by week five symptoms were widespread except at apical inflorescences, and by week six most smaller fan leaves and sugar leaves were yellow except at the midrib and extreme margins while some older fan leaves remained largely unaffected.

At symptom onset, lower-canopy foliage in the magnesium-withheld treatment contained about one-third the magnesium of upper-canopy foliage; the treatment averaged 748 g fresh inflorescence mass versus 1110 g in controls, approximately 30% lower in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment, while cannabinoid concentrations were not significantly affected.

Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel flowering-stage magnesium-deficiency progression spanning the first mild lower-fan-leaf chlorosis, whole-plant distribution, detached-leaf severity, inflorescence context, and advanced whole-plant symptoms.

Potassium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for two weeks; in week three, larger sugar leaves developed dark-brown lesions around secondary branch veins, while lower fan leaves developed lighter browning at leaflet tips and marginal teeth one week later.

By week five both potassium-deficiency pathways appeared on the same plant: sugar-leaf lesions predominated near the top and fan-leaf injury was strongest in the middle third, with light-brown fan-leaf injury moving inward especially through interveinal tissue.

By week six, green tissue was largely limited to inflorescences, sugar-leaf midribs, and some lower fan leaves; by week seven most non-inflorescence leaves were brown, curled, and dry, and some inflorescence leaves developed tip browning.

Potassium-withheld plants averaged 535 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls and had the second-lowest root dry mass in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; higher THCA concentration did not offset the lower plant-level yield.
Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage potassium-deficiency progression showing distinct sugar-leaf and fan-leaf symptoms at week four and their middle-canopy distribution by week five.

media.alt: Four-panel flowering Cannabis sulfur-deficiency progression showing upper sugar-leaf yellowing, upward-angled upper fan leaves, fan-leaf interveinal chlorosis, and later whole-plant distribution
media.caption: Controlled flowering-stage sulfur-withholding composite: younger sugar leaves yellow first, upper fan leaves angle upward, fan-leaf interveinal chlorosis advances, and later injury is most severe on lower fan leaves.
media.creator: David Llewellyn, Scott Golem, A. Maxwell P. Jones, and Youbin Zheng
media.requiredAttribution: Llewellyn D, Golem S, Jones AMP, Zheng Y (2023), Plants 12(3):422, Figure 7, CC BY 4.0; link the source and license and indicate modifications.
useLimitations: One cultivar, three plants per treatment, flowering-stage deep-water culture, and complete sulfur withholding do not establish universal field symptoms, timing, or yield effects.

The four panels span sugar leaves, upper-canopy fan-leaf angle, a detached fan-leaf severity sequence, and whole-plant distribution; each requires its own view, tissue, stage, and severity annotation.
Natural late-flower senescence and nitrogen deficiency can overlap the later yellowing, so source treatment and analytical linkage must remain attached to every derivative.
Reference display only until panels are bounded, individually annotated, scientifically reviewed, source-grouped, and assigned a leakage-safe dataset split.

name: Zinc deficiency / low-zinc treatment response
summary: Low zinc produced two different controlled Cannabis presentations: marginal yellowing and necrosis on newer foliage in vegetative T1, and young-leaf mottled interveinal chlorosis with restricted flowering growth in Annapurna. The latter study found a major phosphorus interaction and cautioned that its visible leaf symptom may not be directly zinc-specific.
affectedParts: roots and root zone for availability checks
stages: vegetative evidence from a transplant-onward withholding experiment
vegetative-to-flowering evidence from a five-concentration dose-response experiment
indicators: Marginal yellowing begins on newer and expanding leaves in the controlled T1 withholding sequence
Yellowing is concentrated along leaflet margins and toothed portions before tan, irregular marginal necrosis develops
A separate low-zinc treatment produced mottled interveinal chlorosis on young leaves
Shorter plants with unchanged main-stem node count indicate reduced internode elongation in the Annapurna experiment
Reduced elongation rate and smaller stem diameter provide longitudinal and morphological context beyond leaf color
Yield reduction can occur without a visible leaf syndrome: the 0.1 mg/L Annapurna treatment reduced inflorescence yield but visible chlorosis was reported only at 0.05 mg/L
exclusions: New-leaf interveinal chlorosis is better supported by iron or manganese results after properly positioned tissue analysis
Older leaves are affected first with interveinal chlorosis, favoring magnesium rather than the controlled zinc sequences
Uniform whole-plant or older-leaf yellowing supports nitrogen shortage or late-cycle senescence more strongly
High leaf phosphorus or a documented phosphorus imbalance could explain the mottled chlorosis seen under low zinc
Necrosis is limited to leaf tips after a high-zinc input, matching the controlled excess-zinc response rather than deficiency
Damage maps to lamp-facing tissue, a heat or light event, spray droplets, residue, rubbing points, or another documented exposure
Fine stippling, silver scars, webbing, eggs, mites, thrips, or fecal spots are found on magnified inspection
Mosaic, distortion, vein clearing, brittle growth, or laboratory evidence supports a virus, viroid, or other pathogen
Root decay, saturation, hypoxia, abnormal temperature, salinity, pH, or irrigation history better explains impaired uptake
Short stature or sectoring is stable within the cultivar and lacks progressive leaf symptoms or analytical evidence of low zinc

progression.description: In flowering Annapurna, 0.1 mg/L zinc reduced inflorescence yield without reported visible chlorosis, so a normal-looking canopy does not exclude a low-zinc treatment response.
After nine weeks of zinc withholding from transplant, newer and expanding leaves developed marginal yellowing concentrated along leaflet edges and toothed portions.
Yellow marginal areas became tan, irregularly shaped necrotic regions along leaflet margins.
At 0.05 mg/L zinc, young leaves were mottled and interveinally chlorotic; elongation slowed by day 29, and plants finished shorter with thinner stems but unchanged node count.
Track subsequent leaf expansion, internode elongation, stem growth, new-lesion rate, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue values; old necrotic tissue will not become a clean reference.

lookAlikes: Nitrogen deficiency or normal late-flower senescence
Waterlogging, root-zone hypoxia, or root disease
Zinc toxicity or nonspecific fertilizer tip burn
Broad mite, spider mite, or thrips injury
Camera white-balance, exposure, or grow-light color shift
confirmation: Keep image- and video-only labels low confidence: newer-leaf chlorosis, marginal necrosis, short internodes, and a visually normal canopy can neither confirm nor exclude low zinc.

Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, new and mature leaves on both surfaces, internodes with scale, roots, and inflorescences under neutral repeatable lighting with a healthy same-cultivar reference.

Record cultivar, stage, zinc concentration and formulation or chelate, phosphorus and complete fertilizer inputs, source-water chemistry, irrigation history, substrate or solution type, and recent environmental or product changes.
Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content, temperature, drainage, and oxygenation as appropriate to the production system, and inspect washed roots before changing zinc supply.

Submit correctly positioned leaf tissue plus appropriate solution, substrate, soil, or water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret zinc together with phosphorus, iron, manganese, copper, sulfur, and other nutrients using crop-, organ-, stage-, and method-appropriate references.
Inspect both leaf surfaces and growing tips with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when arthropods, root disease, viruses, viroids, or other pathogens remain plausible.
Treat response of subsequent growth as supporting evidence only; improvement after correcting a documented cause does not retroactively turn the original image into zinc-deficiency ground truth.
immediateActions: Mark the plant and preserve pre-treatment serial images, feed and irrigation records, root-zone measurements, growth measurements, and representative tissue before changing nutrition.
Correct documented pH, salinity, saturation, temperature, oxygenation, or root-health problems before assuming zinc concentration is inadequate.
Avoid adding zinc or reducing phosphorus from appearance alone because the controlled Cannabis evidence includes a zinc-phosphorus interaction and non-specific visual outcomes.
correctivePlan: When analytical and production records support inadequate zinc supply or availability and roots are functional, restore a balanced crop- and system-appropriate micronutrient program gradually under current local agronomic guidance.
Track subsequent leaves, internode elongation, stem diameter, root growth, yield trajectory, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue results.
If zinc status is adequate or the pattern continues, reopen phosphorus, iron, manganese, sulfur, magnesium, root disease, arthropod, pathogen, environmental, exposure, and genetic differentials.
prevention: Record zinc and phosphorus concentrations, chelates or formulations, complete fertilizer composition, source-water chemistry, pH, EC, and irrigation conditions against plant and media identifiers.
Use routine same-position tissue sampling and production-system-appropriate root-zone or soil testing before visible injury.
Maintain healthy same-cultivar references and neutral-light serial imaging with repeatable whole-plant, leaf, internode, root, and inflorescence views.
warnings: The T1 nine-week onset, 10.70 mg/kg most-recent-mature-leaf zinc, and marginal sequence came from one cultivar in silica sand with zinc withheld from transplant and are not universal thresholds.

The Annapurna 0.05-0.1 mg/L supply levels, 14.7-23.5 mg/kg leaf values, growth effects, and maturity images came from one clonal cultivar in perlite and must not be generalized to other cultivars, media, water chemistry, chelates, or stages.

The 2026 study authors explicitly stated that high leaf phosphorus may have caused the visible mottling at 0.05 mg/L zinc; the pictured chlorosis is a treatment-associated observation, not mechanism-specific visual ground truth.
The 0.1 mg/L treatment reduced inflorescence yield without reported visible chlorosis, so symptom absence cannot exclude a low-zinc treatment response.

The CC BY dose-response figure contains five zinc levels, multiple organs and views, both suspected deficiency and excess tip injury, and a mechanistically uncertain chlorosis label; it is excluded from automated training pending panel-level annotation and human review.
All symptom-only, symptom-negative, and growth-only samples require human review and linked analytical evidence before ground-truth use.
