The published Figure 4 caption and column labels identify initial, intermediate, and advanced copper-deficiency panels in the right column, although the copper subsection text cites Figure 5; Figure 5 is captioned as manganese- and boron-toxicity progression, so this source-level numbering inconsistency must remain attached to copper panel review.

Magnesium-withheld T1 plants first developed slight interveinal yellowing on lower and older foliage after seven weeks; the contrast between green veins and yellow interveinal tissue intensified and some regions became necrotic.

At first magnesium-deficiency symptom expression, magnesium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.12% magnesium compared with 0.61% in controls, 80% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced sulfur-, magnesium-, and potassium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its center column represents magnesium deficiency.

Potassium-withheld T1 plants first developed yellowing at leaflet margins and saw-tooth serrations on lower and older foliage after nine weeks; yellowing intensified and moved inward toward the midrib, followed by tan necrosis concentrated along serrated margins.

At first potassium-deficiency symptom expression, potassium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.41% potassium compared with 2.85% in controls, 86% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 27% less biomass.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite whose right column shows initial, intermediate, and advanced potassium-deficiency phenotypes; the sulfur and magnesium columns are separate diagnoses and the asset is indexed once under the magnesium record to avoid duplicate media hashes.

Zinc-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks as marginal yellowing on newer and expanding leaves, concentrated along leaflet margins and toothed portions; tan, irregularly shaped marginal necrosis developed as the disorder progressed.

At first zinc-deficiency symptom expression, zinc-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 10.70 mg/kg zinc compared with 25.33 mg/kg in controls, 58% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

Sulfur-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after seven weeks as slight overall yellowing, especially in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases; yellowing intensified at leaflet bases and on newly expanding leaves, then advanced to very pale yellow tissue around the midrib and leaflet bases.

At first sulfur-deficiency symptom expression, sulfur-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.11% sulfur compared with 0.41% in controls, 73% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

sources.title: The power of zinc: excess and deficiency of Zn decrease cannabinoids in cannabis without Zn toxicity concerns to consumers
sources.organization: Journal of Cannabis Research (Shiponi and Bernstein)
supportedClaims: Six clonal Annapurna plants per treatment were grown in perlite at five Zn-EDTA concentrations (0.05, 0.1, 0.35, 1, and 4 mg/L); treatments ran for 71 days, including 57 days under a flowering photoperiod, with fertigation adjusted to pH 6.0 and treatment concentrations analytically checked.

At 0.05 mg/L zinc, young leaves showed mottled interveinal chlorosis, plants were shorter, elongation rate was repressed by day 29, stems were thinner, and total biomass was lower; inflorescence yield was reduced in the 0.05-0.1 mg/L range while main-stem node count was unchanged.
Leaves contained 14.7 and 23.5 mg/kg dry-weight zinc at 0.05 and 0.1 mg/L supply, respectively, and yield was reduced at both concentrations, but visible chlorosis was reported only at 0.05 mg/L.

The authors found leaf phosphorus reached 15.6 mg/g at 0.05 mg/L zinc and explicitly cautioned that the visible leaf symptoms may represent phosphorus toxicity rather than a direct zinc-deficiency symptom; the image label is therefore mechanistically uncertain.

Figure 1 is a CC BY 4.0 maturity-stage composite comparing whole plants, youngest fully developed leaves, roots, and apical inflorescences across all five zinc-supply treatments; it also contains high-zinc tip necrosis and must not receive a single whole-image deficiency label.

media.alt: Five-column controlled Cannabis zinc dose-response composite comparing whole plants, young leaves, roots, and inflorescences at 0.05 through 4 milligrams per liter zinc
media.caption: Maturity-stage Annapurna dose response. Columns compare 0.05, 0.1, 0.35, 1, and 4 mg/L zinc; rows show whole plants, youngest fully developed leaves, roots, and apical inflorescences. Low-zinc leaf mottling may be phosphorus-mediated, while the highest-zinc column includes tip necrosis.
media.creator: Sivan Shiponi and Nirit Bernstein
media.requiredAttribution: Shiponi S and Bernstein N (2026), Journal of Cannabis Research 8:33, Figure 1, CC BY 4.0; link the article and license and indicate modifications.
useLimitations: One clonal cultivar, perlite culture, Zn-EDTA, fixed nutrient recipe, and maturity-stage imaging do not establish universal symptoms, thresholds, or timing.
The five columns are distinct zinc treatments and the rows are distinct organs or views; whole-image classification and random panel splitting are invalid.

The 0.05 mg/L chlorosis may reflect phosphorus toxicity associated with low zinc, while the 4 mg/L column contains excess-zinc tip injury; both require separate labels and mechanistic uncertainty metadata.
Reference display only until panels are bounded, dose-, organ-, and diagnosis-annotated, scientifically reviewed, and assigned a leakage-safe dataset split.

name: Boron toxicity
summary: A Cannabis micronutrient toxicity that begins as older- or lower-leaf marginal chlorosis and advances inward to brown or bronze necrosis. Controlled trials link this pattern to elevated boron exposure and leaf-tissue boron, but marginal burn is nonspecific and requires water, input, root-zone, and tissue confirmation.
affectedParts: lower and older fan leaves in the published T1 sequence
upper and lower fan leaves in a separate White Shark trial
interior leaf tissue as injury advances inward
roots, source water, and root zone for causal checks
stages: chronic exposure across multiple growth stages
indicators: Marginal yellowing begins on lower or older fan leaves in the controlled T1 sequence
Yellowing follows the leaflet edge and advances inward toward the midrib
Affected margins turn brown or bronze and become necrotic
Severely chlorotic or necrotic leaves can abscise
A separate three-plant-per-treatment White Shark trial observed margin chlorosis within three weeks, rapidly followed by bronze necrosis on both upper and lower leaves
In a widespread exposure, comparable marginal injury appears across many leaves rather than at one contact point
Elevated boron is documented in representative leaf tissue and a plausible source is identified in nutrient solution, source water, soil, substrate, or amendment
exclusions: Yellowing and necrosis are restricted to the hottest or brightest canopy edge and measured leaf temperature or light exposure explains the pattern
Marginal injury follows a spray, foliar product, fan abrasion, or contact event and stops when the exposure ends
Root-zone EC is high with broad multi-ion tip burn and tissue boron is not elevated
Older leaves show potassium-type saw-tooth marginal yellowing or necrosis and potassium/root-zone evidence explains the pattern better
Margins are damaged but webbing, mites, thrips, fecal spots, chewing, or frass are confirmed
Discrete lesions, halos, fungal structures, or laboratory pathogen results support infectious disease
Cold, waterlogging, drought, unsuitable pH, or root decay is documented and tissue or water analysis does not support excess boron
Purple, bronze, or yellow color is produced only by cultivar pigmentation, senescence, lighting, white balance, or compression artifact

progression.description: Boron accumulates from a source such as nutrient solution, water, substrate, soil, amendment, or calculation error; a photograph alone cannot distinguish it from salinity, potassium disorder, or contact injury.
Lower or older leaflet margins become yellow in the T1 study. In the White Shark DWC trial, marginal chlorosis was visible within three weeks of the 0.05 mM boron treatment.
Marginal chlorosis intensifies and moves inward; tan, brown, or bronze necrosis develops along tips and serrated margins.
Leaf margins become broadly necrotic, remaining tissue can be severely chlorotic, and some affected leaves may abscise.
Use new-lesion rate, new leaf quality, water and root-zone testing, and follow-up tissue boron to assess response; existing necrotic margins will not recover.

lookAlikes: Cultivar pigmentation or camera color artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm boron toxicity from marginal burn, bronze color, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected-toxicity label until elevated boron and a plausible exposure source are linked to the photographed plant.

Capture serial whole-plant, upper- and lower-canopy, leaf upper-surface, leaf underside, margin close-up, root, and root-zone views under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched healthy same-cultivar plant.

Record leaf node and physiological age, cultivar, stage, fertilizer and amendment formulations, mixing calculations, source-water history, irrigation and drainage, root-zone pH, EC, water content, and temperature.

Submit representative leaf tissue from a defined node and maturity class to an agricultural laboratory; interpret boron with a Cannabis-, stage-, plant-part-, and method-appropriate reference rather than treating 671.75 mg per kg from the T1 experiment as a universal threshold.

Test source water, stock solutions, final nutrient solution, soil or substrate, and relevant amendments for boron and salinity; inspect dosing equipment and reverse-osmosis performance where applicable.

Inspect both leaf surfaces and roots and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when pests, foliar injury, or pathogens remain plausible; improvement after source correction supports but does not alone prove the original causal label.
immediateActions: Stop discretionary boron-containing additives while preserving product labels, batch records, solution samples, pre-treatment images, and representative tissue for testing.
Verify source-water, stock, final-solution, root-zone, and tissue results before flushing or changing the complete nutrient program.
Separate suspect plants from training-ground-truth collections until the exposure and laboratory evidence are linked.
correctivePlan: Remove or correct the verified boron source and restore a balanced crop- and stage-appropriate nutrient solution using current local agronomic guidance.
Correct documented salinity, drainage, irrigation, pH, temperature, or root-health problems without assuming that every burned margin was caused by boron.
Track new growth, new-lesion rate, water or solution boron, EC and pH, and follow-up tissue results; reopen differentials if the expected exposure-response relationship is absent.
prevention: Test source water periodically for boron and salinity, especially after treatment-system, well, or reverse-osmosis changes.
Use verified mixing calculations and calibrated dosing equipment for micronutrient concentrates; record lot, concentration, date, and plant group.
Keep same-cultivar healthy references and consistent leaf-node tissue-sampling procedures so changes in leaf age or genotype are not mistaken for toxicity.
warnings: The T1 study induced toxicity with tenfold boron in one silica-sand system; its seven-week timing and 671.75 mg per kg tissue value are experiment-specific, not universal thresholds.
The White Shark report used three clones per treatment in deep-water culture; its three-week onset and canopy-wide distribution require replication across cultivars and production systems.
Marginal chlorosis and necrosis are highly nonspecific and must not become image-only ground truth.
The two source trials did not justify a universal yield-loss estimate; severe-looking leaf injury did not correspond to a clear yield loss in the small White Shark trial.
The CC BY figure contains both manganese- and boron-toxicity columns and is excluded from automated training until panel-level crops, labels, and dataset splits are reviewed.
The Niagara College project captured weekly 360-degree videos, but no original asset URLs or reuse license are publicly exposed; none are admitted as video references.
All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Cannabis sativa T1 plants were grown in silica sand with a complete modified Hoagland solution or a solution withholding one nutrient, observed daily, photographed through initial, intermediate, and advanced symptoms, and sampled at first symptom expression for most-recent-mature-leaf tissue analysis.

Nitrogen-withheld plants developed symptoms after six weeks: slight stunting and lower-foliage paling progressed upward into middle foliage, then affected leaves became fully yellow, necrotic, and abscised.

At first symptom expression, nitrogen-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.62% nitrogen dry weight compared with 4.28% in controls, and treated plants produced 50% less dry biomass under the experiment conditions.
Only the left column of Figure 2 represents nitrogen deficiency; the center and right columns are phosphorus and calcium deficiency and must retain separate labels.
The one-cultivar, silica-sand, complete-withholding experiment does not establish universal onset timing, tissue thresholds, production symptoms, or response to partial nitrogen limitation.

Phosphorus-withheld plants first showed slight stunting and irregular olive-green spots on lower and older leaflets after seven weeks; spots enlarged, appeared sunken and almost wet, developed some marginal necrosis, and advanced to extensive olive spotting and large necrotic portions.

At first phosphorus-deficiency symptom expression, phosphorus-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.09% phosphorus dry weight compared with 0.43% in controls, a 79% difference under the experiment conditions.

The study used one cultivar, began nutrient withholding at transplant, and reported no statistically significant biomass difference for phosphorus-withheld plants at the symptom-onset harvest, so its timing, tissue value, and appearance are not universal diagnostic thresholds.
Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced nitrogen-, phosphorus-, and calcium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1.

In calcium-withheld T1 plants, symptoms appeared after five weeks as slight stunting and irregular growing tips and newly expanding leaves; leaflet bases stayed narrow and paler than tips, then basal and interveinal chlorosis, marginal necrosis, distorted geometry, growing-tip death, and axillary branching developed.

At first calcium-deficiency symptom expression, most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.39% calcium dry weight compared with 3.73% in controls, but the one-cultivar silica-sand withholding experiment does not establish a universal tissue threshold or field sequence.

Iron-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks: slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases, progressed to interveinal chlorosis on growing-tip and newly expanding leaves and spread through the upper half while middle and lower foliage remained healthy dark green.

At first iron-deficiency symptom expression, iron-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 60.08 mg/kg iron compared with 111.75 mg/kg in controls, 46% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.
Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 composite with initial, intermediate, and advanced iron-deficiency images in its left column and zinc-deficiency images in its right column.

Manganese-withheld T1 plants developed bright-yellow netted interveinal chlorosis on upper and central foliage after six weeks; the netting began near leaflet midribs, spread toward margins, retained green veins, and later developed small tan necrotic regions.

At first manganese-deficiency symptom expression, manganese-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 7.56 mg/kg manganese compared with 29.40 mg/kg in controls, 74% lower under the experiment conditions; dry biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

The control manganese concentration was itself below the cited general crop survey range, and the study used one cultivar in silica sand with complete withholding, so neither treatment value is a universal Cannabis diagnostic threshold.

Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced manganese-, boron-, and copper-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its left column represents manganese deficiency.

Copper-withheld T1 plants first developed visible symptoms after nine weeks, beginning with slight whole-plant stunting and mild distortion of newer and expanding leaves, especially narrowed and slightly yellow leaflet bases.

As copper-withholding symptoms advanced, basal narrowing and distortion intensified, marginal interveinal chlorosis developed, and the whole leaf progressed to fine interveinal chlorosis with slightly inward- and downward-curled margins and reduced turgidity.

At first copper-deficiency symptom expression, copper-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.41 mg/kg copper compared with 4.65 mg/kg in controls, 70% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 45% less biomass.

The control copper concentration of 4.65 mg/kg was itself slightly below the general crop survey range cited by the authors, and the one-cultivar complete-withholding result does not establish a universal Cannabis threshold.

The published Figure 4 caption and column labels identify initial, intermediate, and advanced copper-deficiency panels in the right column, although the copper subsection text cites Figure 5; Figure 5 is captioned as manganese- and boron-toxicity progression, so this source-level numbering inconsistency must remain attached to copper panel review.

Magnesium-withheld T1 plants first developed slight interveinal yellowing on lower and older foliage after seven weeks; the contrast between green veins and yellow interveinal tissue intensified and some regions became necrotic.

At first magnesium-deficiency symptom expression, magnesium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.12% magnesium compared with 0.61% in controls, 80% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced sulfur-, magnesium-, and potassium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its center column represents magnesium deficiency.

Potassium-withheld T1 plants first developed yellowing at leaflet margins and saw-tooth serrations on lower and older foliage after nine weeks; yellowing intensified and moved inward toward the midrib, followed by tan necrosis concentrated along serrated margins.

At first potassium-deficiency symptom expression, potassium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.41% potassium compared with 2.85% in controls, 86% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 27% less biomass.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite whose right column shows initial, intermediate, and advanced potassium-deficiency phenotypes; the sulfur and magnesium columns are separate diagnoses and the asset is indexed once under the magnesium record to avoid duplicate media hashes.

Zinc-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks as marginal yellowing on newer and expanding leaves, concentrated along leaflet margins and toothed portions; tan, irregularly shaped marginal necrosis developed as the disorder progressed.

At first zinc-deficiency symptom expression, zinc-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 10.70 mg/kg zinc compared with 25.33 mg/kg in controls, 58% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

Sulfur-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after seven weeks as slight overall yellowing, especially in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases; yellowing intensified at leaflet bases and on newly expanding leaves, then advanced to very pale yellow tissue around the midrib and leaflet bases.

At first sulfur-deficiency symptom expression, sulfur-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.11% sulfur compared with 0.41% in controls, 73% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

sources.title: Documentation of Boron Deficiency and Phytotoxicity in Cannabis sativa to Aid in Development of the GrowDoc Application
sources.organization: Horticultural & Environmental Sciences Innovation Centre, Niagara College
sources.publisher: Niagara College Horticultural & Environmental Sciences Innovation Centre
supportedClaims: Three White Shark Cannabis clones per treatment were grown in deep-water culture with 0.0063 mM boron control solution, zero-boron solution, or 0.05 mM boron toxicity solution; pH and EC were monitored and mature leaf tissue was analyzed by an external laboratory.

The 0.05 mM treatment developed marginal chlorosis within three weeks, quickly followed by bronze necrosis; the injury occurred on both upper and lower leaves and affected nearly every leaf in the three treated plants.
The boron-toxicity tissue analysis was elevated while other measured nutrients were described as sufficient, strengthening the treatment-to-symptom link under this small controlled trial.

In this trial, toxicity caused persistent leaf-margin injury but height, SPAD, yield, and measured THC remained close to controls, showing that visual severity must not be converted into a universal yield-loss estimate.

Researchers captured weekly close-ups, whole-plant photographs, and 360-degree video, but the public report does not expose original video asset URLs or a reuse license; those unlinked assets cannot be admitted to this dataset.

media.alt: Six-panel Cannabis nutrient-toxicity figure with manganese toxicity in the left column, boron toxicity in the right column, and initial, intermediate, and advanced rows
media.caption: Controlled-study composite. The right column shows boron-toxicity progression from marginal yellowing to inward-spreading chlorosis and advanced brown necrosis; the left manganese column is a separate diagnosis.
media.creator: Paul Cockson, Hunter Landis, Turner Smith, Kristin Hicks, and Brian E. Whipker
media.requiredAttribution: Cockson P, Landis H, Smith T, Hicks K, Whipker BE (2019), Applied Sciences 9(20):4432, CC BY 4.0; link the source and license and indicate modifications.
useLimitations: Scientific reference only until the right-side boron panels are separately cropped, bounded, and assigned a dataset split.
The composite contains two diagnosis classes: manganese toxicity in the left column and boron toxicity in the right; do not train or infer one label from the full image.
One cultivar and tenfold-supply protocol do not establish universal symptom timing, tissue thresholds, or production-system response.
media.stage: initial, intermediate, and advanced vegetative toxicity

name: Manganese toxicity / high-manganese response
summary: A measurement-dependent Cannabis differential with conflicting published visual descriptions: a controlled T1 study reported lower-leaf marginal chlorosis progressing inward, while field diagnostic observations described interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis. Neither pattern is specific enough for image- or video-only confirmation.
indicators: In the controlled T1 study, marginal yellowing began on lower leaves seven weeks after the high-Mn treatment
Controlled-study yellowing intensified inward toward the midrib; advanced leaves became severely chlorotic with necrotic margins and sometimes abscised
Separate field diagnostic observations described interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis
A repeated canopy pattern plus measured fertilizer, water, root-zone, or tissue evidence supports abnormal manganese exposure; color alone does not
exclusions: Boron toxicity or potassium deficiency better explains the same older-leaf marginal chlorosis-to-necrosis sequence
High root-zone EC, water stress, root injury, or normal senescence explains the lower-canopy pattern
Discrete lesions, halos, fruiting bodies, or asymmetric spread support a leaf-spot pathogen instead of a nutrient exposure
Mite feeding, stippling, webbing, or visible arthropods explain fine chlorosis
No plausible manganese source, pH condition, or analytical abnormality is found

progression.description: After seven weeks of tenfold Mn treatment in one T1 study, lower-leaf margins became yellow.
Marginal chlorosis intensified and moved inward toward the midrib.
Margins became necrotic, leaves were severely chlorotic, and some symptomatic leaves abscised.
A separate hemp survey described interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis without establishing that every case follows the controlled-study sequence.

confirmation: Do not confirm manganese toxicity from an image or video. Capture standardized whole-canopy, upper/middle/lower-canopy, and both-surface close-ups over time; record leaf/node age and whether injury is marginal, interveinal, or lesion-centered.

Before correction, document fertilizer formulation and batch, injector settings, source-water chemistry, irrigation history, and root-zone pH and EC from representative affected and unaffected plants.
Use a defined-age representative tissue sample and interpret manganese with the analytical laboratory, cultivar, substrate, and crop stage; do not use 47.88 mg/kg as a universal toxicity threshold.
If lesions are discrete or spreading independently of exposure zones, submit fresh tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory and inspect both leaf surfaces under magnification for pathogens and mites.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-correction root-zone, input-water, fertilizer, and tissue evidence before changing the program.
Map affected plants against irrigation zones, stock tanks, substrate lots, and cultivar blocks, and isolate any suspected mixing or injector error.
correctivePlan: Correct only a confirmed manganese source, formulation, injector, or root-zone pH problem using crop-appropriate professional guidance.
Track new leaves and repeated pH, EC, and tissue measurements; necrotic tissue and abscised leaves will not reverse.
prevention: Verify micronutrient formulation, stock-tank math, injector calibration, and source-water contribution.
Trend root-zone pH/EC and periodic tissue results by cultivar and stage instead of relying on a single visual threshold.
warnings: The controlled evidence used one Cannabis sativa T1 cultivar, silica sand, and 180 micromolar Mn (tenfold the complete formula); its seven-week timing is not a universal field threshold.
Treated foliar Mn was 47.88 mg/kg, within the study-cited 41–93 mg/kg survey range, and dry weight did not differ significantly from controls; the authors called for higher-concentration work.

The published visual patterns differ: the controlled study reported marginal injury and the field survey reported interveinal injury, so either pathway requires human review and analytical confirmation.

The licensed Figure 5 reference already stored under boron toxicity is a mixed-class composite with manganese in the left column and boron in the right; it is cross-reference context, not a clean manganese training sample, and is not duplicated here.
Visual chlorosis and necrosis are not manganese-specific, and no image or video in this record is ground truth.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Single-element withholding in Cannabis sativa T1 documented boron deficiency, manganese toxicity, and the absence of a visible molybdenum-deficiency phenotype during the nine-week experiment.
Boron-deficient plants developed growing-tip stunting, distorted new leaves, marginal necrosis, death of growing tips, root-tip loss, and severe wilting in advanced stages.

In Cannabis sativa T1, manganese-toxicity symptoms appeared seven weeks after treatment: marginal yellowing began on lower leaves, intensified inward toward the midrib, and advanced to marginal necrosis, severe chlorosis, and occasional leaf abscission.

The manganese-toxicity treatment used a tenfold increase over the complete formula (180 micromolar Mn versus 18 micromolar), but treated foliar Mn was 47.88 mg/kg, within the cited 41–93 mg/kg survey range; dry weight did not differ significantly from controls and the authors called for higher-concentration work to refine the threshold.
Figure 5 is a six-panel composite: manganese toxicity occupies the left column and boron toxicity the right, with initial, intermediate, and advanced symptom rows.

Molybdenum-withheld plants had foliar Mo 96% lower than controls yet developed no visual symptoms and no significant dry-weight difference by nine weeks, so a camera-visible Mo-deficiency phenotype was not established.
The experiment used one cultivar and complete withholding or tenfold treatments; tissue values and timing are experimental observations rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.

name: Nitrogen toxicity
summary: A measurement-dependent Cannabis nitrogen disorder with two distinct controlled contexts: excessive total nitrogen during vegetative growth produced smaller dark-green shoots and restricted roots, while excessive ammonium fraction during reproductive growth caused growing-tip curl and marginal necrosis, later wilting, systemic necrosis, root damage, and possible plant death. These pathways must not be collapsed into a generic dark-leaf or claw label.
affectedParts: whole plant and organs for relative size
growing tips and apical foliage under severe ammonium-form injury
apical and side inflorescences during reproductive-stage ammonium exposure
irrigation solution, leachate, substrate, and root zone for causal measurement
indicators: Documented nitrogen supply exceeds the crop, stage, cultivar, and production-system demand or the ammonium fraction is excessive relative to nitrate
At 320 mg/L total nitrogen in the controlled vegetative study, the whole plant, leaves, and roots were smaller than at the experiment optimum and foliage was dark green
Root restriction appeared at 240 mg/L total nitrogen even though shoot development and coloration remained visually similar to the 160 mg/L treatment
Dark-green color spans adequate and excessive total-nitrogen treatments and is supporting context only, never a diagnostic feature by itself
Under 100% ammonium at fixed total nitrogen, early apical growth was stunted and growing-tip leaves curled with marginal necrosis
Severe ammonium-form injury progressed from growing tips to widespread necrosis, wilting, severe root damage, and plant death
A 50% ammonium treatment remained visually normal through most of the experiment before necrosis and wilting appeared in the final two weeks
Serial measurements show reduced growth or biomass together with excess nitrogen exposure, elevated tissue nitrogen, high leachate nitrogen, or an excessive ammonium-to-nitrate ratio
exclusions: Dark green foliage is the only finding; the controlled total-nitrogen study showed similar color from 160 through 320 mg/L
Downward leaf clawing occurs without verified high nitrogen or ammonium exposure and without the published growth, root, or marginal-necrosis context
Root-zone EC or osmotic stress is high but nitrogen concentration, form, tissue status, and leachate do not isolate nitrogen from broad salinity injury
Growing tips are curled or necrotic and broad mites, russet mites, thrips, boron disorder, spray injury, heat, or light exposure explains the distribution better
Wilt follows drought, excessive vapor demand, waterlogging, root hypoxia, root temperature, or vascular/root disease without a nitrogen exposure-response link
Marginal necrosis follows a potassium, boron, salinity, contact, foliar-product, wind, or pathogen pattern and analytical evidence does not support nitrogen-form injury
Plants are small because of nitrogen deficiency, unsuitable pH, root binding, irrigation failure, cultivar architecture, stage, or another measured nutrient disorder
Color, gloss, or apparent curl changes only under grow lights, altered white balance, glare, shadow, lens distortion, compression, or stable genetic leaf form

progression.stage: Excess total nitrogen before reliable visual separation
progression.description: Tissue nitrogen and leachate nitrogen may increase and nitrogen-use efficiency may decline before a unique image phenotype develops; high treatment EC and formulation remain confounders.
At the highest controlled dose, plants and organs are smaller and dark green; root restriction can begin at a lower excessive dose while the shoot still resembles the study optimum.
By day 17 under 100% ammonium, apical growth is stunted and growing-tip leaves curl with marginal necrosis.
At 50% ammonium, plants can appear normal for most of the crop cycle before leaves become necrotic and wilt during the final two weeks.
Necrosis spreads through the plant, roots are severely damaged, growth remains restricted, wilting intensifies, and plants may die.
Judge subsequent growth, root condition, new lesion formation, root-zone and leachate chemistry, and follow-up tissue analysis; existing necrosis will not recover.

lookAlikes: High-EC nutrient burn or broad salinity stress
Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, or other root disease
Genetic leaf curl or compact architecture
Camera white-balance, exposure, glare, or grow-light color shift
confirmation: Do not confirm nitrogen toxicity from dark foliage, gloss, leaf clawing, tip burn, curl, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected label until nitrogen dose or form, root-zone measurements, and plant response are linked.

Separate suspected excessive total-nitrogen dose from suspected ammonium-form toxicity; record nitrate and ammonium concentrations and proportions rather than only a product EC or total fertilizer rate.

Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, growing tips, youngest fully developed leaves, both leaf surfaces and margins, stems, side branches, inflorescences when present, and washed roots under neutral repeatable lighting with scale and a healthy same-cultivar reference.

Record cultivar, stage, days since onset, complete fertilizer formulation, each nitrogen source, stock and injector calculations, water alkalinity, irrigation volume, drainage fraction, substrate or solution type, temperature, humidity, light, and recent product changes.

Measure calibrated input and representative root-zone or solution pH and EC, and test input, reservoir, leachate, or drainage for total nitrogen, nitrate, and ammonium as appropriate to the system; compare supply with actual water use and drainage.

Submit defined-position leaf tissue and appropriate solution, substrate, soil, leachate, or water samples to an agricultural or plant diagnostic laboratory; interpret nitrogen with cultivar, stage, organ, method, salinity, and competing nutrients rather than using 160, 240, or 320 mg/L as universal thresholds.

Inspect growing tips and both leaf surfaces with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when mites, thrips, root disease, viruses, viroids, vascular pathogens, or foliar injury remain plausible.
Treat response of subsequent growth after a measured correction as supporting evidence only; it does not retroactively make the original image ground-truth nitrogen toxicity.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-treatment images, fertilizer labels, mixing records, solution samples, root-zone measurements, representative tissue, and matched healthy controls before changing the program.

Pause discretionary nitrogen-heavy additives while verifying total nitrogen, nitrate-to-ammonium ratio, pH, EC, irrigation, drainage, and root health; do not automatically flush an oxygen-limited or already saturated root zone.
Quarantine severe wilt or root decline from ground-truth collections and exclude infectious and arthropod causes before attributing the response to nutrition.
correctivePlan: When measurements confirm excessive total nitrogen, reduce cumulative nitrogen exposure gradually within a balanced crop-, cultivar-, stage-, and system-appropriate program under current local agronomic guidance.

When an excessive ammonium fraction is confirmed, correct nitrogen form as well as total concentration while monitoring pH movement, salinity, calcium, magnesium, potassium, roots, irrigation, and drainage.

Track subsequent root growth, apical leaf geometry, new marginal necrosis, plant expansion, root-zone and leachate chemistry, and follow-up tissue results; reopen differentials if the exposure-response relationship is absent.
prevention: Record nitrogen concentration and nitrate-to-ammonium ratio for source water, each fertilizer component, final solution, and representative tissue instead of relying on product dose or EC alone.
Calibrate dosing equipment and pH/EC meters, verify stock calculations, and monitor irrigation volume, drainage fraction, leachate chemistry, dryback, root-zone temperature, and oxygenation.
Maintain same-cultivar healthy references and consistent node-, organ-, and stage-specific imaging and tissue sampling so naturally dark foliage or compact architecture is not mislabeled.
warnings: The vegetative dose study used one medical Cannabis cultivar, five plants per treatment, soilless media, long photoperiod, and a specific nutrient formulation; its 160 mg/L optimum and 240–320 mg/L restrictions are not universal Cannabis thresholds.
Irrigation EC increased with nitrogen dose in the vegetative study, so the highest-dose phenotype cannot be separated from treatment-specific salinity and ion-balance effects by an image.

The reproductive study held total nitrogen at 200 mg/L while exchanging nitrate for ammonium; high-ammonium injury is not interchangeable with excessive total nitrogen, and the authors noted that reduced or absent nitrate may contribute.
The 50% ammonium plants appeared normal for most of the experiment before late necrosis and wilting; a normal image cannot exclude a harmful nitrogen-form treatment or predict yield.
The controlled sources do not support dark clawed leaves, gloss, soft stems, burned tips, or delayed flowering as standalone Cannabis nitrogen-toxicity ground truth; those legacy claims were removed.

The dose-response Figure 1 combines five treatment columns and three organ/view rows and remains training-ineligible until every panel is dose-, organ-, time-, and source-group annotated with a leakage-safe split.
The 100% ammonium apical image is CC BY 4.0 but represents an extreme treatment confounded by nitrate absence; it remains training-ineligible and requires human scientific review.
All symptom-only, dark-leaf-only, claw-only, and unmeasured-EC samples remain low confidence and require human review.

sources.title: Response of Medical Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) to Nitrogen Supply Under Long Photoperiod
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Saloner and Bernstein)
supportedClaims: A controlled long-photoperiod experiment compared one medical Cannabis cultivar at 30, 80, 160, 240, and 320 mg/L total nitrogen in soilless media, with five replicate plants per treatment and repeated plant-development measurements.

At 320 mg/L nitrogen the plants and plant organs were smaller and dark green; at 240 mg/L shoot coloration and development appeared similar to the 160 mg/L treatment while root development was already restricted.

Supply above 160 mg/L restricted growth and biomass in this experiment, while nitrogen use efficiency declined and leaf, stem, and root total nitrogen and nitrate generally increased across the tested range.
The 160–320 mg/L treatments had similar dark-green leaf color, so dark foliage by itself did not distinguish the study optimum from excessive supply.

At high nitrogen, photosynthetic pigments continued to increase but photosynthesis did not; the authors associated the high-supply decline with stomatal closure and reduced stomatal conductance, transpiration, and intercellular carbon dioxide.

Irrigation EC rose with nitrogen treatment from 2080 µS/cm at 160 mg/L to 2510 and 2760 µS/cm at 240 and 320 mg/L, and high-treatment leachate nitrogen exceeded input concentration; nitrogen-dose effects therefore cannot be separated from the experiment-specific salt and formulation context by an image alone.

Figure 1 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing whole plants, youngest fully developed leaves, and roots across the five nitrogen doses; the columns are treatment levels rather than independent diagnosis classes.

sources.title: Nitrogen Source Matters: High NH4/NO3 Ratio Reduces Cannabinoids, Terpenoids, and Yield in Medical Cannabis
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Saloner and Bernstein)
supportedClaims: A controlled reproductive-stage experiment held total nitrogen at 200 mg/L and compared 0, 10, 30, 50, and 100% ammonium fractions, with five replicate medical Cannabis plants per treatment.

Plants receiving 0–30% ammonium appeared similar and did not show toxicity symptoms, while 50% ammonium plants appeared normal through most of the experiment before leaf necrosis and wilting emerged during the last two weeks.

At 50% ammonium, 40% of plants wilted in the final week and inflorescence biomass was 46% lower than in the nitrate-only treatment; this late response cannot be inferred reliably from an earlier normal-looking image.
The 100% ammonium treatment caused early stunting, curly leaves with marginal necrosis at growing tips, severe root damage, spread of necrosis to all plant parts, wilting, and plant death.

The early 100% ammonium growing-tip image was taken 17 days after treatment began, while whole-plant, inflorescence, and root images were captured at maturation and the sampled leaf image ten days earlier.
The authors cautioned that damage under 50–100% ammonium may also reflect reduced or absent nitrate supply, making ammonium-form toxicity mechanistically different from excessive total nitrogen dose.
Figures 1 and 2 are CC BY 4.0 visual references; Figure 1 mixes five ammonium ratios, organs, and capture times, while Figure 2 shows one apical view from the 100% ammonium treatment.

media.alt: Fifteen-panel controlled medical Cannabis nitrogen-dose composite with whole plants, youngest fully developed leaves, and roots at five nitrogen concentrations
media.caption: Controlled vegetative dose response. Columns show 30, 80, 160, 240, and 320 mg/L total nitrogen; rows show whole plants, youngest fully developed leaves, and roots. The 320 mg/L treatment was smaller and dark green, while root restriction was already evident at 240 mg/L.
media.creator: Avia Saloner and Nirit Bernstein
media.requiredAttribution: Saloner A and Bernstein N (2020), Frontiers in Plant Science 11:572293, Figure 1, CC BY 4.0; credit the authors, link the source and license, and indicate modifications.
useLimitations: Five columns are distinct nitrogen doses and three rows are distinct organs or views; whole-image single-class labeling and random panel splitting are invalid.
Only the 320 mg/L column was described as visually overdosed; 240 mg/L showed restricted roots while shoot coloration and development remained similar to the 160 mg/L treatment.
One cultivar, long photoperiod, soilless media, treatment-specific EC, and one formulation do not establish universal visual or analytical thresholds.
Reference display only until panels are bounded, dose-, organ-, time-, and diagnosis-annotated, scientifically reviewed, source-grouped, and assigned a leakage-safe split.

media.alt: Apical medical Cannabis foliage with severe curl and marginal necrosis after seventeen days of a one-hundred-percent ammonium nitrogen treatment
media.caption: Controlled early severe ammonium-form injury at the growing tip, photographed 17 days after initiation of the 100% ammonium and 0% nitrate treatment.
media.creator: Avia Saloner and Nirit Bernstein
media.requiredAttribution: Saloner A and Bernstein N (2022), Frontiers in Plant Science 13:830224, Figure 2, CC BY 4.0; credit the authors, link the source and license, and indicate modifications.
useLimitations: The image represents an extreme 100% ammonium and 0% nitrate treatment at fixed 200 mg/L total nitrogen, not generic excess total nitrogen.
The authors cautioned that reduced or absent nitrate may contribute to injury, so the image cannot establish a single unconfounded mechanism.
One cultivar, five replicates, reproductive-stage controlled conditions, and one formulation do not establish universal symptoms or timing.
Reference display only until the image and any derivatives are scientifically reviewed, source-grouped, and assigned a leakage-safe split with extreme-treatment metadata.

name: Downy mildew
summary: A foliar oomycete disease of Cannabis. Angular chlorotic-to-brown lesions and dark underside sporulation are stronger clues than top-surface discoloration alone.
indicators: Angular chlorotic or brown lesions develop on leaves
Dark sporulation is visible on the underside of corresponding lesions under conducive humidity
Leaves may curl and defoliate as severity increases
Severe field disease can extend to inflorescence tissue and reduce marketable yield
exclusions: White superficial colonies wipe or scrape away and fit powdery mildew better
Sooty conidial masses are identified as Pseudocercospora
No underside sporulation or pathogen evidence is present and nutrient or chemical injury explains the pattern

progression.description: Angular chlorotic lesions appear.
Dark oomycete sporulation develops on lesion undersides under humid conditions.
Lesions become necrotic, leaves curl or drop, and severe plants can lose substantial healthy foliage.

confirmation: Inspect the underside of fresh lesions under magnification and submit tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory when confirmation matters.
Treat Pseudoperonospora as an oomycete, not a true fungus; laboratory morphology or molecular testing is preferred for organism-level labels.
immediateActions: Separate heavily symptomatic material and reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness while preserving a diagnostic sample.
correctivePlan: Use an oomycete-appropriate disease management program allowed for the crop and production setting.
prevention: Scout undersides during humid periods and improve foliage drying/air movement where appropriate.
warnings: Pseudoperonospora is an oomycete, not a true fungus; disease-management and diagnostic interpretation should preserve that distinction.
Cultivar susceptibility varies widely, so severity cannot be generalized from one cultivar.

sources.title: First Report of Downy Mildew Caused by Pseudoperonospora cannabina on Cannabis sativa in New York
supportedClaims: Downy mildew on hemp was documented with chlorotic and necrotic lesions and sporangiophore production under humid conditions, affecting leaves and inflorescences in severe field cases.
The causal agent is the oomycete Pseudoperonospora cannabina; it is not a true fungus despite the mildew name.

sources.title: Evaluation of downy mildew resistance in the USDA Hemp Germplasm Repository using high-throughput and traditional phenotyping methods
supportedClaims: Pseudoperonospora cannabina causes angular brown foliar lesions and dark sporulation on leaf undersides, often with curling and defoliation.
A 108-entry hemp resistance study documented wide susceptibility variation, reinforcing that severity is genotype-dependent and not a universal image threshold.

name: Cannabis aphid
summary: A Cannabis-adapted aphid found on hemp leaves and stems indoors and outdoors. Confirm by observing and identifying the insect; generalized curling, yellowing, or reduced vigor is not species-level evidence.
affectedParts: whole canopy when populations are heavy
indicators: Colonies of small soft-bodied aphids are visible on cannabis leaves or stems
Wingless aphids show pale abdominal striping while winged forms may show dark spotting
Aphid cast skins or sticky honeydew occur near an active colony
New growth is stressed in the same areas where aphids are actively feeding
exclusions: No aphids, cast skins, or honeydew are found after repeated underside and stem inspection
Only roots contain aphids while foliage and stems are free of colonies
Fine stippling, webbing, mites, or eggs dominate the underside evidence
Silvery feeding scars with dark fecal specks support thrips instead

progression.description: Small colonies establish on stems, petioles, or leaves and may be missed without close inspection.
More aphids, cast skins, and honeydew become visible and feeding stress may affect nearby growth.
Dense colonies can contribute to broader canopy stress, but plant symptoms remain nonspecific without the insects.

confirmation: Inspect leaf undersides, petioles, stems, and shoot tips with magnification and document intact aphids.
Use morphological identification or an entomology reference when species-level identification matters; body color alone is not diagnostic.
immediateActions: Separate heavily infested material from clean propagation stock and inspect neighboring plants.
Record where colonies occur and preserve clear close-up images or a specimen before treatment.
correctivePlan: Use an integrated pest-management response appropriate to the production system and local pesticide/biocontrol rules.
Reinspect new growth and undersides after intervention rather than judging success from old damaged tissue.
prevention: Inspect incoming clones and mother-stock material before integration.
Use routine underside and stem scouting so small colonies are detected before they spread.
warnings: Do not identify Phorodon cannabis from leaf yellowing, curling, or aphid color alone.
Do not assume every aphid found around the root zone is cannabis aphid; rice root aphid is a distinct Cannabis-associated pest.

sources.title: Cannabis aphid, Phorodon cannabis
supportedClaims: Cannabis aphids are small, soft-bodied, long-antennaed aphids with piercing-sucking mouthparts and occur on leaves and stems of hemp plants grown indoors and outdoors.

Cannabis aphids may be pale to light green or light brown; winged forms have dark spotting and wingless forms often show pale abdominal stripes, so body color alone is not a reliable species identifier.

sources.title: Assessing the adaptive role of cannabidiol (CBD) in Cannabis sativa defense against cannabis aphids
supportedClaims: Phorodon cannabis is a Cannabis-adapted aphid and was studied directly on Cannabis sativa hemp in whole-plant assays.
The study supports cannabis aphid as a biologically relevant hemp pest but does not make generic leaf yellowing or curling species-level ground truth.

media.alt: Cannabis plants infested with cannabis aphids alongside magnified adult and winged Phorodon cannabis.
media.caption: Cannabis plants of the Congo Durban variety infested with Phorodon cannabis, with adult and winged adult aphids shown under a stereo microscope at 20× magnification (Lopez Restrepo and Kovalchuk 2025, Figure 2).
media.creator: Daniel Lopez Restrepo and Igor Kovalchuk
media.requiredAttribution: Lopez Restrepo D, Kovalchuk I. 2025. Investigating the Effects of Entomopathogenic Fungi on Mortality of Phorodon cannabis Populations in Cannabis Plants. Plants 14(6):931. CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: cannabis-aphid — Phorodon cannabis infestation and adult morphology on Cannabis sativa
useLimitations: Multi-panel plant-and-organism figure; reference-only as a whole image.
Do not infer cannabis aphid from yellowing, wilting, or leaf distortion without directly observing aphids or other insect evidence.
Keep training-ineligible until panel-level source grouping and crop review are complete.

name: Fungus gnats / root-feeding Bradysia larvae
summary: A greenhouse root-zone pest complex in which adult fungus gnats signal moist-media populations and larvae can feed on roots and interact with soil-borne disease. Evidence is cross-crop greenhouse literature, so Cannabis symptoms alone are not diagnostic.
indicators: Small dark gnat-like adults repeatedly emerge from or rest near moist growing media
Translucent slender larvae with dark head capsules are found in the root zone
Poor growth or yellowing occurs together with confirmed fungus-gnat larvae in wet organic media
exclusions: No adults or larvae are found after sticky-card and root-zone inspection
Root-associated aphids rather than fly larvae are present
Root decay is confirmed without fungus-gnat larvae
Canopy symptoms track a measured nutrient, pH, EC, light, or irrigation problem instead

progression.description: Small adults are noticed around moist media or lower canopy.
Larvae occupy organic media and can feed on fine roots or other plant material.
Root injury and pathogen interactions can contribute to poor growth, but the causal contribution must be separated from root disease and irrigation conditions.

confirmation: Use sticky cards for adults and inspect moist media/root zones for characteristic larvae.
Confirm root health independently because fungus gnats may coexist with soil-borne pathogens.
immediateActions: Inspect moisture management, algae, plant debris, and the root zone.
Document adults and larvae before attributing canopy symptoms to fungus gnats.
correctivePlan: Use sanitation, moisture management, physical or biological controls that are appropriate to the crop system and local rules.
Continue monitoring adults and larvae while separately tracking root recovery.
prevention: Avoid chronic surface wetness and remove algae and decomposing plant debris.
Monitor greenhouse/media pest pressure before symptoms appear.
warnings: This profile uses greenhouse cross-crop evidence for Bradysia biology; it does not make generic yellowing a Cannabis-specific fungus-gnat signature.
Do not treat a few adult gnats as proof that they are the primary cause of a major root or canopy disorder.

sources.title: Ecology of Fungus Gnats (Bradysia spp.) in Greenhouse Production Systems Associated with Disease-Interactions and Alternative Management Strategies
supportedClaims: Bradysia fungus gnats are important greenhouse horticultural pests whose larvae feed on roots and may contribute to disease interactions.

This is cross-crop greenhouse evidence rather than Cannabis-specific symptom validation, so plant yellowing or stunting cannot identify fungus gnats without observing adults, larvae, or other root-zone evidence.

sources.title: Fungus Gnats fact sheet
sources.publisher: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
supportedClaims: Greenhouse fungus-gnat larvae can feed on roots or inside stems and may be associated with poor plant growth, yellowing, and stunting.
Adults around moist growing media are a useful inspection cue, but above-ground plant symptoms remain nonspecific.

name: Rice root aphid on cannabis
summary: A root-associated aphid that has become a common host-associated pest of indoor Cannabis in North America. Root-zone insect evidence is required because above-ground decline is nonspecific.
indicators: Aphid colonies are visible on cannabis roots after careful root-zone inspection
Winged aphids emerge from or cluster around the growing medium while root colonies are present
Root-associated aphids are documented while stems and leaf undersides lack the typical cannabis-aphid colony pattern
exclusions: No aphids are found on roots after representative inspection of the root ball or root zone
Aphids are concentrated on leaves and stems rather than roots
Small dark flies and translucent black-headed larvae support fungus gnats instead
Brown slimy roots and wilt occur without root aphids and a root pathogen or oxygen problem explains the decline better

progression.description: Populations remain largely hidden around roots and may be missed by canopy-only scouting.
More root-associated aphids are present and winged adults may emerge from the growing medium.
Large numbers of alates may emerge from soil near plant maturity; above-ground stress still requires separate causal evaluation.

confirmation: Expose representative roots and document aphids directly associated with roots.
Use morphological identification when distinguishing rice root aphid from other aphids is operationally important.
immediateActions: Inspect nearby root zones and isolate infested propagation material where practical.
Record root condition separately so root feeding is not confused with concurrent root disease or irrigation stress.
correctivePlan: Use a root-zone IPM plan appropriate to the production system and local rules.
Verify population decline by repeat root inspection rather than relying only on fewer flying adults.
prevention: Inspect root balls of incoming plants and rooted cuttings.
Include root-zone scouting when unexplained flying aphids appear indoors.
warnings: Do not diagnose rice root aphid from yellowing, stunting, or flying insects alone.
Root aphids and root disease can coexist; finding one does not exclude the other.

sources.title: Cannabis sativa as a Host of Rice Root Aphid (Hemiptera: Aphididae) in North America
supportedClaims: Indoor Cannabis sativa has emerged as a common North American host of rice root aphid, Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale.
On Cannabis this aphid is found primarily in association with plant roots, and winged adults may emerge from soil in large numbers as plants approach maturity.
A root-zone aphid observation is much more discriminating than nonspecific above-ground stress symptoms.

media.alt: Rice root aphids visible at the base and roots of aeroponically grown Cannabis sativa.
media.caption: Rice root aphids living on the roots of aeroponically grown Cannabis sativa (Cranshaw and Wainwright-Evans 2020, Figure 2).
media.creator: Whitney Cranshaw and Suzanne Wainwright-Evans; figure photographer not separately stated in the caption
media.requiredAttribution: Cranshaw W, Wainwright-Evans S. 2020. Cannabis sativa as a Host of Rice Root Aphid (Hemiptera: Aphididae) in North America. Journal of Integrated Pest Management 11(1):15. CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: rice-root-aphid — Rice root aphid (Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale) on Cannabis roots
useLimitations: Reference-only until source-group and panel-level training review are complete.
The presence of rice root aphids is visible; generalized canopy decline is not uniquely diagnostic of this pest.
Do not use this asset to infer root disease, nutrient status, or above-ground symptom severity.

name: Hemp witches’ broom (phytoplasma-associated)
scientificName: Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii and other phytoplasmas
summary: A leafhopper-associated systemic syndrome in which cannabis can develop shortened nodes, clusters of proliferating axillary or apical shoots, stunting, small distorted leaves, chlorosis, mottling, and curling; the same visual pattern can involve Beet curly top virus, Spiroplasma citri, or mixed infection.
stages: field-grown leaf-bearing plants; cannabis-specific stage effects are not established
indicators: Clusters of excessive apical or axillary shoots forming a broom-like tip
Shortened internodes and compact branch clusters
Small, distorted, curled, or upward-rolled leaves
Leaf chlorosis with mottling or mosaic
Vein-bounded green islands on the upper leaf surface
Interveinal discoloration with a pale pustule-like appearance from below
Whole-plant stunting with abnormal branching
exclusions: Validated testing identifies Beet curly top virus without detecting phytoplasma in properly sampled tissue
Validated testing identifies Spiroplasma citri or another agent and does not detect phytoplasma
Microscopy confirms broad mites or hemp russet mites in the distorted growing tips
Abnormal branching follows deliberate topping or training and subsequent leaves remain normal
Distortion maps to documented herbicide or plant-growth-regulator exposure
Short internodes and branching remain stable in healthy clones without chlorosis, mottling, progressive distortion, or pathogen detection

progression.description: Leaves may curl, roll upward, mottle, become chlorotic, or develop vein-bounded green islands above with pale interveinal discoloration visible below.
Internodes shorten while apical or axillary shoots proliferate into compact highly branched clusters; leaves on affected branches may remain small and distorted and the plant may become stunted.

Primary cannabis reports document variable symptoms during the growing season but do not establish a universal order or rate. Capture the same plant serially and do not infer infection age from one image.

confirmation: Do not confirm phytoplasma from witches’ broom architecture, a photograph, video, or leafhopper observation.
Submit the most symptomatic young leaves with petioles to a plant diagnostic laboratory using that laboratory’s current sampling and shipping protocol; include a healthy comparator when requested.

Use a validated phytoplasma molecular assay followed by sequence or classification evidence when group-level identity matters; the Nevada report combined real-time PCR, nested 16S rRNA PCR, Sanger sequencing, BLASTn, and iPhyClassifier analysis.
Request a differential panel that includes Beet curly top virus and Spiroplasma citri because the three agents can produce overlapping symptoms and can occur together.

Record whole-plant architecture, both leaf surfaces, affected shoot position, field location, onset date, and serial change to preserve image and video context without treating those observations as proof.
immediateActions: Flag suspect plants and pause distribution of their cuttings pending laboratory results.
Scout nearby plants and leafhoppers while keeping vector presence separate from pathogen confirmation.
Keep all symptom-only images out of phytoplasma, Spiroplasma, and BCTV ground-truth classes.
correctivePlan: Base removal and vector-management decisions on laboratory results, production policy, and locally legal recommendations.
If phytoplasma is not detected, continue testing or differential review for BCTV, Spiroplasma citri, mites, chemical injury, and physiological causes.
Continue serial observation because one plant or branch can combine architecture, foliar color, and distortion differently over time.
prevention: Use tested and traceable propagation material.
Monitor leafhoppers and regional alerts without assuming every vector carries the same pathogen.
Control weed reservoirs and vectors only with locally appropriate, crop-legal practices.
warnings: Witches’ broom is a syndrome, not a species-level visual diagnosis.
Cannabis symptom overlap and documented mixed infections make image-only ground truth unsafe.
The three institutional photographs below are metadata-only license-review candidates: no reuse license is stated, so they are hidden and prohibited from automated training.
Cannabis-specific evidence does not establish a universal symptom order, cultivar response, or infection-to-symptom interval.

sources.title: First Report of ‘Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii’ Associated with a Witches’ Broom Disease in Cannabis sativa in Nevada, U.S.A
supportedClaims: Symptomatic Nevada cannabis had leaf curling, mottling, chlorosis, witches’ broom, stunting, and shortened nodes.
Upper leaf surfaces showed vein-bounded green islands while lower surfaces showed interveinal discoloration with a pale pustule-like appearance.

Phytoplasma was detected from petioles of the most symptomatic leaves by 23S rRNA real-time PCR; nested 16S rRNA PCR, Sanger sequencing, BLASTn, and iPhyClassifier analysis supported identification near Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii.

sources.title: Hemp Abnormal Growth Is Attributed to Mono-, Di-, or Tri-Infections of Spiroplasma citri, Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii, and Beet Curly Top Virus
supportedClaims: Across 67 symptomatic Nevada hemp samples, abnormal growth included stunting, yellowing, excessive apical branching, witches’ broom clusters, upward leaf rolling, mottling, and mosaic.
Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii was detected in 14 samples, Beet curly top virus in 57, and Spiroplasma citri in two; dual and triple infections occurred.

The overlapping syndrome cannot assign one causal agent visually, so diagnostic testing should consider phytoplasma, Spiroplasma citri, and Beet curly top virus rather than treating witches’ broom as a species-specific image label.

sources.title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Witches’ Broom
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: Cannabis witches’ broom expression varies with the phytoplasma involved; typical plants are stunted with highly branched stems, axillary shoot proliferation, and small, distorted, chlorotic leaves.
Phytoplasmas are leafhopper-transmitted, regional pathogen types vary, and vector presence or symptoms alone do not identify the phytoplasma involved.
The three cannabis symptom photographs are credited to C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University, 2022; the landing page states copyright but supplies no reuse license.

media.alt: Hemp leaves with cupping, curling, and deformation associated with phytoplasma infection by Oregon State University Extension
media.caption: Metadata-only institutional reference showing distorted and curled hemp leaves. Hidden until explicit reuse permission is documented and never sufficient as phytoplasma ground truth.
media.creator: C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University
media.license: Copyright © Oregon State University; no reuse license stated on the landing page
media.requiredAttribution: C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University, 2022; obtain permission before display, copying, modification, or training use.
useLimitations: Reference-link metadata only; no image file is stored.
Do not display, copy, modify, or train without documented permission.
Symptom association does not identify the phytoplasma or exclude mixed infection.

media.creator: C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University
media.license: Copyright © Oregon State University; no reuse license stated on the landing page
media.requiredAttribution: C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University, 2022; obtain permission before display, copying, modification, or training use.
useLimitations: Reference-link metadata only; no image file is stored.
Do not display, copy, modify, or train without documented permission.
Detached leaves omit canopy distribution; yellowing alone is not diagnostic.

media.caption: Metadata-only institutional branch view of excessive meristem proliferation. Hidden pending permission and not usable as a pathogen-specific visual label.
