useLimitations: Reference-link metadata only; no image file is stored.
Do not display, copy, modify, or train without documented permission.
Architecture can overlap with training response, BCTV, Spiroplasma, and mixed infection.

name: Root binding / container-restriction stress
summary: A physical root-zone restriction documented in hemp transplants. Canopy stunting or stress is nonspecific; confirmation requires seeing the root system and separating mechanical restriction from drought, salinity, hypoxia, and root pathogens.
indicators: Roots densely circle or mat along the container boundary with limited free substrate volume
Plant growth is restricted relative to matched plants despite otherwise reasonable nutrition and irrigation
Stress persists around transplant establishment and root architecture remains constrained
exclusions: Root system is not physically congested
Roots are brown, slimy, necrotic, or lesioned enough to support disease
Measured drought, salinity, or hypoxia explains the response
Stem girdling or transplant damage is the dominant mechanical problem

progression.description: Roots occupy most available container volume.
Circling and dense matting increase while water and nutrient buffering become less stable.
A severely bound root system may establish poorly and can coexist with secondary root pathogens.

confirmation: Remove or expose the root ball and document root density, circling, root color, odor, and substrate condition.
Measure moisture and EC and inspect for disease because root binding can coexist with pathogens.
immediateActions: Document the intact root ball before disturbing it when diagnosis matters.
Check irrigation uniformity and root health rather than assuming every small container is root-bound.
correctivePlan: Relieve confirmed physical restriction using transplant/root-management practices appropriate to crop stage and system.
Monitor new root expansion and canopy recovery while screening for secondary disease.
prevention: Match container volume and transplant timing to growth rate.
Inspect purchased transplants before integration.
warnings: Small container size alone does not prove pathological root binding.
Root binding and Fusarium/Pythium can coexist, so finding circling roots does not exclude disease.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.

name: Fusarium crown and root rot / wilt complex
summary: A Cannabis crown/root/wilt disease complex associated with multiple Fusarium species. Yellowing and wilt are nonspecific; dark sunken crown tissue, root necrosis, and internal discoloration increase suspicion, while laboratory isolation or molecular work is required for organism-level confirmation.
indicators: Dark sunken crown lesions extend upward from the cannabis root zone
Reddish-brown or dark internal stem discoloration originates at the crown
Roots are necrotic while crown tissue is darkened or rotted
Canopy yellowing and wilt occur together with documented crown or internal stem decay
exclusions: Roots and crown are firm and healthy with no internal discoloration
Brown slimy roots occur without crown or internal stem lesions and Pythium or oxygen stress is better supported
Wilt resolves promptly after correcting a documented irrigation deficit without crown decay
Only one-sided mechanical stem injury explains the crown discoloration

progression.description: Root or crown tissue darkens and growth may slow before the canopy pattern is distinctive.
General or sometimes asymmetric yellowing and wilt develops as crown/root damage advances.
Internal decay may extend upward from the crown and plants can rapidly wilt, defoliate, collapse, or die.

confirmation: Inspect roots, crown, and a clean stem cross-section for the distribution of decay and internal discoloration.
Use a plant-diagnostic laboratory for isolation plus molecular or sequence-based identification when Fusarium confirmation changes management.
immediateActions: Quarantine severely affected plants and avoid moving contaminated root-zone material or runoff to clean plants.
Document crown/root/internal symptoms before destructive sampling and preserve representative tissue for diagnosis.
correctivePlan: Base sanitation, culling, irrigation-system, and crop-protection decisions on confirmed pathogen and production-system evidence.
Inspect propagation stock and adjacent plants because Fusarium can move through infected plant material and contaminated production environments.
prevention: Start with clean propagation stock and sanitized tools, containers, and root-zone systems.
Prevent recirculation or movement of contaminated irrigation water where pathogen spread is a concern.
warnings: A photograph of yellowing or wilt cannot confirm Fusarium.
Multiple Fusarium species and Pythium can occur in similar Cannabis crown/root disease complexes; do not make species-level claims without laboratory evidence.
The Fusarium species list on Cannabis continues to expand; a model should rank a Fusarium syndrome separately from a laboratory-confirmed species label.

sources.title: Root and crown rot pathogens causing wilt symptoms on field-grown marijuana (Cannabis sativa L.) plants
supportedClaims: Affected field-grown Cannabis plants showed general or one-sided yellowing, rapid wilting, and collapse, with dark sunken crown lesions and internal discoloration extending upward from the root/crown zone.

Fusarium oxysporum, F. brachygibbosum, F. solani, F. equiseti, and Pythium aphanidermatum were recovered from affected tissues; pathogenicity work demonstrates that visual wilt alone does not identify one causal species.
Darkened or necrotic roots, crown rot, and reddish-brown internal decay are more discriminating observations than general canopy yellowing.

sources.title: Diseases of Cannabis sativa Caused by Diverse Fusarium Species
supportedClaims: Multiple Fusarium species are associated with Cannabis root, crown, stem, wilt, and flower disease syndromes.
Reported Cannabis Fusarium diagnoses use culture and sequence-based or other laboratory identification together with pathogenicity evidence; symptom appearance is not species-level confirmation.

sources.title: First Report of Fusarium falciforme (FSSC 3 + 4) Causing Rot of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in California
supportedClaims: Fusarium falciforme isolates caused internal hemp stem rot in pathogenicity work and were reisolated from inoculated stems.
Field root rot was associated with the same organism, but the report specifically confirmed stem-rot ability more directly than root-rot ability.

sources.title: First Report of Fusarium commune Causing Damping Off and Wilt in Cannabis sativa in Pennsylvania
supportedClaims: Fusarium commune was reported from indoor Cannabis with wilted yellowing foliage, browning stems and roots, and withering, expanding the documented Fusarium species associated with Cannabis wilt/root disease.
The case supports maintaining a Fusarium complex label unless laboratory work resolves the causal species.

media.alt: Multi-panel reference figure showing Fusarium-associated disease signs and pathogen evidence on greenhouse-grown Cannabis plants.
media.caption: Infection of greenhouse-grown Cannabis plants by Fusarium species, including yellowing, crown infection and decay, pith necrosis, crown rot, diseased cuttings, flower infection, cultures, and pathogenicity-test symptoms (Gwinn et al. 2022, Figure 4).
media.creator: Zamir Punja (photographs), published in Gwinn et al. 2022
media.requiredAttribution: Gwinn KD, Hansen Z, Kelly H, Ownley BH. 2022. Diseases of Cannabis sativa Caused by Diverse Fusarium Species. Frontiers in Agronomy 3:796062. Figure photographs courtesy of Zamir Punja. CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: fusarium-crown-root-rot — Fusarium-associated Cannabis crown/root/wilt disease composite
useLimitations: Multi-panel and multi-species composite: reference-only as a whole figure.
Do not treat the full composite as one single-class training example.
Do not visually confirm a Fusarium species in an unknown plant from resemblance to this figure.
Use the source article and laboratory confirmation guidance for causal identification.

name: Acidic or extreme substrate-pH root stress
summary: A measured root-zone condition in which persistently acidic peat-based substrate suppresses Cannabis shoot and root development, while either acidic or high-pH extremes can restrict visible root growth. There is no unique leaf appearance: cultivar, fertility, EC, substrate, and exposure duration materially change what a camera can see.
affectedParts: root tips and developing root system
lower foliage when low pH is combined with excessive micronutrient fertility in a susceptible cultivar
leaf tips and leaflet interior during treatment-associated bronzing and necrosis
root-zone solution and substrate for direct pH and EC measurement
indicators: Repeated calibrated substrate measurements remain at an extreme rather than a single irrigation or runoff reading
Root-tip development is reduced relative to matched healthy plants before a specific foliar pattern is reliable
Whole-plant diameter and accumulated shoot biomass lag despite plant height sometimes remaining similar
At acidic pH, leaf-tissue micronutrient concentrations may rise without visible toxicity
In the Sweetened pH 3.8 plus fourfold-micronutrient treatment, lower-leaf tips bronzed, became necrotic, spread inward, and developed chlorosis
The same low-pH and high-micronutrient treatment did not produce the same foliage response in Cherry Wine
exclusions: Only nutrient-solution input pH was measured and the actual substrate or root-zone pH is unknown
A single runoff, reservoir, or slurry reading is outside target but repeat representative measurements are not
High EC, fertilizer imbalance, or source-water alkalinity explains the response without a persistent measured substrate-pH extreme
Roots are restricted by saturation, compaction, container binding, drought, temperature, oxygen limitation, transplant damage, or root disease
Foliar bronzing or necrosis is localized to heat, light, spray, contact, pest feeding, or infectious lesions
Tissue analysis supports a specific nutrient deficiency or toxicity and measured root-zone pH is not outside the production-system target
Color differences appear only under altered lighting, white balance, cultivar pigmentation, senescence, or compression artifact

progression.description: Substrate pH persists outside the intended system range; solution pH alone does not establish the root-zone exposure.
Root-tip expansion can slow before a diagnostic foliage pattern appears. In Baox, separation at pH 3.1 and 7.1 was evident by 21 days after planting.
Plant diameter, root mass, or shoot dry mass can fall while height remains deceptively similar; compare serial whole-plant and root-zone measurements with matched controls.
Low pH plus excessive micronutrients may cause lower-leaf tip bronzing, chlorosis, and spreading necrosis in a susceptible cultivar, but absence of those symptoms does not exclude pH stress.
New root tips, canopy expansion, and new-leaf quality should be followed over time; existing necrosis will not reverse and response alone does not prove the original diagnosis.

confirmation: Do not diagnose pH stress from leaf color, tip burn, stunting, one photograph, one video, or a generic nutrient-availability chart.

Measure the actual substrate or root-zone pH repeatedly with a calibrated meter and a method appropriate to the medium; record sampling location, depth, irrigation timing, extraction method, meter calibration, temperature, and replicate values.

Measure root-zone and input EC alongside pH, and document source-water pH and alkalinity, fertilizer formulation, acid or base additions, lime charge, substrate batch, irrigation volume, leaching fraction, and drainage.

Capture serial whole-plant top and side views, root-zone and cleaned-root views, upper- and lower-canopy views, and close-ups of both leaf surfaces under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched same-cultivar control.

Record cultivar, plant age, stage, days of exposure, container volume, substrate composition, water content, root-zone temperature, dissolved oxygen where relevant, and root-tip quantity or standardized root coverage.

Use representative leaf-tissue and root-zone or substrate analysis to separate a pH-associated exposure from a specific nutrient disorder; use a plant diagnostic laboratory when discolored or decaying roots, lesions, or pests remain plausible.
Retain a measured-exposure or suspected label unless the pH history, root or growth response, competing exposures, and analytical evidence are linked to the photographed plant.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-correction pH, EC, alkalinity, solution, substrate, tissue, root, and image records before changing the system.
Verify the measuring method and calibration with repeat samples; avoid large unmeasured acid, base, lime, fertilizer, or flush corrections.
Quarantine uncertain images and videos from diagnostic ground truth until exposure and confounder evidence is linked.
correctivePlan: Correct the verified cause gradually using substrate- and water-appropriate guidance, considering alkalinity and buffering rather than input pH alone.
Restore a balanced fertilizer and irrigation program while monitoring substrate pH, EC, water content, drainage, and new root growth.
Reassess root pathogens, salinity, water status, temperature, and nutrient-specific differentials if new root tips and growth do not improve after the measured pH returns to the intended range.
prevention: Establish a production-system-specific substrate pH and EC monitoring protocol with calibrated meters, consistent extraction methods, replicate sampling, and trend alerts.
Test source-water alkalinity and account for substrate lime and fertilizer acidity before making recurring pH adjustments.
Keep same-cultivar controls and serial root and canopy images so gradual growth restriction is not mistaken for a specific leaf disorder.
warnings: The study supports a measured substrate-pH stress record, not a universal image phenotype or a universal nutrient-lockout chart.
The 5.5 to 6.5 recommendation came from peat-based greenhouse experiments and must not be copied unchanged to soil, field, coco, rockwool, aeroponic, or deep-water systems.
At normal micronutrient supply, low pH increased tissue accumulation without a universal visible toxicity; absence of bronzing does not establish that the root zone is acceptable.
The lower-leaf bronzing sequence occurred in Sweetened under pH 3.8 plus fourfold micronutrients and was absent in Cherry Wine; it is not low-pH-specific ground truth.
A single runoff or reservoir pH value does not prove the pH experienced throughout the root system.
No image or video is admitted for this record because no stable original asset URL was independently verified during this review.
All symptom-only or uncalibrated-pH samples remain low confidence and require human review.

sources.title: Impact of substrate pH and micronutrient fertility rates on Cannabis sativa
sources.publisher: Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America and the American Society of Agronomy
supportedClaims: In a controlled peat-perlite experiment, industrial hemp shoot dry weight was lower at substrate pH 3.0 and 4.0 than at pH 5.0 through 7.0; plant diameter was smaller at pH 3.0, while mean plant height did not differ across that pH range.
Visible root-tip counts in Cannabis sativa Baox mini-rhizotrons were lowest at both measured extremes, pH 3.1 and 7.1, by 21 days after planting, while counts at pH 3.7 through 5.9 were similar.
Termination EC was higher at pH 3.0 and 7.0 than at intermediate pH values in the first experiment, so pH response cannot be interpreted without the accompanying salt and fertility context.

Lower pH increased several leaf-tissue micronutrient concentrations, but normal micronutrient supply did not produce a universal toxicity phenotype; the authors concluded that Cannabis growth was inhibited below pH 5.0 and recommended a greenhouse substrate range of 5.5 to 6.5 for the systems evaluated.

With fourfold micronutrients at target pH 3.8, Sweetened developed lower-foliage tip bronzing that advanced to necrosis, inward spread, and chlorosis, whereas Cherry Wine did not show the same response, demonstrating cultivar- and fertility-dependent appearance.

The experiments evaluated peat-based greenhouse substrates and three cultivars; their pH values, timing, tissue concentrations, and symptom expression are treatment-specific and do not establish universal soil, coco, rockwool, or hydroponic thresholds.

name: Pythium root rot
summary: An oomycete root disease favored by wet, low-oxygen conditions; affected roots discolor, soften, and lose function.
indicators: Brown slimy roots
Wilting despite moisture
Stunting and yellowing
Crown rot in severe cases
exclusions: Roots are tan from media staining but firm
Container is very light and dry
Only one leaf shows damage

progression.description: Root tips lose white color and growth slows.
Roots brown and soften while foliage wilts or yellows.
Root systems collapse and crown tissue may rot.

confirmation: Inspect cleaned roots for texture and active white tips.
Laboratory testing is required to distinguish similar root pathogens.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone water and tools.
Restore oxygenation and correct saturation.
correctivePlan: Remove irrecoverable plants where appropriate and sanitize wetted equipment.
Use only legal crop-appropriate treatments.
prevention: Control water temperature, sanitation, oxygen, and irrigation duration.
warnings: Visual symptoms cannot reliably identify Pythium to species.
Pythium species differ in temperature and production-system ecology; do not treat one environmental threshold as universal for the entire complex.

sources.title: Several Pythium species cause crown and root rot on cannabis plants grown under commercial greenhouse conditions
sources.organization: Canadian Journal of Plant Pathology (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: Multiple Pythium species cause crown and root rot in greenhouse cannabis, and pathogen identity cannot be resolved reliably from above-ground symptoms alone.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium ultimum Crown and Root Rot of Industrial Hemp in the United States
supportedClaims: Pythium ultimum was pathogenic to industrial hemp in replicated inoculation work; symptoms began within about one week and the organism was reisolated and PCR-confirmed.
Cool early planting, low-lying/flood-prone conditions, and soil crusting after intense rainfall were risk context in the report, not species-level visual identifiers.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium aphanidermatum Crown and Root Rot of Industrial Hemp in the United States
supportedClaims: Industrial hemp with Pythium aphanidermatum crown/root rot showed chlorosis, stunting, wilt, brown root lesions, feeder-root loss, and sometimes brown water-soaked stem lesions.
The above-ground syndrome overlaps other root diseases and water stress, reinforcing the need for cleaned-root and laboratory evidence.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium myriotylum Causing Root Rot in Cannabis sativa in California
supportedClaims: Greenhouse medical Cannabis with Pythium myriotylum root rot showed stunting, chlorosis, senescence, reduced root mass and root-hair density, and necrotic root lesions.
The Cannabis-specific phenotype does not make canopy appearance species-specific.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium aphanidermatum Causing Crown and Root Rot in Cannabis sativa in Florida
supportedClaims: Pythium aphanidermatum crown/root rot has been confirmed in indoor Cannabis grown in rockwool across multiple cultivars in Florida.
Species occurrence across production systems supports retaining a Pythium complex label unless laboratory evidence resolves species.

sources.title: First Report of Pythium myriotylum Causing Damping off and Root Rot in Cannabis sativa in Florida
supportedClaims: Pythium myriotylum was confirmed causing damping-off and root rot in indoor Cannabis cuttings from five cultivars in Florida.
The expanded cultivar evidence supports propagation-stage scouting and reinforces that Pythium disease can occur before a mature-plant canopy syndrome is available.

media.alt: Hemp plants from a controlled pathogenicity trial comparing Pythium, Globisporangium, Fusarium, and uninoculated treatments.
media.caption: Hemp 'Wife' plants 14 days after inoculation with pathogenic Pythium myriotylum, Globisporangium irregulare, or Fusarium oxysporum isolates, plus the uninoculated control (McGehee and Raudales 2021, Figure 7).
media.creator: Cora S. McGehee and Rosa E. Raudales
media.requiredAttribution: McGehee CS, Raudales RE. 2021. First Report of Pathogens Associated With Root Rot and Wilt of Cannabis sativa in Connecticut. Frontiers in Agronomy 3:706138. CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: pythium-root-rot — controlled hemp root-pathogen pathogenicity comparison including Pythium myriotylum
useLimitations: Multi-pathogen treatment composite; reference-only as a whole figure.
Whole-plant chlorosis, wilt, and growth reduction are not Pythium-specific.
Do not use this figure to visually confirm Pythium in an unknown plant; root/crown evidence and laboratory identification remain required.

name: Rhizoctonia sore shin / root and crown rot
summary: A Cannabis root/crown disease documented as wilting with necrotic lesions at the plant base just above the soil line. Characteristic right-angle branching hyphae and laboratory identification are needed because the canopy response overlaps other root diseases.
affectedParts: lower stem just above soil line
indicators: Plants wilt while necrotic lesions develop at the stem base near the soil line
Roots/crown show compatible necrotic disease
Pigmented septate hyphae from lesions branch at roughly 90 degrees with basal constriction
ITS/18S or other laboratory evidence supports Rhizoctonia solani
exclusions: White cottony basal mycelium with round brown sclerotia strongly supports southern blight
Soft/slimy roots and oomycete evidence support Pythium
Vascular discoloration and Fusarium evidence support Fusarium wilt/crown disease
No basal/root lesions exist and water-status measurements explain wilt

progression.description: Necrotic lesions develop around crown/lower stem or roots.
Root function declines and above-ground wilt becomes more evident.

confirmation: Inspect and photograph roots/crown and lower-stem lesions; submit lesion tissue for fungal morphology and molecular identification.
Do not confirm Rhizoctonia from wilted foliage alone.
immediateActions: Separate suspect root-zone material and preserve a fresh lesion sample.
Check irrigation/moisture and root binding concurrently.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed root-disease sanitation and crop-appropriate management.
Correct measured root-zone stressors that may worsen disease.
prevention: Use clean media/containers and avoid moving contaminated soil.
Inspect transplants for crown lesions and bound/diseased roots.
warnings: Rhizoctonia can coexist with other root stresses/pathogens.
Canopy wilt is not organism-specific.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

name: White root rot
summary: A pathogenicity-confirmed hemp root disease characterized by declining canopy tissue together with white root-surface mycelium and fan-like mycelial growth beneath root bark. Root signs are essential because yellowing and wilt are nonspecific.
indicators: Roots are covered by conspicuous white fungal mycelium
Fan-like mycelial growth occurs beneath root bark
Canopy yellowing and apical wilt progress rapidly in a plant with compatible root signs
Laboratory morphology and molecular evidence identify Dematophora/Rosellinia necatrix
exclusions: No white or fan-like root mycelium is present and another root pathogen is confirmed
White cottony growth and spherical basal sclerotia support southern blight
Small black crown sclerotia support Sclerotinia crown rot
Wilt occurs with physically healthy roots and a measured water deficit explains symptoms

progression.description: White mycelium develops on affected roots and beneath bark.
Yellowing and apical wilt appear as root function deteriorates.
In the reported hemp outbreak, affected plants could die within weeks after visible decline began.

confirmation: Expose and photograph roots before cleaning, then inspect beneath bark for fan-like mycelium.
Use culture and molecular identification for organism-level confirmation.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone soil, tools, and debris from clean production areas.
Preserve representative colonized roots for laboratory diagnosis.
correctivePlan: Base sanitation, culling, soil/root-zone management, and crop-protection decisions on confirmed disease and locally legal options.
prevention: Avoid moving contaminated soil and infected root debris.
Inspect planting sites with a history of susceptible perennial crops or unexplained root-rot mortality.
warnings: Canopy wilt or chlorosis cannot diagnose white root rot.
White fungal growth must be interpreted at the root/crown location and distinguished from other soilborne fungi.

sources.title: First Report of White Root Rot of Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Caused by Dematophora necatrix in Campania Region (Southern Italy)
supportedClaims: Affected hemp developed yellowing, apical wilt, root rot, white mycelium covering roots, and fan-like mycelium beneath root bark before death.
In the reported field, death generally occurred within two to three weeks after first symptoms and about 10% of plants were affected.
Inoculated hemp reproduced chlorosis, apical wilt, and death while controls remained healthy; the fungus was reisolated and confirmed by morphology and molecular analysis.
Root signs and laboratory confirmation are required because canopy yellowing and wilt overlap many Cannabis root-zone disorders.

name: Drought / water-deficit stress
summary: A water-availability stress state that can reduce Cannabis leaf area, growth, photosynthesis, and biomass. Genotypes differ markedly in stomatal behavior, leaf shedding, and visual response, so moisture and plant-water evidence are more reliable than a generic wilt appearance.
indicators: Substrate or soil moisture is measurably below the established irrigation target while the plant shows water-deficit stress
Canopy wilt or reduced expansion coincides with a documented dry root zone and improves after appropriate rehydration
Leaf area or biomass growth declines during a sustained measured water deficit without root rot evidence
exclusions: Root zone is adequately moist while wilt persists
Roots or crown are necrotic, slimy, or discolored enough to support root disease
Root-zone EC is elevated enough to create osmotic stress despite adequate water content
Heat, light, vascular damage, or another exposure explains the wilt pattern better

progression.description: Plant water status declines and stomatal regulation can change before dramatic visible symptoms appear.
Leaf expansion, leaf area, photosynthesis, or shoot growth may decline; genotype-specific leaf retention or shedding can occur.
Severe or prolonged stress can sharply reduce biomass and yield, but response magnitude varies among Cannabis genotypes and stages.

lookAlikes: Fusarium crown and root rot / wilt complex
confirmation: Measure root-zone water content or moisture status and compare with the crop-specific irrigation target and recent irrigation history.
If the cause remains unclear, compare root health, EC, temperature/VPD, and recovery after controlled rehydration rather than relying on leaf posture alone.
immediateActions: Verify actual root-zone moisture before irrigating.
Check emitter function, irrigation uniformity, root volume, and drainage so a dry-looking canopy is not misread.
correctivePlan: Restore an appropriate irrigation regime without forcing severe dry/wet oscillations.
Track new growth, leaf posture, substrate moisture, and root-zone EC after correction.
prevention: Use a repeatable irrigation/dryback monitoring method appropriate to the medium and container size.
Account for cultivar, canopy size, environment, and developmental stage when setting irrigation frequency.
warnings: Do not use one wilted photograph as proof of drought.
Cannabis genotypes can respond to water deficit by different combinations of stomatal closure, leaf shedding, and growth reduction.

sources.title: Genotypic Variation in Photosynthesis and Biomass Partitioning Underlies Agronomic Performance and Cannabinoid Profile in Cannabis sativa Under Drought
supportedClaims: Water deficit imposed at early flowering reduced leaf area and affected plant water status, photosynthesis, biomass partitioning, and cannabinoid response in a genotype-dependent way.
Different Cannabis genotypes used different physiological drought responses, so visual canopy appearance or one moisture reading is not a universal drought-severity scale.

sources.title: Variation in Hydric Response of Two Industrial Hemp Varieties (Cannabis sativa) to Induced Water Stress
supportedClaims: Two hemp varieties showed notably different water-stress strategies, including partial stomatal closure in one and rapid leaf shedding in another.
The genotype-dependent responses support using substrate moisture and plant water-status context rather than a single visual symptom to identify water deficit.

name: Salinity / elevated root-zone EC stress
summary: A measured root-zone stress state in which elevated dissolved salts can reduce Cannabis growth, alter water relations, and create secondary nutrient imbalance. Visual symptoms are nonspecific; diagnosis requires EC and source/root-zone chemistry context.
affectedParts: older and newer foliage depending on severity and formulation
indicators: Measured irrigation or root-zone EC is elevated relative to the established crop baseline while growth declines
Growth suppression occurs together with a documented saline or high-salt root-zone exposure
Leaf nutrient imbalance appears after a measured salinity increase rather than an isolated single-element withholding pattern
exclusions: EC is stable within the crop baseline and no saline/high-salt exposure is documented
Symptoms map cleanly to a single nutrient deficiency with tissue and root-zone measurements supporting that diagnosis
Wilt is explained by a dry root zone without elevated EC
Root decay or pest evidence explains the plant decline better

progression.description: Root-zone osmotic load rises after saline irrigation, fertilizer concentration, recirculation, or salt accumulation.
Water relations and nutrient balance become disrupted and growth slows.
Biomass and yield can decline; exact symptom appearance depends on genotype, medium, nutrient formulation, and salt composition.

lookAlikes: General nutrient lockout from abnormal pH
confirmation: Measure input and representative root-zone/runoff EC using a method appropriate to the medium and compare with the crop baseline.
Review fertilizer concentration, source-water chemistry, sodium/chloride exposure, irrigation volume, and recirculation history; use tissue or water analysis when the salt source is uncertain.
immediateActions: Verify EC with a calibrated meter before making a large corrective change.
Check root-zone moisture and drainage so osmotic stress is not confused with simple drought or hypoxia.
correctivePlan: Correct the documented salt source and root-zone chemistry gradually using a medium-appropriate plan rather than adding another nutrient by symptom color.
Trend EC and new growth after correction; old necrotic tissue will not recover.
prevention: Track input and root-zone EC over time.
Account for source-water salts, fertilizer formulation, irrigation frequency, and recirculation when setting a crop baseline.
warnings: The EC values used in published salinity experiments are experimental treatment levels, not universal Cannabis toxicity thresholds.
Do not diagnose “nutrient burn” from brown tips alone; elevated EC must be measured in context.

sources.title: Effect of saline irrigation and plant-based biostimulant application on fiber hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) growth and phytocannabinoid composition
supportedClaims: Fiber hemp exposed to NaCl irrigation at 2, 4, and 6 dS/m was compared with a tap-water control.

The 4 and 6 dS/m saline treatments significantly reduced biomass and were associated with altered leaf mineral profiles, showing that measured salinity can create broad growth and nutrient-balance effects.
The experimental EC values are treatment conditions, not universal Cannabis toxicity thresholds for every genotype, medium, fertilizer, or irrigation strategy.

sources.title: Aquaponic and Hydroponic Solutions Modulate NaCl-Induced Stress in Drug-Type Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: A controlled indoor flowering experiment tested increasing NaCl concentrations in hydroponic and aquaponic solutions and measured growth, gas exchange, water-use physiology, solution pH/EC, yield, and cannabinoids.
Response to salinity depends on production-system and treatment context, so image appearance alone cannot establish that elevated EC or sodium is the primary cause.

name: Hop latent viroid
summary: A systemic viroid that may remain asymptomatic or produce stunting, brittle stems, short internodes, weak rooting, and reduced reproductive performance.
indicators: Short internodes
Brittle stems or leaves
Stunted growth
Weak flower production
exclusions: Symptoms resolve after correcting a measured root-zone problem
One branch alone is mechanically damaged
No comparison with a healthy clone exists

progression.description: Plant may show no reliable visual symptoms.
Reduced vigor, short internodes, brittle growth, or poor rooting develops.
Yield and quality decline; secondary stress may intensify.

confirmation: Use a validated RT-PCR or equivalent laboratory test.
Retest representative tissue when timing or sampling may affect detection.
immediateActions: Quarantine suspect plants and stop sharing tools or propagation material.
correctivePlan: Base culling and sanitation decisions on validated testing and facility protocol.
prevention: Test mother stock and incoming clones.
Disinfect tools between plants with a validated viroid protocol.
warnings: HLVd cannot be confirmed from a photograph.
Do not label a plant infected without laboratory evidence.

sources.title: Hop Latent Viroid: A Hidden Threat to the Cannabis Industry
supportedClaims: Hop latent viroid can be asymptomatic or associated with reduced vigor, shortened internodes, brittle growth, poor rooting, and reduced yield or quality; molecular testing is needed for confirmation.

media.alt: Cannabis stock plants shown with molecular HLVd detection results from matched leaf and root samples.
media.caption: Cannabis stock plants and HLVd detection results from leaf and root tissues, with HLVd bands confirmed by sequence analysis (Punja et al. 2025, Figure 1).
media.creator: Zamir K. Punja, Cameron Scott, Heather H. Tso, Jack Munz, and Liam Buirs; figure photographer not separately stated
media.requiredAttribution: Punja ZK, Scott C, Tso HH, Munz J, Buirs L. 2025. Hop Latent Viroid in Cannabis sativa: Root Distribution and Transmission in Production Systems. Plants 14(5):830. CC BY 4.0.
media.diagnosticLabel: hop-latent-viroid — molecularly anchored Cannabis HLVd reference composite
useLimitations: HLVd is laboratory-bounded; the image is a molecularly anchored reference, not a visual confirmation tool.
Stunting, small leaves, weak roots, yellowing, and reduced flowering overlap many non-HLVd causes.
Keep the full composite training-ineligible because it mixes plant appearance and molecular-assay panels.

name: Beet curly top virus disease
summary: A beet-leafhopper-vectored viral disease of field-grown hemp that can produce uneven stunting, bushy or shortened shoots, twisted and upward-curled young leaves, and pale-green, yellow, mosaic, or fully chlorotic foliage.
indicators: Stunted or bushy plant architecture
Twisted, puckered, or upward-curled young leaves
Pale-green to yellow new foliage
Yellow mosaic or generalized chlorosis
Shortened stem growth
Symptomatic shoots beside apparently healthy shoots on the same plant
exclusions: Microscopy confirms broad mites or hemp russet mites in protected new growth
Distortion follows a documented herbicide or plant-growth-regulator exposure pattern
Symptoms are uniform only on the hottest or brightest canopy surface and measured environmental stress explains the distribution
Only older leaves follow a mobile-nutrient pattern without twisted new shoots
A validated laboratory assay is negative on properly collected tissue and another cause is confirmed

progression.description: New growth may begin twisting or puckering while shoots slow; pale-green or yellow coloration can develop, but appearance varies by cultivar, growth stage, temperature, and virus strain.
Plants become stunted or bushy with shortened stems and distorted, upward-curled, yellowed, or mosaic foliage; shoots may differ markedly within one plant.
Early infections are generally more severe, yet some plants appear to outgrow visible symptoms or retain a mixture of symptomatic and apparently healthy shoot portions.

confirmation: Do not confirm BCTV from an image or from beet-leafhopper presence; submit representative symptomatic tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory using a validated BCTV-targeted molecular assay.
Sample newly symptomatic shoots rather than only old damaged leaves, and include an apparently healthy comparison when the laboratory protocol allows.
Ask the laboratory to consider other viruses or mixed infection when symptoms or assay results do not fully agree; BCTV can occur in mixed strain or mixed pathogen infections.
Record field position, onset date, affected growth stage, nearby weed hosts, and beet-leafhopper observations to support epidemiological interpretation without treating them as proof of infection.
immediateActions: Mark and isolate suspect propagation material; stop taking or distributing cuttings until laboratory results are available.
Scout the crop, field edges, leaf undersides, and nearby weeds for beet leafhoppers and additional symptomatic plants.
Prevent unverified symptom images from being assigned a virus ground-truth label.
correctivePlan: Base roguing or retention decisions on laboratory confirmation and the facility or field disease protocol.
Manage beet-leafhopper exposure with locally recommended legal practices; vector control does not cure an infected plant.
Continue monitoring because visible symptoms may vary among shoots or appear to recede.
prevention: Use tested propagation material and maintain source records.
Monitor beet leafhoppers from spring onward with crop inspection and field-edge trapping appropriate to the production system.
Reduce unmanaged weed and volunteer hosts around field borders using legal, agronomically appropriate practices.
warnings: Visual symptoms are not specific enough to confirm a virus.
A beet leafhopper on a plant does not establish that the insect or plant carries BCTV.

The two institutional hemp photographs below are metadata-only license-review candidates: no reuse license is stated, so they are hidden from the public gallery and prohibited from automated training.

sources.title: Curly Top Disease of Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in California Is Caused by Mild-Type Strains of Beet curly top virus Often in Mixed Infection
supportedClaims: California hemp plants with curly-top-like disease were characteristically stunted and bushy with distorted, upward-curled, yellowed leaves.
A multiplex PCR detected Beet curly top virus in 89% of hemp samples with curly-top-like symptoms, while other symptom types had low BCTV incidence and were associated with other factors.
An infectious BCTV-CO clone reproduced curly-top-like symptoms in hemp, fulfilling Koch’s postulates; mixed BCTV strain infections also occurred.

sources.title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Curly Top
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: Hemp curly-top symptoms vary with variety, growth stage, temperature, and virus strain; predominant signs include stunting, twisted or curled leaves, and pale-green-to-yellow foliage.
Leaves may pucker and curl upward, or remain green while new growth twists and stem growth is stunted; earlier infection generally produces more severe symptoms.
Individual plants can contain symptomatic and apparently healthy shoot portions or appear to outgrow visible symptoms.
The four hemp symptom photographs are credited to C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University, 2021; the landing page states copyright but provides no reuse license.

sources.title: Curly Top Virus
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Infected field-grown hemp can become stunted and develop yellow mosaic or generalized leaf chlorosis.
Beet leafhoppers transmit curly-top viruses during probing and feeding; scouting is especially important while plants are small and should include leaf undersides, field edges, and nearby weeds.
Yellow mosaic hemp samples should be submitted to a plant diagnostic laboratory, and tomato spotted wilt virus is an early-season look-alike.

name: Waterlogging or root-zone hypoxia
summary: A persistently saturated root zone can suppress Cannabis root elongation, leaf expansion, relative chlorophyll, gas exchange, and biomass; the canopy response overlaps drought, nutrient, transplant, and root-disease injury, so exposure measurements are required.
indicators: Root zone remains saturated or stands in water across repeated observations
Whole-plant growth and canopy expansion slow relative to a matched healthy plant
Root system is shorter or has less new growth than a matched control
Canopy greenness declines over time rather than forming discrete lesions
Leaf-area development and biomass accumulation remain depressed after drainage
exclusions: Container weight or substrate-water measurement shows the root zone is dry rather than saturated
The pattern is restricted to one mechanically damaged branch
Discrete leaf lesions, fungal growth, vascular discoloration, root galls, or organisms provide a better causal explanation
Roots are brown, soft, or decayed and a laboratory test identifies Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, or another pathogen
Measured salinity or pH is outside the crop target and explains the distribution better
Only canopy posture is available without irrigation, drainage, root, or time-series context

progression.description: The container or soil zone remains saturated or flooded; canopy appearance can still be nonspecific, so the event should be labeled from measured exposure rather than leaf posture.
Controlled waterlogging reduced root length, leaf area, leaf-area index, relative chlorophyll, stomatal conductance, and plant biomass in Cannabis cv. G1.
In the same experiment, waterlogged plants remained below controls and water-shortage plants after seven days of recovery, especially for root length, leaf area, and biomass.
Longer exposure reduced canopy leaf area, relative chlorophyll, photosynthetic efficiency, root and shoot biomass, and flower biomass; exact timing and magnitude remain genotype- and stage-limited.

lookAlikes: High root-zone EC or pH-related nutrient unavailability
confirmation: Document irrigation volume and timing, drainage duration, runoff, standing water, container weight, or calibrated substrate-water content across time; a canopy photograph alone cannot confirm waterlogging.

Compare the entire plant and cleaned root system with a healthy plant of the same cultivar, age, medium, and stage, recording root length, active root tips, leaf-area expansion, and recovery after drainage is restored.
Measure root-zone pH and EC because salinity and nutrient availability can produce overlapping canopy decline.
If roots or crowns are discolored, soft, necrotic, or decayed, submit representative root and crown tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory before assigning an abiotic-only label.
immediateActions: Stop adding unnecessary irrigation and remove standing water while preserving a documented sample of the pre-correction root-zone condition.
Separate drainage and runoff from healthy plants when infectious root disease remains possible.
Inspect roots, emitters, drain paths, and neighboring containers before choosing a correction.
correctivePlan: Correct the measured cause of persistent saturation, such as blocked drainage, excessive shot size or frequency, poor container drainage, compacted media, or flooding.
Return irrigation gradually to a measured dryback pattern appropriate to the crop stage and medium, then score only new growth and root recovery.
Use laboratory results and locally legal crop protocols if a root pathogen is confirmed; drainage correction alone does not establish or cure a pathogen diagnosis.
prevention: Record irrigation input, runoff, container weight or substrate water content, and dryback duration instead of relying on a fixed calendar.
Use matched healthy controls and photograph the whole plant, root zone, and cleaned roots across time.
Keep drainage paths functional and prevent shared runoff from moving between containers.
warnings: Reduced growth, pale foliage, or leaf posture is not specific to excess water and must not be used as image-only ground truth.
The controlled waterlogging results come from one Cannabis genotype and defined seven-to-21-day treatments; symptom timing and severity should not be generalized as universal thresholds.
Brown or decayed roots cannot safely be labeled abiotic hypoxia without excluding Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, and other root diseases.
No symptom photograph with adequate Cannabis-specific confirmation and reusable provenance was admitted in this batch.

sources.title: Impact of varying water stress periods (water shortage vs. waterlogging) on Cannabis sativa growth, leaf physiology, and CBD content
sources.publisher: University of Agricultural Sciences and Veterinary Medicine Cluj-Napoca
supportedClaims: In a controlled Cannabis sativa cv. G1 experiment, waterlogging was imposed by standing potted plants in a two-centimetre sheet of water; diagnosis therefore depended on verified root-zone exposure rather than canopy appearance alone.

After seven vegetative-stage days, waterlogged plants had shorter roots, lower leaf area, lower leaf-area index, lower chlorophyll-meter readings, and less biomass than controls; their growth remained lowest after a seven-day recovery period.

During reproductive-stage exposure, waterlogging reduced leaf-area index, root and shoot biomass, stomatal conductance, relative chlorophyll content, and photosystem-II efficiency as duration increased, but responses varied with stage and duration.

Water shortage produced overlapping reductions in several above-ground measurements, so reduced canopy growth or greenness cannot distinguish excess water from insufficient water without root-zone measurements.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A 2017–2018 North Carolina survey based on 572 agronomic and 117 plant-clinic hemp submissions attributed common environmental disorders to excessive rainfall flooding roots and to poor root development in transplanted clones.
The same diagnostic survey found Pythium diseases in greenhouse hemp, supporting explicit separation of abiotic flooding injury from root-pathogen diagnoses.
